54351.e: The “Outback” is the name for the remote interior of Australia. The great deserts lie there.
54351.m: The dry interior of Australia is called the Outback.

54352.q: Who has lived in the deserts of Australia for tens of thousands of years?
54352.e: Aboriginal people are the original inhabitants of Australia. They have known the water holes and edible plants of the desert for generations.
54352.m: Aboriginal people have lived in Australia's deserts since ancient times.

54353.q: Where do the wild camels in Australia's deserts come from?
a: People brought them in the 19th century.
54353.e: In the 19th century camels were brought to Australia as pack animals. Later many were set free, and today a great many wild camels live there.
54353.m: Australia's camels were brought in by people.

54354.q: In which two countries is the Sonoran Desert?
54354.e: The Sonoran Desert lies in the south-west of the USA, mainly in Arizona and California, and in north-west Mexico.
54354.m: The Sonoran Desert lies in the USA and Mexico.

54355.q: Which giant column-shaped cactus is the symbol of the Sonoran Desert?
54355.e: The saguaro grows almost only in the Sonoran Desert. With its raised arms, it is a well-known image of the Wild West.
54355.m: The saguaro is the giant cactus of the Sonoran Desert.

54356.q: Which big city lies in the Sonoran Desert?
54356.e: Phoenix, the capital of Arizona, lies in the middle of the Sonoran Desert. In summer it often gets hotter than 40 °C there.
54356.m: Phoenix is a big city in the desert.

54357.q: Which venomous reptile lives in the Sonoran Desert?
54357.e: The Gila monster is one of the few venomous lizards. It lives in the south-west of the USA and in Mexico.
54357.m: The Gila monster is a venomous desert lizard.

54358.q: How tall can a saguaro cactus grow?
54358.e: A saguaro grows very slowly but lives for more than 100 years. Large ones are 12 to 15 metres tall.
54358.m: A saguaro can grow as tall as a house.

54359.q: Why do especially many plants grow in the Sonoran Desert?
a: There are two rainy seasons a year.
It rains a little every day.
54359.e: In the Sonoran Desert it rains in winter and in summer. That is why it is one of the deserts richest in plants in the world.
54359.m: Two rainy seasons make the Sonoran Desert green.

54360.q: Which arm of the sea does the Sonoran Desert border?
54360.e: The Gulf of California separates the Baja California peninsula from mainland Mexico. The Sonoran Desert reaches both shores.
54360.m: The Sonoran Desert borders the Gulf of California.

54361.q: How does a saguaro cactus store water?
54361.e: The stem has ribs like an accordion. After rain it expands and stores a lot of water.
54361.m: The saguaro stores water in its stem.

54362.q: What are the hills of sand piled up by the wind in a desert called?
54362.e: The wind piles the sand up into dunes. In Erg Chebbi in Morocco they reach more than 100 metres high.
54362.m: Sand hills in the desert are called dunes.

54363.q: What do you call loose grains of rock that are coarser than sand?
54363.e: Grains of sand are at most 2 millimetres in size. Larger grains are called gravel, finer ones silt and clay.

54364.q: Where does the sand in a sandy desert come from?
54364.e: Heat, cold and wind break rock into smaller pieces over a long time. The wind gathers the fine grains together.

54365.q: Why do grains of sand move about in a sandy desert?
a: The wind carries and rolls them.
54365.e: The wind lifts grains of sand briefly and makes them hop along in jumps. So a sandy desert is always changing.
54365.m: The wind moves the desert sand.

54367.q: Why do rocks crack apart in the desert?
a: because of big differences in temperature
54367.e: During the day the rock expands in the heat, and at night it contracts in the cold. This causes cracks and the rock breaks apart.
54367.m: Heat by day and cold by night split rocks.

54368.q: What does a rocky desert look like?
54368.e: There is hardly any sand in a rocky desert. You mainly see bare rock, slabs of stone and sharp-edged lumps.
54368.m: A rocky desert is made of bare rock.

54370.q: What covers the ground in a gravel desert?
54370.e: In a gravel desert, wide areas are covered with small stones. They are often rounded because rivers used to carry them.
54370.m: In a gravel desert there is gravel everywhere.

54371.q: Which type of desert forms when the wind blows the sand away and only gravel is left?
54371.e: The wind can carry fine sand away, but not heavy little stones. What remains is an area of gravel.
54371.m: Where the wind blows the sand away, gravel is left behind.

54372.q: What does a barchan dune look like from above?
54372.e: A barchan is a crescent dune. It forms when the wind always blows from the same direction and there is little sand.
54372.m: A barchan is a crescent dune.

54373.q: On which side is a dune steeper?
a: on the side facing away from the wind
on the side facing the wind
54373.e: On the windward side, sand is blown gently upwards. On the leeward side it slides down steeply.
54373.m: The leeward side of a dune is steeper than the windward side.

54374.q: What are dunes that move along with the wind called?
54374.e: The wind blows sand up the gentle side and over the crest. There it slides down, and so the dune slowly moves on.
54374.m: Shifting dunes move with the wind.

54375.q: Which dune forms when the wind blows from many directions?
54375.e: Changing winds shape dunes with several arms. From above they look like a star.
54375.m: Star dunes form when the wind blows from many directions.

54376.q: What can some dunes do when the sand slides?
54376.e: When dry sand slides down a dune, a deep humming can be heard. These are called singing dunes.
54376.m: Some dunes hum when sand slides down.

54377.q: In which country is the Dune du Pilat, the highest dune in Europe?
54377.e: The Dune du Pilat lies on the Atlantic coast near Bordeaux. It is about 100 metres high.
54377.m: The highest dune in Europe is in France.

54378.q: What often forms at the mouth of a wadi, where floods deposit rubble?
54378.e: When the water flows out of the narrow valley onto the plain, it slows down. It leaves gravel and sand behind in a fan shape.
54378.m: An alluvial fan often forms at the mouth of a wadi.

54379.q: Which language does the word “wadi” come from?
54379.e: “Wadi” is an Arabic word for a valley or riverbed. It is used all over the world for dry desert valleys.

54380.q: Why is it dangerous to camp in a wadi?
54380.e: If it rains far away, a flood wave can rush through the dry valley without warning. Many people have drowned in this way.
54380.m: A flash flood can suddenly come through a wadi.

54381.q: What does a wadi look like for most of the year?
54381.e: A wadi only carries water after heavy rain. Otherwise it is a dry valley with sand and rubble.
54381.m: A wadi is usually a dry riverbed.

54382.q: Why do more plants often grow in a wadi than in the land around it?
54382.e: Moisture often remains in the ground beneath a wadi. Plants with long roots can reach this groundwater.
54382.m: In a wadi plants find water more easily.

54383.q: In which country is the famous desert valley of Wadi Rum?
54383.e: Wadi Rum in southern Jordan is known for its red sandstone rocks. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

54384.q: Why does rainwater run off so quickly in a wadi?
a: The hard, dry ground hardly soaks up any water.
The wind blows the water away.
54384.e: Parched ground absorbs water only slowly. So rain collects quickly and rushes through the valley as a flood.
54384.m: Dry desert ground makes rain run off quickly.

54385.q: What happens to the lake you seem to see in a desert mirage when you walk towards it?
54385.e: The mirage depends on the angle you look from. When you get closer, the angle is no longer right and the image disappears.
54385.m: You can never reach a mirage lake in the desert.

a: Light is bent in warm and cold layers of air.
Sand reflects light like a mirror.
54386.e: Warm air is thinner than cold air. At such layers light changes direction and is bent, creating a mirror image.
54386.m: Light bent in layers of air creates the Fata Morgana.

54387.q: What do desert travellers often think they see in a mirage?
54387.e: Over hot ground, light from the blue sky is bent upwards. It looks like a shining surface of water.
54387.m: The apparent lake is reflected sky.

54388.q: Where can you also see a mirage in Switzerland?
54388.e: On hot summer days the road further ahead seems to be wet. This is the same kind of mirage as in the desert.
54388.m: You often see a mirage over hot tarmac.

54389.q: Who is the Fata Morgana named after?
54389.e: “Fata” is Italian for fairy. Morgan le Fay from the legends of King Arthur was said to create illusions.
54389.m: The Fata Morgana is named after a fairy.

54390.q: In which country was the name “Fata Morgana” first used?
54390.e: In the Strait of Messina, between Sicily and the Italian mainland, people saw floating illusions. “Fata” is Italian and means fairy.
54390.m: The name Fata Morgana comes from Italy.

54391.q: Why does the air shimmer over hot ground?
a: Rising warm air keeps bending the light differently.
Dust grains glow in the sun.
The heat makes the eyes tired.
54391.e: Over hot ground, bubbles of warm air rise and mix with cooler air. This keeps bending the light in slightly different ways.
54391.m: Warm, rising air makes images shimmer.

54392.q: What can you sometimes see in a mirage over a cold sea?
54392.e: When cold air lies beneath warm air, light is bent downwards. Distant ships then appear raised or upside down.
54392.m: Over a cold sea, ships can seem to float.

54393.q: Which weather event especially speeds up desertification?
54393.e: If there is no rain for years, plants die. The unprotected soil is then easily carried away by the wind.

54394.q: Which human activity especially encourages desertification?
54394.e: If too many animals graze on one area, they eat the plants down. The bare soil is then worn away by wind and rain.
54394.m: Too many grazing animals encourage desertification.

54395.q: Which region south of the Sahara is especially threatened by desertification?
54395.e: The Sahel is a belt between the Sahara and the savannah. Droughts and overuse have dried out a lot of land there.
54395.m: The Sahel is badly threatened by desertification.

54396.q: What is the “Great Green Wall” in Africa?
a: a project to plant trees across Africa
54396.e: Several African countries want to make land green again along the southern edge of the Sahara. Trees and plants are meant to slow the spread of the desert.
54396.m: The Great Green Wall is meant to stop the desert.

54397.q: Which organisation agreed a worldwide convention against desertification?
54397.e: In 1994 the UN adopted a Convention to Combat Desertification. Switzerland has joined it too.
54397.m: The UN fights desertification with a convention.

54398.q: Which continent is especially badly affected by desertification?
54398.e: The desert is spreading above all on the edge of the Sahara. Droughts and overuse make a lot of land infertile there.
54398.m: Africa is especially badly affected by desertification.

54399.e: Plants hold the soil in place with their roots and protect it from the wind. Careful grazing lets them grow back.
54399.m: Plants protect the soil from the desert.

54400.q: What problem arises when dry soils are irrigated the wrong way?
a: The soil becomes as sour as vinegar.
54400.e: The water evaporates quickly in the heat and the dissolved salts are left behind. Hardly any plants grow on salty soil.

54401.q: Which is the largest desert on Earth?
54401.e: Whether an area is a desert does not depend on heat. Antarctica covers about 14 million km², making it bigger than any hot desert.
54401.m: Antarctica is the largest desert on Earth.

54402.q: Why is Antarctica considered a desert even though there is a lot of ice there?
a: There is a lot of sand there.
54402.e: A desert is an area with very little precipitation. The ice of Antarctica has built up over hundreds of thousands of years.
54402.m: A desert is defined by little precipitation.

54403.q: Below how much precipitation a year is an area usually called a desert?
54403.e: If less than about 250 millimetres of rain or snow fall in a year, an area usually counts as a desert. Zurich gets about four times as much.
54403.m: Deserts get less than 250 millimetres of precipitation a year.

54404.q: Why are there even valleys without ice and snow in Antarctica?
a: Hardly any snow falls and strong winds dry everything out
It is very hot there in summer
54404.e: In the McMurdo Dry Valleys almost no precipitation falls, and icy winds blowing down the slopes carry snow away. They are among the driest places on Earth.
54404.m: Antarctica has dry valleys free of ice.

54405.q: Which desert is the second largest on Earth after Antarctica?
54405.e: The Arctic around the North Pole also gets very little precipitation. At almost 14 million km² it is the second largest desert.
54405.m: The Arctic is the second largest desert on Earth.

54406.q: Why does so little snow fall in cold deserts?
a: Cold air contains little water vapour.
The wind is too weak there.
54406.e: The colder the air, the less water vapour it can hold. So hardly any precipitation forms.

54407.q: Which plants mainly grow in the ice-free areas of Antarctica?
54407.e: Only a few areas of Antarctica are free of ice. There mainly mosses and lichens survive, as they can cope with cold and dryness.
54407.m: Mainly mosses and lichens grow in Antarctica.

54408.q: Which warm wind carries dust from the Sahara across the Mediterranean to Italy?
54408.e: The sirocco blows from the south or south-east from North Africa. It brings warm air and often Saharan dust to southern Europe.
54408.m: The sirocco brings Saharan air to Italy.

54409.q: Which small predatory dinosaur with a sickle-shaped claw was discovered in the Gobi?
54409.e: The first Velociraptor fossils were found in the Mongolian Gobi in 1923. It was about the size of a turkey.

54410.q: What did scientists find in the dry sand on the edge of the Taklamakan?
54410.e: The so-called Tarim mummies are several thousand years old. The dry air and the salty ground preserved them naturally.
54410.m: Dry desert sand can preserve mummies.

54411.q: In which state is Australia's Great Sandy Desert?
54411.e: The Great Sandy Desert lies in north-west Australia in the state of Western Australia. It is the country's second largest desert.
54411.m: The Great Sandy Desert lies in Western Australia.

54412.q: In which layer of the atmosphere does almost all weather happen?
54412.e: The troposphere is the lowest layer of the atmosphere and reaches about 8 to 17 kilometres high. Almost all the water vapour is there, so that is where clouds and precipitation form.

54413.q: What is the science that studies climate called?
54413.e: Climatology studies how the atmosphere behaves over many years. To do this it analyses measurements over many decades.
54413.m: Climatology is the science of climate.

54414.q: What do you call the general course of the weather over several days to weeks?
54414.e: A spell of weather lies in time between short-term weather and long-term climate. You might talk, for example, about a sunny spell in autumn.
54414.m: A spell of weather describes the weather over a few days or weeks.

54415.q: What does MeteoSwiss call a day on which the highest temperature reaches 30 °C or more?
54415.e: A hot day has a highest temperature of at least 30 °C. From 25 °C it is already called a summer day.
54415.m: On a hot day it gets at least 30 degrees warm.

54416.q: Which sentence describes the climate and not the weather?
a: In Ticino the winters are usually mild.
Tomorrow it will snow in Davos.
Today it is raining heavily in Bern.
Yesterday it was hot in Basel.
54416.e: A statement about the climate describes what a place is normally like over many years. The other sentences describe the weather on a single day.
54416.m: If you say what it is usually like, you are talking about climate.

54417.e: A thermometer shows the temperature, in Switzerland usually in degrees Celsius. Weather stations measure air temperature about 2 metres above the ground in the shade.
54417.m: The thermometer measures how warm or cold it is.

54418.e: The hygrometer shows how much water vapour is in the air. Relative humidity is given as a percentage.
54418.m: The hygrometer measures how moist the air is.

54419.q: What do the blue bars in a climate chart show?
a: The hours of sunshine each month
54419.e: In a climate chart the months are on the horizontal axis. The bars show how much precipitation falls on average in each month.
54419.m: The bars in a climate chart show precipitation.

54420.q: What does the red line in a climate chart show?
54420.e: The red curve joins the average temperatures of the twelve months. So you can see which months are warm or cold.
54420.m: The red curve in a climate chart shows the temperature.

54421.q: Roughly how much precipitation falls in Zurich on average each year?
54421.e: Over the long-term average (1991 to 2020), about 1000 to 1100 millimetres of precipitation fall in Zurich each year. That is about 1000 litres of water on every square metre.
54421.m: About one metre of precipitation falls in Zurich each year.

54422.q: How much water does 1 millimetre of precipitation on one square metre mean?
54422.e: One square metre times 1 millimetre of height makes 1 cubic decimetre. That is exactly 1 litre of water.
54422.m: One millimetre of precipitation equals one litre per square metre.

54423.q: In a Walter and Lieth climate chart, 10 °C is at the same height as which amount of precipitation?
54423.e: In Walter and Lieth charts the precipitation axis is labelled with numbers twice as large as the temperature axis. So 10 °C is at the same height as 20 mm.
54423.m: In a Walter and Lieth chart, 10 degrees equals 20 millimetres.

54424.q: What are months called in which the temperature curve lies above the precipitation bars in a climate chart?
54424.e: When the temperature curve is higher than the precipitation, more water evaporates than falls from the sky. Such dry months are called arid.
54424.m: In arid months it is too dry, because more water evaporates than falls.

54425.q: The warmest month in a place is 19 °C, the coldest -1 °C. What is the annual temperature range?
54425.e: The annual range is the difference between the warmest and the coldest month. Calculation: 19 minus (-1) = 20 °C.
54425.m: The annual range is the gap between the warmest and coldest month.

54426.q: A climate chart shows that the warmest month is January. Where is the place probably?
54426.e: In the Southern Hemisphere it is summer in January, because the seasons are reversed there. Places such as Sydney or Buenos Aires therefore have their warmest time in January.
54426.m: In the Southern Hemisphere it is summer in January.

54427.q: Roughly what is the average air pressure at sea level?
54427.e: The average air pressure at sea level is 1013.25 hectopascals. Values above this count as rather high, values below as rather low.
54427.m: At sea level the air pressure averages about 1013 hectopascals.

54428.q: What does the air do in the centre of a low-pressure area?
54428.e: In a low, air rises and cools down. Water vapour condenses into clouds, and there is often precipitation.
54428.m: In a low, the air rises and forms clouds.

54429.q: In which direction does the wind basically blow?
54429.e: Air flows from the area of high pressure to the area of low pressure to even out the difference. The bigger the difference in pressure, the stronger the wind.
54429.m: The wind always blows from high to low pressure.

54430.q: What is the boundary between a warm and a cold air mass called?
54430.e: At a front, air masses of different temperatures meet. Clouds and precipitation often form there; there are warm fronts and cold fronts.
54430.m: At a weather front, warm and cold air meet.

54431.q: How does air pressure change when you climb a mountain?
54431.e: The higher you climb, the less air there is above you. That is why the air pressure on the Jungfraujoch is much lower than in Zurich.
54431.m: In the mountains the air pressure is lower than in the valley.

54432.q: Which high-pressure area over the Atlantic often brings Switzerland fine weather in summer?
54432.e: The Azores High usually lies over the Atlantic near the Azores. If it stretches as far as central Europe in summer, Switzerland often has sunny, warm days.
54432.m: The Azores High often brings fine weather in summer.

54433.q: How does air flow around a low-pressure area in the Northern Hemisphere?
54433.e: Because the Earth rotates, the air flowing in is deflected. In the Northern Hemisphere it therefore circles a low anticlockwise.
54433.m: In the Northern Hemisphere the wind turns anticlockwise around a low.

54434.q: Where does a west wind come from?
54434.e: Winds are named after the direction they come from. So a west wind blows from west to east.
54434.m: A wind is named after the direction it comes from.

54435.q: What does the Beaufort scale show?
54435.e: The Beaufort scale was developed by the British admiral Francis Beaufort. It divides wind into forces according to its effects.
54435.m: The Beaufort scale describes how strongly the wind blows.

54436.q: Which force on the Beaufort scale means a hurricane?
54436.e: The scale goes from 0 for calm to 12 for hurricane. A hurricane has wind speeds from about 118 km/h.
54436.m: A hurricane is the highest force on the Beaufort scale.

54437.e: An anemometer often has small cups that turn in the wind. The faster they turn, the stronger the wind.
54437.m: The anemometer measures the speed of the wind.

54438.q: What is the warm, dry wind called that blows down Alpine valleys such as the Reuss valley or the Rhine valley?
54438.e: With the föhn, air rises over the Alps, drops its rain on one side and comes down warm and dry into the valley on the other side. It can reach storm force.
54438.m: The föhn is a warm, dry wind blowing down the Alps.

54439.q: What is the cold north wind called that blows through the Rhone valley in southern France to the Mediterranean?
54439.e: The mistral is channelled between the Alps and the Massif Central and often reaches storm force. In Provence it usually brings clear, dry weather.
54439.m: The mistral is a cold wind in the Rhone valley in France.

54440.q: In which direction does the valley wind blow in an Alpine valley on a sunny day?
54440.e: During the day the mountain slopes warm up a lot and the warm air rises. Air flows in from the mouth of the valley, so the valley wind blows up the valley; at night the mountain wind blows down the valley instead.
54440.m: During the day the valley wind blows up the valley.

54441.q: On a coast, where does the wind usually blow from during a sunny day?
a: From the sea to the land
From the land to the sea
54441.e: During the day the land warms up faster than the water, and the warm air rises. Cooler air then flows in from the sea; this is called a sea breeze.
54441.m: During the day the sea breeze blows from the sea to the land.

54442.q: In which region of the Earth do the trade winds blow?
a: Between the subtropics and the equator
54442.e: The trade winds blow fairly steadily all year round in the tropics. They are among the most regular winds on Earth.
54442.m: The trade winds are steady winds in the tropics.

54443.q: What is the trade wind in the Northern Hemisphere called?
54443.e: The air flows from the subtropics towards the equator and is deflected by the Earth's rotation. That is why the trade wind in the Northern Hemisphere comes from the north-east.
54443.m: In the Northern Hemisphere the north-east trade wind blows.

54444.q: In which direction does the Intertropical Convergence Zone shift in July?
a: Not at all, it stays fixed at the equator
54444.e: The Intertropical Convergence Zone follows the highest position of the sun with a slight delay. In the northern summer it therefore lies north of the equator, in the northern winter south of it.
54444.m: The Intertropical Convergence Zone moves with the position of the sun.

54445.q: What happens to the air where the trade winds meet at the equator?
a: It flows away to the poles
54445.e: The warm, moist air rises and cools down. Tall thunderclouds form with heavy downpours.
54445.m: At the equator moist air rises and it often rains.

54446.q: Where does the name “horse latitudes” for calm areas of sea probably come from?
a: From horses thrown overboard from becalmed sailing ships
From waves that look like horses
From a ship called the Horse
54446.e: Without wind, sailing ships often lay still there for weeks. When drinking water ran short, horses were said to have been thrown overboard.
54446.m: There is little wind in the horse latitudes.

54447.q: Why did sailing ships at the equator sometimes lie still for days in the past?
a: Because there is often hardly any wind there
Because there are too many waves there
Because pirates lay in wait there
54447.e: At the equator warm air mainly rises straight up. That is why there is often hardly any wind there. Sailors call this zone the doldrums.
54447.m: At the equator there is a zone with little wind, the doldrums.

54448.q: Where does warm air rise in the Hadley cell, a large circulation of air?
54448.e: It is very hot at the equator, so warm air rises there. It sinks in the subtropics and flows back to the equator as the trade wind.
54448.m: In the Hadley cell, warm air rises at the equator.

54449.q: Which sailor used the north-east trade wind in 1492 to sail across the Atlantic to America?
54449.e: Columbus sailed west from the Canary Islands and let the trade wind carry him across the Atlantic. Later many sailing ships used this route.
54449.m: In 1492 Columbus sailed to America with the trade wind.

54451.q: Which kind of precipitation does not fall from the sky but forms directly on grass in the morning?
54451.e: Dew forms when the air cools at night and water vapour condenses on cold surfaces. It is a kind of precipitation that settles rather than falls.
54451.m: Dew forms directly on cool surfaces.

54452.q: What are the ice crystals called that form directly on plants and car windows when it is frosty?
54452.e: With hoar frost, water vapour turns straight into ice at temperatures below 0 °C. It forms white crystals on cold objects.
54452.m: Hoar frost forms when water vapour turns straight into ice in frosty weather.

54453.q: What is the rain called that forms when moist air has to rise over mountains?
54453.e: The air cools as it rises, the water vapour condenses and it rains. That is why a lot of precipitation falls on the northern edge of the Alps.
54453.m: Air rising over mountains brings relief rain.

54454.q: What is the side of a mountain range facing away from the wind, which usually stays drier, called?
54454.e: On the windward side the air drops its rain, and on the leeward side it sinks down dry. This is called a rain shadow, as in central Valais.
54454.m: The leeward side of a mountain range lies in the rain shadow.

54455.q: What is a short, heavy fall of rain that starts suddenly and soon stops again called?
54455.e: Showers fall from individual heaped clouds and usually last only a short time. Steady rain, by contrast, falls for a long time and evenly from a closed layer of cloud.
54455.m: A shower is short and heavy.

54456.q: What is rain made of very fine droplets, smaller than half a millimetre, called?
54456.e: Drizzle often falls from low, grey clouds. The droplets are so small that they almost seem to float in the air.
54456.m: Drizzle is rain made of tiny droplets.

54457.q: What is the rain in the tropics called that falls when the midday sun is almost directly overhead?
54457.e: When the sun is at its zenith, the ground heats up a lot and moist air rises. In the afternoon there are then heavy thundery downpours.
54457.m: Zenithal rain falls in the tropics when the sun is directly overhead.

54458.q: What is the huge thundercloud called that often looks like an anvil at the top?
54458.e: A cumulonimbus often reaches more than 10 kilometres high. It brings lightning, thunder, heavy rain and sometimes hail.

54459.q: Which high, wispy clouds are made of ice crystals?
54459.e: Cirrus clouds float very high up, where it is very cold. That is why they are made of ice crystals and look like fine feathers.
54459.m: Cirrus clouds are high, feathery clouds made of ice.

54460.q: What are the white, cauliflower-like fair-weather clouds called?
54460.e: “Cumulus” is Latin for heap, so they are also called heap clouds. They form when warm air rises from the ground.
54460.m: Cumulus clouds are white heap clouds.

54461.q: What is the low, grey cloud called that covers the sky like an even blanket?
54461.e: Stratus means “spread out”. This layer cloud lies low and can bring light drizzle.
54461.m: The stratus cloud is a grey layer cloud.

54462.q: What is the thick, dark layer cloud called from which long-lasting rain or snow falls?
54462.e: “Nimbus” means rain cloud. Nimbostratus covers the whole sky and often brings hours of steady rain.
54462.m: Nimbostratus is the typical rain cloud.

54463.q: Around 1802 Luke Howard gave clouds names such as cumulus and stratus. Which language do these names come from?
54463.e: Luke Howard chose Latin names so that scientists in all countries could understand them. Cumulus, for example, means heap and stratus means layer.
54463.m: Luke Howard's cloud names are Latin.

54464.q: Which clouds look like lots of little white balls of cotton wool in the sky?
54464.e: Fleecy clouds are made up of many small white puffs of cloud. They look like a flock of sheep in the sky.
54464.m: Fleecy clouds look like a flock of sheep in the sky.

54465.q: What is the grey layer of cloud called that often lies over the Swiss Plateau for days in winter while it is sunny in the mountains?
54465.e: In high-pressure weather, cold air collects on the Plateau beneath warmer air. A layer of cloud forms at the boundary, while the mountain peaks above it lie in the sun.
54465.m: Above the high fog the sun often shines.

54466.q: Which energy drives the Earth's water cycle?
a: The heat from inside the Earth
54466.e: The sun warms the water, which then evaporates and rises into the air. Without solar energy the cycle would stop.
54466.m: The sun keeps the water cycle going.

54467.q: What is the process called in which liquid water turns into water vapour without boiling?
54467.e: In evaporation, water passes into the air from the surface of seas, lakes and soils. Heat speeds up this process.
54467.m: In evaporation, water becomes water vapour.

54468.q: What is the process called in which water vapour in the air turns into tiny droplets?
54468.e: When moist air cools down, it can no longer hold as much water vapour. The vapour condenses into droplets and clouds form.
54468.m: Clouds form from water vapour through condensation.

54469.q: What is it called when rainwater soaks into the ground and flows to the groundwater?
54469.e: Part of the rain seeps through soil and rock. This creates groundwater, from which Switzerland gets a large part of its drinking water.
54469.m: Rainwater that soaks into the ground becomes groundwater.

54470.q: What is the release of water vapour through the leaves of plants called?
54470.e: Plants take up water with their roots and release it again through tiny openings in their leaves. A large tree can give off hundreds of litres of water this way on a summer's day.
54470.m: Plants release water vapour through their leaves.

54471.q: Where does most water on Earth evaporate?
54471.e: The oceans cover about 71 per cent of the Earth's surface. So most of the evaporated water comes from the sea.
54471.m: Most water evaporates over the seas.

54472.q: What is the process called when ice or snow turns straight into water vapour without melting first?
54472.e: In sublimation, a substance goes straight from solid to gas. This is how snow can disappear in dry, sunny air without melting.
54472.m: In sublimation, ice turns straight into vapour.

54473.q: What happens to water vapour when it cools down in the air?
a: It forms tiny droplets and clouds form
54473.e: Cold air can hold less water vapour. The vapour condenses into fine droplets, which we see as clouds. When they become heavy enough, precipitation falls.

54474.q: Roughly how cold would the Earth be on average without the natural greenhouse effect?
54474.e: Without greenhouse gases, heat would escape into space almost freely. The average temperature would then be about -18 °C instead of about 15 °C.
54474.m: Without the natural greenhouse effect, the Earth would be an ice planet.

54475.q: Which greenhouse gas do humans release the most of?
54475.e: Carbon dioxide (CO2) contributes most to human-made warming. It stays in the atmosphere for a very long time.
54475.m: Carbon dioxide is the most important greenhouse gas caused by humans.

54476.q: Which greenhouse gas is produced, among other places, in the stomachs of cows and in rice fields?
54476.e: Methane is produced when ruminants digest food and when plants break down without oxygen. It is much more powerful than CO2 but stays in the air for a shorter time.
54476.m: Cows and rice fields release methane.

54477.q: Which radiation do greenhouse gases hold back in the atmosphere?
54477.e: Sunlight warms the ground, which then gives off heat radiation (infrared). Greenhouse gases absorb some of it and radiate it back to the Earth.
54477.m: Greenhouse gases hold back heat radiation in the atmosphere.

54478.q: What is the biggest source of the extra CO2 in the atmosphere?
54478.e: Fossil fuels contain carbon from plants of millions of years ago. When they are burnt in heating systems, cars and power stations, it is released as CO2.
54478.m: Burning fossil fuels releases a lot of CO2.

54479.q: Where does the greenhouse effect get its name from?
54479.e: In a greenhouse the warmth stays trapped under the glass. The atmosphere acts in a similar way, like a cover around the Earth.
54479.m: The atmosphere acts like the glass roof of a greenhouse.

54481.q: What did the Swedish scientist Svante Arrhenius calculate as early as 1896?
a: More CO2 in the air warms the Earth
The Earth goes round the sun
54481.e: Arrhenius estimated how much the Earth would warm with more carbon dioxide in the air. He was one of the first climate scientists.
54481.m: As early as 1896 it was known that more CO2 warms the Earth.

54482.q: Which two processes mainly make sea levels rise because of warming?
a: Melting land ice and expanding water
More rain and more water in rivers
54482.e: Glaciers and ice sheets on land release meltwater into the sea. In addition, seawater expands as it gets warmer.
54482.m: Melting land ice and warmer water make the sea rise.

54483.q: Why does melting sea ice speed up the warming of the Arctic?
a: Dark water absorbs more of the sun's heat than pale ice
Meltwater releases a lot of carbon dioxide
Without ice there is no more wind in the Arctic
Without ice the sea becomes saltier and so warmer
54483.e: Pale ice reflects a large part of the sunlight; this is called a high albedo. The dark sea, by contrast, absorbs a lot of solar energy and warms up, so even more ice melts.
54483.m: Where the pale ice is missing, the dark sea absorbs more heat.

54484.q: Roughly how much did the average sea level rise between 1901 and 2018?
54484.e: According to the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), sea level rose by about 0.20 metres in this period. The rise has become faster in recent decades.
54484.m: Sea level is rising, and the rise is getting faster.

54485.q: Which country in Europe lies about a quarter below sea level and is protected by dykes?
54485.e: Large parts of the Netherlands were won from the sea and lie lower than sea level. A rising sea makes higher dykes necessary.
54485.m: The Netherlands protect themselves from the sea with dykes.

54486.q: In which year was the Paris climate agreement adopted?
54486.e: In December 2015 almost all countries agreed to keep warming well below 2 °C. The aim is to keep it to 1.5 °C if possible.
54486.m: The Paris climate agreement was adopted in 2015.

54487.q: Which flat island nation in the Indian Ocean is especially threatened by rising sea levels?
54487.e: Most of the islands of the Maldives lie only about one metre above the sea. Even a small rise can flood parts of the country.
54487.m: Flat island nations such as the Maldives are threatened by the rising sea.

54488.q: Roughly how much of their ice volume did Swiss glaciers lose between 2015 and 2025?
54488.e: According to the glacier monitoring network GLAMOS, the volume of Swiss glaciers shrank by about 24 per cent in these ten years. In 2025 alone, about 3 per cent was lost.
54488.m: Swiss glaciers are melting very fast.

54489.q: How much has Switzerland warmed since pre-industrial times compared with the global average (as of 2025)?
54489.e: According to MeteoSwiss, Switzerland has become about 2.9 °C warmer since pre-industrial times, the world about 1.3 °C. Land areas warm up more than seas.
54489.m: Switzerland is warming more than the Earth's average.

54490.q: Which effect of rising sea levels threatens many coastal areas?
54490.e: With a higher sea level, storm surges reach further inland. Salt water can also get into the groundwater.
54490.m: A higher sea level leads to more flooding on the coasts.

54491.q: What does the Spanish name “El Niño” mean in English?
54491.e: “El Niño” literally means “the boy” and refers to the Christ Child. South American fishermen gave this name to the warm water that often appeared around Christmas.
54491.m: El Niño means the Christ Child.

54492.q: In which ocean does the climate pattern El Niño develop?
54492.e: El Niño is a warming of the water in the tropical Pacific. It changes wind and weather in many regions of the world.
54492.m: El Niño develops in the tropical Pacific.

54493.q: Roughly how often does El Niño occur?
54493.e: El Niño does not come in a fixed rhythm but at irregular intervals, on average about every four years. An event usually lasts about a year.
54493.m: El Niño returns at irregular intervals.

54494.q: What is the opposite of El Niño called, when the eastern Pacific is especially cool?
54494.e: La Niña means “the girl”. The water in the eastern Pacific is then colder than normal, and it often rains more in South-East Asia and Australia.
54494.m: La Niña is the cool opposite of El Niño.

54495.q: How does a strong El Niño usually affect the average temperature of the whole Earth?
a: It drops sharply for a few months
54495.e: During El Niño the warm Pacific gives off a lot of heat to the air. That is why years with a strong El Niño, such as 2016 or 2024, were especially warm.
54495.m: A strong El Niño makes the Earth warmer for a while.

54496.q: What does El Niño often bring to the otherwise very dry coastal areas of Peru?
54496.e: A lot of water evaporates over the warm sea, and the moist air rises. On the coast of Peru there is then heavy rain and flooding.
54496.m: El Niño often brings Peru heavy rain.

54497.q: Why do fishermen off Peru catch fewer fish during El Niño?
a: The warm water contains few nutrients
The fish flee inland from storms
The water has become too salty
The fishing boats freeze in the harbour
54497.e: Normally, cold deep water rising up brings lots of nutrients for plankton. During El Niño this water is missing, and fish such as anchovies find hardly any food.
54497.m: Warm water off Peru means less food for fish.

54498.q: What happens to the trade winds over the Pacific during El Niño?
54498.e: Normally the trade winds push warm water west towards Asia. When they weaken, the warm water sloshes back east.
54498.m: During El Niño the trade winds are weak.

54499.q: What do you call the climate near the sea with mild winters and cool summers?
54499.e: The sea stores a lot of heat and evens out temperatures. That is why on coasts such as Ireland or Brittany the differences between summer and winter are small.
54499.m: The sea creates a balanced maritime climate.

54500.q: What weather does a warm front often bring?
54500.e: At a warm front, warm air slowly slides over cold air. This creates a wide layer of cloud from which rain often falls steadily for a long time.
54500.m: A warm front often brings long-lasting rain.

54501.q: From which line on Earth does the polar zone roughly begin?
54501.e: The polar circles lie at about 66.5 degrees latitude. Beyond them it is cold almost all year round.
54501.m: The polar zone begins at the polar circle.

54502.q: What is the narrow band of very strong westerly winds about 10 kilometres up called?
54502.e: The jet stream often blows from west to east at more than 200 km/h in the upper troposphere. Aircraft use it, which is why flights from America to Europe usually take less time than the other way round.
54502.m: The jet stream is a fast wind high up.

54503.q: What is the Köppen-Geiger climate classification used for?
a: It divides the Earth into climate zones
It measures the strength of earthquakes
It counts a country's animal species
54503.e: Köppen and Geiger sorted the Earth's climates by temperature and precipitation. Each climate group has a letter, for example A for tropical and B for dry.
54503.m: The Köppen-Geiger classification divides the Earth into climate zones.

54504.q: Which vegetation is typical of the always-wet tropics?
54504.e: In the always-wet tropics it is warm all year and it rains a great deal. The species-rich tropical rainforest grows there, for example along the Amazon.
54504.m: Rainforest grows in the hot, wet climate of the tropics.

54505.q: What weather does a passing cold front often bring?
54505.e: At a cold front, cold air pushes beneath the warm air and lifts it quickly. Heaped clouds form with showers or thunderstorms, and afterwards it gets cooler.
54505.m: After a cold front it gets cooler.

54506.q: In the Köppen climate classification there is a group of dry climates. Which area belongs to it?
54506.e: Dry climates include deserts and steppes. There more water evaporates than falls as precipitation, as in the Sahara.
54506.m: Deserts such as the Sahara have a dry climate.

54507.q: Why is it warmer at the equator than at the poles?
a: The sun's rays hit the ground more steeply there
The equator is closer to the sun
There are more volcanoes at the equator
The Earth turns more slowly there
54507.e: At the equator the sun's rays fall almost vertically and heat a small area strongly. At the poles they hit at a low angle and spread over a large area.
54507.m: The more steeply the sun shines, the warmer it gets.

54508.q: How tall can the tallest trees in the tropical rainforest grow?
54508.e: Single giant trees rise far above the closed canopy. They are called emergents.
54508.m: The tallest trees in the rainforest grow over 50 metres tall.

54509.q: Roughly how much of the sunlight reaches the floor of a dense tropical rainforest?
54509.e: The dense canopy catches almost all the light. Only about 1 to 2 per cent reaches the ground, so it is dim there.
54509.m: The rainforest floor is dark because the treetops swallow the light.

54510.q: Why do many orchids in the rainforest grow high up on branches?
a: To get closer to the light
Because they suck the tree dry
Because the ground is too hot
54510.e: The rainforest floor is dim. Epiphytes such as orchids use the trees only as a support; they get their water from rain and moist air.
54510.m: Epiphytes grow on trees to get more light.

54511.q: What are the broad buttress roots of many trees in the tropical rainforest for?
a: They give the tall trees support
They store water for the dry season
54511.e: The roots of rainforest trees usually do not reach deep into the ground. The board-like extensions at the base of the trunk support the huge trees like buttresses.
54511.m: Buttress roots support the giant trees like pillars.

54512.q: Why is the soil in the tropical rainforest poor in nutrients, despite the lush plant life?
a: Most of the nutrients are inside the plants themselves
Too little rain falls for humus
The ground is frozen all year
There are no decomposers such as fungi there
54512.e: In the warm, wet climate, dead plant parts are broken down very quickly and the nutrients are taken up again by the roots at once. So almost all the nutrients stay in the plants' cycle and hardly any in the soil.
54512.m: In the rainforest the wealth is in the plants, not in the soil.

54513.q: Why is the climate of the tropical rainforest described as a diurnal climate?
a: The temperature varies more over a day than over a year
It rains every day at exactly the same time
The days are much longer in summer than in winter
There are four different seasons every day
54513.e: At the equator it is similarly warm all year, and there are hardly any seasons. The difference between day and night is bigger than that between the warmest and coldest month.
54513.m: In the rainforest, day and night differ more than summer and winter.

54514.q: Which plant sprouts high up in the canopy, wraps its roots around its host tree and can finally strangle it?
54514.e: The seeds of the strangler fig are carried onto branches by birds. Its aerial roots grow down to the ground and enclose the trunk until the host tree dies.
54514.m: The strangler fig slowly crushes its host tree.

54515.q: What are the climbing plants called that root in the ground and grow up the trees to the canopy?
54515.e: Lianas save themselves a thick, load-bearing trunk and climb other trees towards the light. Some grow many dozens of metres long.
54515.m: Lianas climb up trees towards the light.

54516.q: How much precipitation typically falls in the tropical rainforest each year?
54516.e: Tropical rainforests usually get more than 2000 millimetres of rain a year, spread over all the months. Part of it comes from water evaporating from the forest itself.
54516.m: In the tropical rainforest it rains a lot, all year round.

54517.q: What characterises the climate of the savannah?
a: A change between rainy season and dry season
Rain and heat all year round
Hardly any rain in any month
54517.e: Savannahs lie in the seasonally wet tropics. During the rainy season the grass turns green, and in the dry season it withers.
54517.m: In the savannah, rainy and dry seasons take turns.

54518.q: Which type of savannah has the most wet months in a year?
54518.e: The closer a savannah lies to the rainforest, the longer the rainy season. The wet savannah has about 7 to 9 wet months and tall grass.
54518.m: The wet savannah has the longest rainy season of all savannahs.

54519.q: How do many savannah grasses survive the long dry season?
a: The stalks wither, but the roots survive in the ground
They grow a thick trunk to store water
They travel with the wind to wet places
They stay green all year thanks to a waxy layer
54519.e: In the dry season the parts of the grasses above ground die and turn yellow. The roots and buds at ground level stay alive and sprout again with the first rain.
54519.m: Savannah grasses survive the drought in their roots.

54520.q: What is the tree with a flat, wide crown that is typical of the East African savannah called?
54520.e: The umbrella thorn acacia has a flat crown that looks like an open umbrella. Its thorns protect it from many plant-eaters, but giraffes still eat its leaves.
54520.m: The umbrella thorn acacia is the typical tree of the East African savannah.

54521.q: In which country is Serengeti National Park?
54521.e: Serengeti National Park lies in northern Tanzania in East Africa. It is known for its huge herds of animals on the savannah.
54521.m: The Serengeti is a famous savannah in Tanzania.

54522.q: Why do huge herds of wildebeest travel through the Serengeti every year?
a: They follow the rain and the fresh grass
They flee from the winter snow
They look for shade in the rainforest
They travel to the sea to drink
54522.e: Wildebeest, zebras and gazelles migrate in a circle through the Serengeti and neighbouring areas. They follow the rains, after which fresh grass grows.
54522.m: The savannah herds travel to where it has rained.

54523.q: What part do bushfires play in the savannah?
a: They keep the landscape open and help grasses
They make the soil permanently infertile
They almost never happen in savannahs
54523.e: In the dry season, fires mainly burn young trees and shrubs. The grasses quickly sprout again from their roots, so the savannah stays open.
54523.m: Fires belong to the savannah and help the grasses.

54524.q: Which animals in the African savannah often build mounds of earth several metres high?
54524.e: Termite mounds are made of earth, saliva and droppings and have a clever ventilation system. The termites break down a lot of dead plant material.
54524.m: Termites are the builders of the savannah.

54525.q: Which country in Asia is largely steppe and known for nomads who live in yurts?
54525.e: Mongolia lies in the interior of Asia and is shaped by wide steppes. Many families travel there with their herds and live in round tents called yurts.
54525.m: Nomads live with their herds on the steppes of Mongolia.

54526.q: What are the round, dried-up plants called that the wind rolls across the steppe, scattering seeds as they go?
54526.e: In autumn, tumbleweeds break off from their roots and are blown across the open plain by the wind. On the way their seeds fall out.
54526.m: Tumbleweeds use the wind to spread their seeds.

54527.q: What is the large grassland in Argentina called?
54527.e: The Pampas are a wide, flat grassland in Argentina and Uruguay. Today they are used mainly for cattle farming and growing crops.
54527.m: The steppe of South America is called the Pampas.

54528.q: What is the steppe landscape in Hungary called?
54528.e: The Puszta is a steppe landscape on the Great Hungarian Plain. Part of it is protected as Hortobágy National Park.
54528.m: The Hungarian steppe is called the Puszta.

54529.q: Which very fertile soil has formed in many steppes?
54529.e: In the steppe, lots of grasses die every year and form a thick, dark layer of humus. This created black earth, one of the most fertile soils in the world.
54529.m: The black earth of the steppe is especially fertile.

54530.q: What are many steppe areas of Ukraine and North America mainly used for today?
54530.e: Thanks to the fertile soils, most steppes have been turned into farmland. Mainly wheat and maize grow there, which is why they are also called breadbaskets.
54530.m: The former steppes are now great breadbaskets.

54531.q: What climate is found in the steppes of Central Asia?
a: Continental climate with hot summers and cold winters
Tropical climate with rain in every month
Polar climate without a proper summer
54531.e: Steppes lie far from the sea, which could even out the temperatures. So the summers are hot and the winters very cold.
54531.m: In the interior of continents, summers are hot and winters cold.

54532.q: What do the leaves of many Mediterranean trees, such as the holm oak, do in winter?
a: They stay green on the tree
They turn as white as snow
54532.e: Many Mediterranean trees are evergreen. Their small, leathery leaves stay on the tree all year.

54533.q: What are the hard, leathery leaves of many Mediterranean plants for?
a: They keep snow off the branches
They attract birds to build nests
54533.e: The leaves have a thick, often waxy skin through which little water evaporates. That is why these plants are called sclerophyllous, or hard-leaved, plants.
54533.m: Hard leaves help plants survive the dry summers.

54534.q: Which tree is considered a typical crop of the Mediterranean region?
54534.e: The olive tree has been grown around the Mediterranean for thousands of years. It is well adapted to dry summers and can live to a great age.
54534.m: The olive tree is the typical tree of the Mediterranean region.

54535.q: What is the dense, evergreen scrubland of the Mediterranean called, which often formed after forests were cut down?
54535.e: Maquis consists of shrubs up to several metres high, such as strawberry tree, myrtle and tree heath. It often grew where evergreen forests once stood.
54535.m: Maquis is a dense scrubland on the Mediterranean.

54536.q: Which fragrant herbs grow wild on the dry hills of southern France?
54536.e: On poor limestone soils grows a low scrub called garrigue. Typical are fragrant herbs such as thyme, rosemary and lavender.
54536.m: In southern France the hills smell of thyme and lavender.

54537.q: From the bark of which Mediterranean tree is cork obtained?
54537.e: The cork oak grows thick bark that can be stripped about every nine years without the tree dying. Portugal is the world's largest producer of cork.
54537.m: Cork is the bark of the cork oak.

54538.q: In which of these regions is there also a Mediterranean climate with hard-leaved vegetation?
54538.e: A Mediterranean climate is also found in California, central Chile, south-west South Africa and parts of Australia. In California the scrubland is called chaparral.
54538.m: There is a Mediterranean climate outside Europe too, for example in California.

54539.q: Why are there often forest fires and bushfires in the Mediterranean region in summer?
a: Long heat and drought dry out the plants
There is a lot of snow there in summer
The plants contain a lot of water in summer
It rains almost every day in summer
54539.e: In summer it hardly rains for weeks and the plants are very dry. Many hard-leaved plants also contain flammable essential oils.
54539.m: Heat and drought make summer the fire season on the Mediterranean.

54540.q: Why do deciduous trees in the temperate zone drop their leaves in autumn?
a: So they do not lose water through their leaves in winter
So that animals have enough to eat in winter
Because their leaves are only allowed to live for one summer
So that snow can settle on the branches more easily
54540.e: In winter the ground is often frozen and the roots can hardly take up water. But water would keep evaporating through the leaves, so the tree drops them.
54540.m: Deciduous trees drop their leaves so as not to dry out in winter.

54541.q: Which deciduous tree is the most common in Switzerland?
54541.e: According to the National Forest Inventory, the beech is the most common deciduous tree in Switzerland. Only the spruce, a conifer, is more common.
54541.m: The beech is the most common deciduous tree in Swiss forests.

54542.q: Why do plants such as the wood anemone flower in deciduous woods as early as early spring?
a: Before the trees have leaves, a lot of light reaches the ground
The ground is warmest in spring
Otherwise deer would eat them in summer
There is most rain in spring
54542.e: As soon as the trees are in leaf, the woodland floor becomes shady. Early bloomers use the short time with plenty of light and store reserves in bulbs or rootstocks.
54542.m: Early bloomers use the light before the trees are in leaf.

54543.q: Why do many leaves turn yellow in autumn?
a: The green leaf pigment is broken down
The leaves are bleached by the sun
The frost colours the leaves yellow
The leaves take up yellow pollen
54543.e: The tree breaks down the green chlorophyll and stores valuable substances from it in the trunk. This makes the yellow and orange pigments visible, which were already in the leaf.
54543.m: In autumn the green disappears and the yellow colours show.

54544.q: Which layer of the forest lies directly above the moss layer?
54544.e: From bottom to top, a deciduous wood is divided into the moss layer, herb layer, shrub layer and tree layer. Grasses, ferns and flowers grow in the herb layer.
54544.m: Herbs grow above the moss layer.

54545.q: What climate is found in the zone of deciduous forests?
a: A temperate climate with four seasons
A desert climate with hardly any rain
A polar climate with a very short summer
54545.e: Deciduous forests grow where there are warm summers, cool winters and precipitation in all seasons. This includes a large part of central Europe.
54545.m: Deciduous forests grow where there are four seasons.

54546.q: Which type of soil is especially common under the deciduous forests of central Europe?
54546.e: Fallen leaves are broken down well by soil animals and form a fertile layer of humus. This creates brownish brown earth, a common soil on the Swiss Plateau.
54546.m: Fertile brown earth often forms under deciduous forests.

54547.q: Which animals do most to turn fallen leaves into humus in a deciduous wood?
54547.e: Earthworms pull leaves into the ground, eat them and excrete them as nutrient-rich crumbs. Together with fungi and bacteria, this creates humus.
54547.m: Earthworms turn leaves into fertile soil.

54548.q: Which small rodents of the tundra are known for their populations rising and falling sharply?
54548.e: In some years lemmings multiply in huge numbers, and afterwards their population crashes again. Many predators and birds of prey in the tundra depend heavily on them.
54548.m: Lemmings are the most important small rodents of the tundra.

54549.q: How does the Arctic fox adapt to winter in the tundra?
a: Its fur turns white and very thick
It travels to Africa every winter
It loses its fur in winter
It sleeps under water in winter
54549.e: In summer the Arctic fox's fur is usually brownish grey, in winter white and especially thick. This camouflages it well in the snow and protects it from the cold.
54549.m: In winter the Arctic fox wears a white coat for camouflage.

54550.q: Apart from Canada, which country has the largest share of the tundra?
54550.e: The Arctic tundra stretches along the northern coasts of Russia, Canada and Alaska. Parts of Greenland and Scandinavia also belong to it.
54550.m: Large areas of tundra lie in the north of Russia and Canada.

54551.q: What do reindeer in the tundra mainly eat in winter?
54551.e: Reindeer scrape the snow away with their hooves to reach lichens such as reindeer lichen. This is their most important food in winter.
54551.m: In winter reindeer mainly eat lichens.

54552.q: Which member of the birch family grows in the tundra only as a low, knee-high shrub?
54552.e: The dwarf birch usually grows only knee-high and close to the ground. There, under the snow, it is protected from cold and wind in winter.
54552.m: The dwarf birch hugs the ground in the tundra.

54553.q: What forms in the tundra in summer when the top layer of soil thaws?
54553.e: Below the thawed layer the ground stays frozen, so the meltwater cannot seep away. That is why the tundra is marshy in summer and there are lots of mosquitoes.
54553.m: In the tundra summer the ground is wet and marshy.

54554.q: Why can tundra plants still grow quickly in the short summer?
a: During the polar day there is light almost around the clock
The ground is especially warm in summer
It rains very heavily every day in summer
The animals do not fertilise the ground in summer
54554.e: North of the Arctic Circle the sun at times does not set in midsummer. The plants can then carry out photosynthesis almost without a break.
54554.m: The long summer light helps tundra plants grow.

54555.q: What do you call treeless landscapes like the tundra high in the mountains above the tree line?
54555.e: High in the mountains, as in the far north, it is too cold for trees. So similar low plants grow there; this is called alpine tundra.
54555.m: Tundra is also found high up in the mountains.

a: When it has been frozen for at least two years without a break
When it has been frozen for a single winter
When it is covered with snow
When there is a glacier on it
54556.e: Permafrost is ground or rock whose temperature stays below 0 °C for at least two years without a break. It is found in polar regions and high mountains.
54556.m: Permafrost is ground that stays frozen for years.

54557.q: What is the top layer of ground above the permafrost that thaws in summer called?
54557.e: Above the permanently frozen ground, a layer thaws every summer and freezes again in winter. It is called the active layer and is often only a few tens of centimetres to a few metres thick.
54557.m: The active layer thaws in summer and freezes again in winter.

54558.q: Where is there permafrost in Switzerland?
a: In the high mountains, above about 2500 metres
On the Plateau beneath the cities
On the shores of the large lakes
In Ticino beneath the palm trees
54558.e: In Switzerland, permafrost is found mainly in rock faces and scree slopes high in the Alps. There the ground stays frozen all year.
54558.m: There is permafrost in the Swiss Alps too.

54559.q: Which danger increases in the Alps when the permafrost thaws?
54559.e: Frozen water in rock cracks acts like glue and holds the rock together. When it thaws, rocks and rubble can break off and slide down.
54559.m: When the permafrost thaws, the mountain becomes crumbly.

54560.q: Why is thawing permafrost a problem for the climate?
a: Greenhouse gases such as methane are released
It makes the Earth turn more slowly
It creates more ozone at ground level
54560.e: Huge amounts of dead plant remains are frozen in the permafrost. When they thaw, microorganisms break them down, producing carbon dioxide and methane, which increase warming.
54560.m: Thawing permafrost releases greenhouse gases and heats the climate further.

54561.q: Why do many houses in Siberia stand on stilts?
a: So that the warmth of the house does not thaw the frozen ground
So that bears cannot get into the house
So that water does not get in during floods
So that the houses are shadier in summer
54561.e: A heated house standing directly on the ground would thaw the permafrost beneath it. The ground would become soft and the house could sink or crack.
54561.m: On permafrost, people build on stilts so the ground stays frozen.

54562.q: Under roughly what share of the land area of the Northern Hemisphere is there permafrost?
54562.e: Permafrost is widespread above all in Siberia, Alaska, Canada and on the Tibetan Plateau. In total it lies under about a quarter of the land area of the Northern Hemisphere.
54562.m: Permafrost covers a large part of the far north.

54563.q: In which areas of the Earth is there especially a lot of permafrost?
54563.e: Permafrost is found where winters are very long and cold. In Siberia it reaches very deep into the ground in some places.
54563.m: There is a lot of permafrost in the far north.

54564.q: Which country has the largest area of mangroves in the world?
54564.e: Indonesia consists of thousands of islands with long tropical coasts. About a fifth of all the mangroves on Earth grow there.

54565.q: What are the arched stilt roots of many mangrove trees for?
a: They give support in the soft mud
They store fresh water for droughts
54565.e: The muddy ground is very soft and is moved by the waves. The stilt roots support the tree like lots of little legs.
54565.m: Stilt roots support mangroves in the soft mud.

54566.q: What are the roots of some mangroves for that stick straight up out of the mud?
a: They supply the roots with air
They serve as nesting places for birds
54566.e: There is hardly any oxygen in the wet mud. These breathing roots stick out of the ground and take in air.
54566.m: Breathing roots get air for the mangroves.

54567.q: How do some mangroves cope with salty seawater?
a: They get rid of surplus salt through their leaves
They only drink when it rains
They only grow in fresh water
54567.e: Some mangroves filter out salt at their roots, others get rid of it through glands on their leaves. You can then sometimes see salt crystals on their leaves.
54567.m: Mangroves have adapted to living with salt water.

54568.q: Why are mangrove forests also important for protecting the climate?
a: They store a lot of carbon in wood and mud
They cool the sea with their leaves
They keep the sun's rays off the sea
54568.e: In the oxygen-poor muddy ground, plant remains break down only very slowly. So mangroves store especially large amounts of carbon per area.

54569.q: Why are mangroves seen as a nursery of the sea?
a: Many young fish grow up protected among the roots
All whales lay their eggs there
The water there is especially cold
There are no plants and no enemies there
54569.e: Among the roots, young fish, crabs and prawns find food and protection from large predators. Later many of them move to the open sea or to coral reefs.
54569.m: Mangroves are a nursery for fish.

54570.q: Which use has destroyed especially many mangrove forests in South-East Asia?
54570.e: On many coasts, mangroves have been cleared for prawn farming ponds. After a few years the ponds are often polluted and abandoned.
54570.m: Prawn farming has destroyed many mangrove forests.

54571.q: Which altitude zone in the Alps comes directly above the montane zone?
54571.e: The order from bottom to top is colline, montane, subalpine, alpine and nival. In the subalpine zone mainly coniferous forests grow, up to the forest line.
54571.m: Above the montane comes the subalpine zone.

54572.q: What is the highest altitude zone with permanent snow and ice called?
54572.e: The word nival comes from the Latin “nix”, meaning snow. Only a few scattered plants grow here on snow-free rocks.
54572.m: At the very top lies the nival zone with snow and ice.

54573.q: In which altitude zone are most of Switzerland's vineyards?
54573.e: The colline zone is the hill zone at lower, warm altitudes. Vines, fruit trees and mixed deciduous forests with oaks thrive there.
54573.m: Vines grow in the low, warm colline zone.

54574.q: Which trees dominate the montane zone in the northern Alps?
54574.e: Mixed mountain forests grow in the montane zone of the northern Alps. Beech and silver fir are typical, often mixed with spruce.
54574.m: In the montane zone, beech and fir grow together.

54575.q: Which conifer of the subalpine zone is also called the Swiss stone pine?
54575.e: The Arolla pine, or Swiss stone pine, grows in the central Alps up to the forest line. It can stand great cold, and its wood has a strong scent.
54575.m: The Arolla pine is a tough tree of the high mountains.

54576.q: Which famous Alpine flower with white, felty leaves grows in the alpine zone?
54576.e: Edelweiss grows on stony grassland and rocks in the alpine zone. Its thick hairs protect it from strong sun, cold and drying out.
54576.m: Edelweiss is a typical flower of the alpine zone.

54577.q: What shapes the alpine zone above the forest line?
a: Alpine pastures with grasses, dwarf shrubs and flowers
54577.e: In the alpine zone it is too cold for trees. Grassland, dwarf shrubs and many Alpine flowers grow there, and in summer they are used as Alpine pastures.
54577.m: Above the forest lie the Alpine pastures of the alpine zone.

54578.q: By roughly how much does the air temperature fall on average when you climb 100 metres higher?
54578.e: On average it gets about 0.6 °C cooler for every 100 metres of height. If you climb 1000 metres, it is about 6 °C colder, which is why vegetation changes with height.
54578.m: The higher you climb, the cooler it gets.

54579.q: Why are the altitude zones higher on south-facing slopes than on north-facing ones?
a: South-facing slopes get more sun and are warmer
More snow falls on south-facing slopes
North-facing slopes get more hours of sunshine
54579.e: In the Northern Hemisphere the sun shines more steeply onto south-facing slopes and warms them more. So plants can grow higher up there than on the shady north side.
54579.m: On the sunny side, plants grow higher up.

54580.q: Where is the forest line highest in the Swiss Alps?
a: In the inner central Alps, such as Valais and the Engadine
In the Pre-Alps on the northern edge of the Alps
54580.e: In the inner Alpine valleys the summers are sunnier and warmer than on the edge of the Alps. There the forest reaches about 2300 metres and higher.
54580.m: In Valais and the Engadine the forest grows especially high up.

54581.q: What mainly limits how high up trees can grow in the mountains?
a: The temperature during the growing season being too low
The lack of oxygen at altitude
The lack of insects at altitude
54581.e: Trees need enough warmth to form new wood. If the average summer temperature is too low, they can no longer grow properly.
54581.m: The cold in summer decides where the trees stop.

54582.q: What do you call the transition zone above the forest line with scattered, often stunted trees?
54582.e: Between the forest line and the tree line there are only single trees struggling against cold, wind and snow. Their twisted, stunted growth gives the zone its name, “krummholz”, meaning crooked wood.
54582.m: In the krummholz zone the last trees struggle to survive.

54583.q: How is climate warming changing the tree line in the Alps?
a: It stays the same for ever
It disappears within a few years
54583.e: When it gets warmer, young trees can also grow further up. Because trees grow slowly, the tree line rises only gradually.
54583.m: With warming, the trees slowly climb uphill.

54584.q: Why is the forest line in many Alpine valleys lower than the climate would allow?
a: People cleared forest for Alpine pastures
The soils there are too salty
54584.e: For centuries farmers cleared forest to gain pasture for their livestock. Where Alpine pastures are no longer farmed today, the forest often grows back.
54584.m: Alpine farming has pushed the forest line down in many places.

54585.q: Which two vegetation zones does the polar tree line separate in the far north?
54585.e: In the north of Europe, Asia and America, the coniferous forest of the taiga ends at the polar tree line. Further north comes the treeless tundra.
54585.m: The polar tree line separates the coniferous forest from the tundra.

54586.q: Which low, creeping pine often forms dense thickets at the treeline in the Alps?
54586.e: The mountain pine grows close to the ground with flexible branches. This way the snow protects it, and it can withstand avalanches and the weight of snow.
54586.m: The mountain pine ducks down under the snow.

54587.q: Why is the treeline much higher in the tropics than in the Alps?
a: Because it is warmer there at the same altitude
Because there are fewer avalanches there
Because more animals spread the seeds there
Because the mountains there are made of softer rock
54587.e: Near the equator it is warmer at every altitude than in the Alps. In tropical mountains such as the Andes, trees therefore often still grow above 3500 metres.
54587.m: The closer to the equator, the higher the treeline.

54589.q: Which of these areas is considered a biodiversity hotspot?
54589.e: Madagascar is home to many animals and plants found nowhere else, such as lemurs. However, much of its rainforest has already been cut down.

54590.q: What happens when nature in a biodiversity hotspot is destroyed?
a: Many species die out completely because they only live there
The species simply move to Switzerland
Nothing, because all species also live elsewhere
54590.e: Hotspots are home to many species that exist only there. If their habitat disappears, they become extinct worldwide.
54590.m: When a hotspot is destroyed, species die out for ever.

54591.q: What does it mean if an animal or plant species is endemic?
a: It is found only in one particular, limited area
It is found on every continent
54591.e: Endemic species live in only one place, for example on an island or in a mountain range. If their habitat disappears, they become extinct worldwide.
54591.m: Endemic species live in just one place in the world.

54592.q: Which very species-rich forest in Brazil has now mostly been cut down?
54592.e: The Atlantic Forest, Mata Atlântica in Portuguese, once stretched along the whole coast. Only a small part is left today, yet many species found nowhere else still live there.
54592.m: Only a little of Brazil's Atlantic Forest is left.

a: An area with very many, often threatened species
A place with a particularly hot climate
A volcano that will soon erupt
54593.e: Biodiversity hotspots are home to especially many animal and plant species that exist only there. At the same time, their habitat is under serious threat.

54594.q: What share of all the world's plant species is found only in biodiversity hotspots?
54594.e: Together the hotspots cover only about 2.4 per cent of the Earth's land surface. Even so, about half of all plant species are found only there.
54594.m: On a small area, the hotspots are home to a great many species.

54595.q: Which high mountain range on the border between Europe and Asia is one of the biodiversity hotspots?
54595.e: The Caucasus mountains, with their forests and mountain meadows, are home to many plants found only there. They are one of the world's 36 biodiversity hotspots.
54595.m: The Caucasus is a biodiversity hotspot.

54596.q: Which region near Switzerland is considered a biodiversity hotspot?
54596.e: The Mediterranean region is home to a great many plant species found only there. At the same time, much of its original vegetation has been destroyed.
54596.m: The Mediterranean region is a biodiversity hotspot.

54597.q: What is most rainforest in the Amazon cleared for?
54597.e: Most of the cleared land in the Amazon is used as pasture for livestock. The beef is sold in the country and also exported.
54597.m: In the Amazon, forest mainly gives way to cattle pasture.

54598.q: Which plantations have pushed out especially large areas of rainforest in Indonesia and Malaysia?
54598.e: Palm oil is made from the fruit of the oil palm and is found in many foods and cosmetics. Large areas of rainforest were cleared for the plantations.
54598.m: Much rainforest in Southeast Asia was cleared for palm oil.

54599.q: Which plant is grown in huge amounts as animal feed on cleared land in South America?
54599.e: Soya is very rich in protein and is used worldwide as feed for chickens, pigs and cattle. In South America, forests and savannahs are also cleared for new soya fields.
54599.m: Soya for animal feed needs a lot of farmland.

54600.q: What is the method called where forest is burnt to gain farmland or pasture?
54600.e: In slash-and-burn, trees are cut down or set on fire directly. The ash fertilises the soil only for a short time.

54601.q: Why does cutting down the rainforest contribute to climate change?
a: Burning and rotting trees release CO2
Without forest the Earth immediately gets colder
Without trees there are more clouds
54601.e: Trees store carbon in their wood and leaves. When they are burnt or rot, this carbon enters the air as CO2 and strengthens the greenhouse effect.
54601.m: Forests store carbon; cutting them down releases it.

54602.q: Why can large-scale deforestation in the Amazon lead to less rain?
a: Trees release a lot of water into the air through evaporation
Trees create wind that drives clouds away
Without trees it gets colder there
Trees hold clouds in place with their branches
54602.e: Much of the rain in the Amazon comes from water that trees evaporate through their leaves. Without the forest, fewer clouds form and it becomes drier.
54602.m: The rainforest makes some of its own rain.

54603.q: What is a direct consequence of deforestation for many animals and plants?
a: They lose their habitat and may die out
They find more food than before
54603.e: An especially large number of species live in a small space in the tropical rainforest. When the forest is destroyed, the animals and plants that can only live there disappear too.
54603.m: When the forest goes, its inhabitants go too.

54604.q: What does the FSC label on wood and paper products stand for?
a: Wood that comes only from tropical forests
54604.e: The Forest Stewardship Council label shows that the wood comes from a forest managed according to rules that protect the environment and people. In Switzerland, many wood and paper products carry this label.
54604.m: The FSC label stands for wood from responsible forestry.

54605.q: How is deforestation in the Amazon monitored over large areas today?
54605.e: Satellites regularly photograph the rainforest from space. Brazil analyses these images to spot new clearings quickly.
54605.m: Satellites show from space where forest is disappearing.

54606.q: Roughly how long is the Earth's circumference at the equator?
54606.e: The Earth's circumference at the equator is about 40,075 km. A plane flying at 900 km/h would need almost two days without a break.
54606.m: Once around the equator is about 40,000 kilometres.

54607.q: Roughly how big is the Earth's diameter?
54607.e: The Earth's diameter at the equator is about 12,756 km. From pole to pole it is about 43 km shorter because the Earth is slightly flattened.
54607.m: The Earth's diameter is about 12,700 kilometres.

54608.q: Which Greek scholar calculated the Earth's circumference amazingly accurately around 240 BC?
54608.e: Eratosthenes compared the angles of the sun's shadows in Alexandria and Syene. From the difference in angle and the distance between the cities, he calculated the Earth's circumference.
54608.m: Eratosthenes worked out the Earth's circumference in ancient times using shadows.

54609.q: Which observation showed even in ancient times that the Earth is round?
a: the round shadow of the Earth during a lunar eclipse
the red colour of the sky in the evening
the tides on the sea coast
the changing phases of the moon
54609.e: During a lunar eclipse, the Earth's shadow falls on the moon. Aristotle noticed that this shadow is always round.
54609.m: The Earth's round shadow on the moon reveals its ball shape.

54610.q: Which mountain summit is furthest from the centre of the Earth?
54610.e: Chimborazo in Ecuador lies almost on the equator, where the Earth is thickest. That is why its summit reaches further into space than Mount Everest, even though it is lower above sea level.
54610.m: Because of the bulge at the equator, Chimborazo is the closest point to space.

54611.q: Whose expedition was the first to sail all the way around the Earth, from 1519 to 1522?
54611.e: Magellan set off in 1519 with five ships but died in the Philippines in 1521. Juan Sebastián Elcano brought the last ship back to Spain in 1522.
54611.m: The first circumnavigation began under Magellan and ended in Spain in 1522.

54612.q: Roughly how big is the Earth's entire surface?
54612.e: The Earth's surface covers about 510 million km². About 71 per cent of it is covered by water.
54612.m: The Earth has a surface area of about 510 million square kilometres.

54613.q: Roughly how long does the Earth take to turn once around itself?
54613.e: The Earth turns once on its axis in about 24 hours. That is why day and night take turns.
54613.m: One turn of the Earth takes about a day.

54614.q: How long does the sun appear to take to move on by one degree of longitude?
54614.e: A day has 24 · 60 = 1440 minutes, and in that time the Earth turns through 360°. 1440 : 360 = 4 minutes per degree.
54614.m: Local time shifts by four minutes for each degree of longitude.

54615.q: Roughly how fast does a point on the equator move because of the Earth's rotation?
54615.e: A point on the equator travels about 40,000 km in roughly 24 hours. 40,000 : 24 gives about 1670 km/h.
54615.m: At the equator you speed along with the Earth at about 1670 kilometres per hour.

54616.q: What can you use to show that the Earth is turning?
