54616.e: In 1851 Léon Foucault hung a heavy pendulum in Paris. The direction of its swing slowly turned, because the Earth was turning underneath it.
54616.m: A long pendulum makes the Earth's rotation visible.

54617.q: Why is it always day somewhere on Earth and night somewhere else?
a: The sun only ever lights up one half of the Earth
The sun goes out every night
54617.e: The sun only ever shines on the half of the Earth facing it. Because the Earth turns, the boundary between day and night keeps moving.
54617.m: The sun only ever lights up one half of the Earth.

54618.q: Which apparent force caused by the Earth's rotation deflects winds to the right in the Northern Hemisphere?
54618.e: The Coriolis force arises because the Earth turns beneath moving air. In the Northern Hemisphere winds are deflected to the right, in the Southern Hemisphere to the left.
54618.m: The Coriolis force deflects winds to the right in the Northern Hemisphere.

54619.q: When is the Earth closest to the sun?
54619.e: The Earth reaches its closest point to the sun (perihelion) around 3 January, at a distance of about 147 million km. In July it is furthest away.
54619.m: Of all months, it is in January that the Earth is closest to the sun.

54620.q: Roughly how fast does the Earth move along its path around the sun?
54620.e: On average the Earth travels about 29.8 km per second along its orbit. That is over 100,000 km per hour.
54620.m: The Earth races around the sun at about 30 kilometres per second.

54621.q: When does astronomical summer begin in the Northern Hemisphere?
54621.e: Astronomical summer begins with the summer solstice around 21 June. That is the longest day of the year in the Northern Hemisphere.
54621.m: Astronomical summer begins with the June solstice.

54622.q: What are the two days of the year called when day and night are about the same length everywhere?
54622.e: Around 20 March and around 23 September, the sun stands directly above the equator at midday. Then day and night are about the same length all over the Earth.
54622.m: At the equinoxes, day and night last about twelve hours everywhere.

54623.q: When is the shortest day of the year in the Northern Hemisphere?
54623.e: Around 21 December is the winter solstice. The midday sun is then at its lowest here, and afterwards the days get longer again.
54623.m: At the winter solstice in December, the day is shortest.

54624.q: By how many degrees is the Earth's axis tilted from the perpendicular to its orbit?
54624.e: The Earth's axis is tilted by about 23.4° from the perpendicular to the plane of its orbit. This angle is also called the obliquity of the ecliptic.
54624.m: The Earth's axis is tilted by about 23.4 degrees.

54625.q: How does the Earth's axis move over many thousands of years?
a: It slowly wobbles in a circle like a spinning top
It stays exactly the same for ever
It always points towards the sun
54625.e: Like a tilted spinning top, the Earth's axis slowly traces out a cone. This movement is called precession and is caused mainly by the sun and the moon.
54625.m: The Earth's axis slowly wobbles like a spinning top.

54626.q: Why will a different star be our Pole Star in many thousands of years?
a: The Earth's axis slowly points in a different direction
The Pole Star will soon go out
The Earth will then turn the other way
The moon will cover the Pole Star
54626.e: The Earth's axis wobbles like a spinning top and takes about 26,000 years for one full circle. Along the way, it gradually points at other stars.
54626.m: Because the Earth's axis wobbles, the Pole Star changes over thousands of years.

54627.q: What happens to the direction of the Earth's axis in space during a year?
a: it always points towards the sun
it flips over every six months
54627.e: Throughout the whole orbit, the axis points in the same direction in space. That is why sometimes the Northern and sometimes the Southern Hemisphere faces the sun.
54627.m: The Earth's axis keeps its direction in space as the Earth orbits the sun.

54628.q: Does the tilt of the Earth's axis always stay exactly the same?
a: No, it varies a little over a very long time
No, it changes a lot every day
No, it flips over every winter
54628.e: The tilt swings between about 22 and 24.5 degrees over about 41,000 years. At the moment it is slowly decreasing.
54628.m: The tilt of the Earth's axis varies only slightly over long periods.

54629.q: Which special circles of latitude do you get when you subtract the axial tilt from 90°?
54629.e: The polar circles lie at about 66.6° north and south. Their position depends directly on the tilt of the Earth's axis.
54629.m: The position of the polar circles comes from the tilt of the Earth's axis.

54630.q: What can you experience north of the Arctic Circle in midsummer?
54630.e: Because the Northern Hemisphere is tilted towards the sun in summer, the sun does not set there for at least one day. You can even see it at midnight.
54630.m: Beyond the Arctic Circle, the sun shines even at midnight in summer.

54631.q: What is the latitude of the equator?
54631.e: Latitude is counted from the equator. It is the starting point, at 0°.
54631.m: The equator has a latitude of zero degrees.

54632.q: What is the latitude of the North Pole?
54632.e: From the equator to the pole is a quarter of a circle, so 90°. The North Pole therefore lies at 90° North.
54632.m: The poles lie at 90 degrees north and south latitude.

54633.q: Roughly how far apart are two circles of latitude that differ by 1°?
54633.e: A meridian from the equator to the pole measures about 10,000 km and covers 90°. 10,000 : 90 gives about 111 km per degree of latitude.
54633.m: One degree of latitude is about 111 kilometres.

54634.q: Roughly between which degrees of latitude does Switzerland lie?
54634.e: Switzerland's southernmost point near Chiasso lies at about 45.8° North, its northernmost near Bargen SH at about 47.8° North. So Switzerland spans about 2 degrees of latitude.
54634.m: Switzerland lies between about 45.8 and 47.8 degrees north latitude.

54635.q: Which circle of latitude is the longest?
54635.e: The circles of latitude get smaller and smaller towards the poles. The Earth is widest at the equator, so it is the longest.
54635.m: The equator is the biggest of all circles of latitude.

54636.q: How many minutes of arc is a degree divided into?
54636.e: Just as an hour has 60 minutes, a degree has 60 minutes of arc. A minute of arc in turn has 60 seconds of arc.
54636.m: One degree is made up of 60 minutes of arc.

54637.q: Which city lies at about the same latitude as Zurich?
54637.e: Zurich lies at about 47.4° North, Seattle at about 47.6° North. New York lies much further south, Oslo much further north.
54637.m: Seattle in the USA lies at almost the same latitude as Zurich.

54638.q: What is true of all circles of latitude?
a: They run parallel to the equator
They are all the same length
They run from the North Pole to the South Pole
54638.e: All circles of latitude run parallel to the equator and never cross. That is why they are also called parallels.
54638.m: Circles of latitude are parallels because they never cross.

54639.q: What are the lines on a globe that run from the North Pole to the South Pole called?
54639.e: The half-circles from pole to pole are called meridians or lines of longitude. You read off longitude from them.
54639.m: Meridians connect the North Pole with the South Pole.

54640.q: Where do all the meridians meet?
54640.e: Every meridian starts at the North Pole and ends at the South Pole. That is why they all come together there.
54640.m: All meridians meet at the poles.

54641.q: Roughly between which degrees of longitude does Switzerland lie?
54641.e: The westernmost point near Geneva lies at just under 6° East, the easternmost in the Val Müstair at about 10.5° East. So Switzerland lies east of the prime meridian.
54641.m: Switzerland stretches from about 6 to 10.5 degrees east longitude.

54642.q: How does the distance between two meridians change from the equator towards the poles?
a: it gets smaller, down to zero
it is greatest at the poles
54642.e: The meridians come together towards the poles. That is why a degree of longitude gets narrower and narrower towards the north and south.
54642.m: The distance between meridians shrinks to zero towards the poles.

54643.q: Which device helped sailors in the 18th century work out their longitude at sea?
54643.e: The clockmaker John Harrison built a clock that kept accurate time even on rolling ships. By comparing local time with home time, sailors could then calculate their longitude.
54643.m: With an accurate ship's clock, sailors could work out their longitude.

54644.q: How many meridians, each 1° apart, are there around the Earth?
54644.e: A full circle around the Earth has 360°. With 1° between them, that makes 360 meridians.
54644.m: There are 360 whole degrees of longitude around the Earth.

54645.q: How was the metre originally defined in France in the 1790s?
a: as one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator
as the length of the king's foot
as the distance a ball falls in one second
as one hundredth of the height of Mont Blanc
54645.e: The metre was meant to be one ten-millionth of the meridian arc from the North Pole to the equator. To find it, the meridian between Dunkirk and Barcelona was measured.
54645.m: The metre was originally based on the length of a meridian.

54646.q: What kind of building stands in Greenwich right on the prime meridian?
54646.e: The prime meridian runs through the Royal Observatory in Greenwich near London. A line in the ground marks it there.
54646.m: The prime meridian runs through the observatory at Greenwich.

54647.q: Why do we need a prime meridian?
a: As a starting line for longitude
As the boundary between north and south
As a line for shipping traffic
As the border between two countries
54647.e: Longitude is counted east and west from the prime meridian. Since 1884, the line through Greenwich has been the internationally agreed prime meridian.
54647.m: Counting longitude begins at the prime meridian.

54648.q: Which of these African countries does the prime meridian run through?
54648.e: In Africa, the prime meridian crosses Algeria, Mali, Burkina Faso, Togo and Ghana. Nigeria, Kenya and Egypt lie to the east of it.
54648.m: In West Africa, the prime meridian runs through Ghana, among other countries.

54649.q: Which European countries does the prime meridian run through?
54649.e: From England, the prime meridian crosses the English Channel and runs through western France and eastern Spain into the Mediterranean.
54649.m: In Europe, the prime meridian crosses Great Britain, France and Spain.

54650.q: Which country set its legal time by the meridian of its capital city until as late as 1911?
54650.e: For a long time France counted longitude from the meridian through the Paris Observatory. In 1911 it switched its legal time to Greenwich, and shipping followed in 1914.
54650.m: France held on to a prime meridian through Paris for a long time.

54651.q: Apart from Europe and Africa, which continent does the prime meridian cross?
54651.e: After Africa, the prime meridian runs across the South Atlantic to the South Pole. On the way it crosses Antarctica.
54651.m: The prime meridian runs through Europe, Africa and Antarctica.

54652.q: Which device finds your location in longitude and latitude using satellites?
54652.e: A GPS receiver, for example in a mobile phone, picks up signals from satellites. From them it calculates longitude and latitude, counted from the prime meridian and the equator.
54652.m: GPS gives your location in longitude and latitude.

54653.q: What is the northern tropic called?
54653.e: The northern tropic is called the Tropic of Cancer. Its counterpart in the south is named after a different sign of the zodiac.
54653.m: The northern tropic is called the Tropic of Cancer.

54654.q: Where is the sun directly overhead at midday around 21 June?
54654.e: At the summer solstice, the Northern Hemisphere is tilted most towards the sun. The midday sun then stands directly above the Tropic of Cancer and afterwards turns back.
54654.m: In June, the overhead sun reaches the Tropic of Cancer.

54655.q: What is the area between the two tropics called?
54655.e: Between the tropics, the midday sun is directly overhead at least once a year. This area is called the tropics.
54655.m: The tropics lie between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn.

54656.q: Which of these countries is crossed by the Tropic of Capricorn?
54656.e: The Tropic of Capricorn runs right through Australia, for example near Alice Springs. Kenya and Indonesia lie closer to the equator, New Zealand further south.
54656.m: The Tropic of Capricorn runs right across Australia.

54657.q: Which of these countries is crossed by the Tropic of Cancer?
54657.e: The Tropic of Cancer runs through Mexico, the Sahara, India and southern China, among other places. Brazil and Peru lie south of it, Spain north of it.
54657.m: The Tropic of Cancer crosses Mexico, for example.

54658.q: What is the southern tropic called?
54658.e: The southern tropic is called the Tropic of Capricorn. Around 21 December the midday sun is directly above it.
54658.m: The southern tropic is the Tropic of Capricorn.

54659.q: Where can the midday sun never be directly overhead?
54659.e: The sun is only at the zenith once or twice a year between the tropics. Switzerland lies far north of them.
54659.m: In Switzerland the sun is never directly overhead.

54660.q: Where do the tropics get their names from?
a: from constellations the sun was in at the solstices
from sailors who crossed them first
from mountains that lie exactly on them
from gods of the ancient Greeks
54660.e: About 2000 years ago, at the two solstices, the sun stood in particular constellations of the zodiac. The tropics are named after these constellations.
54660.m: The tropics are named after constellations of the zodiac.

54661.q: Which meridian does the International Date Line roughly follow?
54661.e: The date line lies roughly on the 180th meridian, exactly opposite the prime meridian. But it bends so that island groups and countries are not split.
54661.m: The date line roughly follows the 180th meridian.

54662.q: Which ocean does most of the International Date Line run through?
54662.e: The date line runs from the Bering Strait through the Pacific to Antarctica. That way it divides hardly any inhabited land.
54662.m: The date line lies almost entirely in the Pacific.

54663.q: What happens to the date when you cross the International Date Line from Asia towards America?
a: You live the same day again
The clock jumps forward one hour
54663.e: West of the date line it is already one day later. Anyone travelling east towards America puts the calendar back one day and so experiences one date twice.
54663.m: Crossing the date line eastwards, you get one day twice.

54664.q: Which country celebrates New Year earlier than Switzerland?
54664.e: Australia lies far to the east, near the date line. There the new year begins many hours earlier than here, whereas in America it begins later.
54664.m: In Australia the new year begins earlier than in Switzerland.

54665.q: Which hero of a novel gains a day thanks to the date line and so wins his bet?
54665.e: In Jules Verne's novel “Around the World in Eighty Days”, Phileas Fogg travels east. He thinks he is too late, but he has gained a day by crossing the date line.
54665.m: Phileas Fogg wins his round-the-world bet thanks to the date line.

54666.q: Which strait between Russia and Alaska does the International Date Line run through?
54666.e: In the Bering Strait, Russia and Alaska are only about 80 kilometres apart. The date line separates two calendar days there.
54666.m: The date line runs through the Bering Strait.

54667.q: How many different calendar dates can apply on Earth at the same time?
54667.e: Time zones range from UTC-12 to UTC+14, spanning 26 hours. That is why three different dates apply at the same time for a short while each day.
54667.m: Because time zones span so widely, there are briefly three dates at once.

54669.q: Which time zone applies in Switzerland in winter?
54669.e: In winter, Switzerland uses Central European Time (CET). It is one hour ahead of Coordinated Universal Time, UTC.
54669.m: In winter Switzerland uses Central European Time, which is UTC plus one hour.

54670.q: In winter it is 2 pm in Zurich (UTC+1). What time is it then in Tokyo (UTC+9)?
54670.e: Tokyo is 9 minus 1 = 8 hours ahead. 14 + 8 = 22, so it is 10 pm.
54670.m: In winter Japan is eight hours ahead of Switzerland.

54671.q: In winter a plane takes off from Zurich (UTC+1) at 10 am and flies 6 hours to Dubai (UTC+4). What is the local time when it lands?
54671.e: When it lands, it is 10 + 6 = 16, so 4 pm in Zurich. Dubai is 3 hours ahead, so 16 + 3 = 19, which is 7 pm.
54671.m: When flying east, you have to put your watch forward.

54672.q: How many official time zones does China have, even though it is very wide?
54672.e: Beijing time, UTC+8, applies throughout China. In the far west of the country, the sun therefore rises very late.
54672.m: Despite its size, China has only a single time zone.

54673.q: What is special about India's time zone?
a: It is half an hour off the full hours
India has no time zone at all
54673.e: UTC+5:30 applies throughout India. So the clocks there are half an hour different from most neighbouring zones.
54673.m: India uses a time zone that is off by half an hour.

54674.q: Which country stretches from the Baltic Sea to the Pacific and covers 11 time zones?
54674.e: Russia stretches from the Baltic Sea to the Pacific and covers the time zones UTC+2 to UTC+12.
54674.m: Russia is so wide that it covers 11 time zones.

54675.q: Who pushed especially hard in the 19th century for a single time across large areas?
54675.e: Before that, every town had its own local time based on the position of the sun. For timetables over long distances, the railways needed a shared time.
54675.m: The railways made standard time zones necessary.

54676.q: Why did Switzerland introduce summer time after all in 1981?
a: To have the same time as its neighbouring countries
Because the people demanded it in a vote
Because the sun rose earlier than before
To make the summer holidays longer
54676.e: All the neighbouring countries already had summer time. So that railways, trade and travel would not get muddled, Switzerland fell into line in 1981.
54676.m: Switzerland adapted to its neighbours on summer time.

54677.q: When does summer time begin in Switzerland?
a: on the last Sunday in March
on the first Sunday in March
on the last Sunday in April
54677.e: As in the EU, summer time begins in the night before the last Sunday in March. So the exact date changes every year.
54677.m: Summer time begins on the last Sunday in March.

54678.q: When does summer time end in Switzerland?
a: on the last Sunday in October
on the first Sunday in October
on the last Sunday in September
54678.e: Since 1996, summer time in Europe has ended on the last Sunday in October. Before that it ended in September.
54678.m: Summer time ends on the last Sunday in October.

54679.q: How are the clocks changed when summer time begins?
a: put forward from 2 am to 3 am
put back from 3 am to 2 am
put forward from midnight to 1 am
put back from 1 am to midnight
54679.e: On the night of the change, the clock jumps straight from 2 am to 3 am. The hour in between is skipped.
54679.m: In spring, the clocks go forward from two to three o'clock.

54680.q: How many hours does the day on which summer time ends have?
54680.e: When summer time ends, the clock is put back from 3 am to 2 am. So you live through the hour from 2 to 3 am twice, and the day has 24 + 1 = 25 hours.
54680.m: The day the clocks go back in autumn has 25 hours.

54681.q: What did the Swiss people vote on on 28 May 1978 and narrowly reject?
a: a time law with summer time
54681.e: The time law would have allowed summer time, but it was rejected with only 47.9 per cent voting yes. Afterwards Switzerland was briefly a “time island” in Europe.
54681.m: In 1978 Swiss voters narrowly said no to summer time.

54682.q: When was summer time first introduced in large countries?
a: in the time of the ancient Romans
54682.e: The German Empire and Austria-Hungary introduced summer time in 1916 to save energy during the war. Other countries soon followed.
54682.m: Summer time has existed since the First World War.

54683.q: What was the main original aim of summer time?
a: Saving energy with more daylight in the evening
54683.e: If it stays light longer in the evening, you need less artificial light. That is why summer time was introduced mainly in times of crisis, to save energy.
54683.m: Summer time was originally meant to save energy.

54684.q: What did a large majority want in an EU online survey in 2018?
a: to change the clocks by two hours
to introduce a third clock change
to start summer time as early as February
54684.e: About 84 per cent of the 4.6 million participants wanted to abolish the clock change. So far, however, this has not happened.
54684.m: Many people in Europe would like to abolish the clock change.

54685.q: On which date does the leap day fall?
54685.e: In a leap year, February gets an extra day. It then has 29 days instead of 28.

54686.q: Which of these years was not a leap year, even though it is divisible by 4?
54686.e: Century years are only leap years if they are divisible by 400. 1900 is not divisible by 400, so it was not a leap year.
54686.m: Century years are only leap years if they are divisible by 400.

54687.q: Which Roman ruler introduced a calendar with a leap day every four years in 45 BC?
54687.e: The Julian calendar, named after him, had 365 days and a leap day every four years. It was used in Europe for over 1600 years.
54687.m: Julius Caesar introduced the leap day every four years.

54688.q: What is the calendar we use today called?
54688.e: Pope Gregory XIII had the calendar improved in 1582 because the old Julian calendar was drifting away from the sun. That is why it is called the Gregorian calendar.
54688.m: Our calendar is called the Gregorian calendar.

54689.q: How many days were skipped in the calendar reform of 1582?
54689.e: Thursday 4 October was followed directly by Friday 15 October 1582. This made up for the drift of ten days.
54689.m: In 1582, ten calendar days were skipped.

54690.q: Why did Zurich, Bern and Basel adopt the new calendar more than a hundred years after the Catholic cantons?
a: They were Protestant and rejected the Pope's calendar
They did not know about it
54690.e: The new calendar came from the Pope. So the Protestant cantons refused it for a long time and only switched in 1701.
54690.m: The Protestant cantons adopted the new calendar late.

54691.q: In which canton did two municipalities stick to the old calendar until 1812, longer than anyone else in Western and Central Europe?
54691.e: Schiers and Grüsch in the Prättigau only adopted the Gregorian calendar in 1812. That made them the last in Western and Central Europe.
54691.m: Two municipalities in the Grisons only switched calendars in 1812.

54692.q: Lea was born on 29 February 2000. How many times could she celebrate her birthday on exactly that date by the end of 2024?
54692.e: The leap years after 2000 up to 2024 are 2004, 2008, 2012, 2016, 2020 and 2024. That makes 6 real birthdays.
54692.m: If you were born on 29 February, you only have a real birthday every four years.

54693.q: What is a calendar year without a leap day called?
54693.e: A year with 365 days is called a common year. Its counterpart with an extra day is the leap year.
54693.m: A year without a leap day is called a common year.

54694.q: What would happen over the centuries without leap days?
a: the seasons would drift through the calendar
the days would get shorter and shorter
the Earth would orbit more slowly
54694.e: The calendar year would be about a quarter of a day too short every year. After about 750 years, the start of summer would already fall in December in the calendar.
54694.m: Leap days keep the calendar in step with the seasons.

54695.q: Is the Earth a perfect sphere?
a: No, it is slightly flattened at the poles
No, it is a flat disc
No, it is shaped like a cube
54695.e: Because it spins, the Earth is a little thicker at the equator than from pole to pole. The difference is about 43 kilometres.
54695.m: The Earth is slightly flattened at the poles.

54696.q: Why does the sun rise later in Geneva than in St Gallen?
a: because Geneva lies closer to the lake
54696.e: The Earth turns towards the east, so sunlight reaches places in the east first. St Gallen lies about 3 degrees of longitude further east than Geneva, so the sun rises there about 13 minutes earlier.
54696.m: In eastern Switzerland the sun rises earlier than in the west.

54697.q: How does the Earth's rotation change over a very long time?
54697.e: The tides caused by the moon slow the Earth down very slightly through friction. That is why the days get longer over millions of years.
54697.m: The moon very slowly brakes the Earth's rotation.

54698.e: To make statistics simpler, weather services always start the seasons on the first day of a month. Meteorological spring covers March, April and May.
54698.m: Meteorological spring always begins on 1 March.

54699.q: Which star in the night sky today shows almost exactly where north is?
54699.e: At present the Earth's axis points almost exactly at the Pole Star. That is why it seems to stand still in the sky and shows the direction of north.
54699.m: The Pole Star shows the direction of north.

54700.q: Around which country does the International Date Line bend east in the far north, so that the whole country is on the same side?
54700.e: The 180th meridian cuts through the Chukotka Peninsula in the far east of Russia. So that the same date applies there as in the rest of the country, the date line swerves to the east.
54700.m: The date line bends so that countries are not split.

54701.q: Which country lies mostly west of the prime meridian but still uses Central European Time?
54701.e: Geographically, Spain belongs more in the Greenwich zone, but it has used Central European Time since 1940. That is why the sun rises and sets especially late there.
54701.m: Spain has a time zone that really lies too far east.

54702.q: How many times a year are the clocks changed in Switzerland?
54702.e: In March the clocks go forward one hour, in October they go back one hour. That makes two changes a year.
54702.m: The clocks are changed in spring and in autumn.

54703.q: Which Swiss city lies at about 46.95° North and 7.44° East?
54703.e: Bern lies at about 46.95° North and 7.44° East. Lugano lies further south, Basel further north and Chur further east.
54703.m: With latitude and longitude, any place like Bern can be pinpointed.

54704.q: What does the scale 1:25,000 on a map mean?
a: 1 cm on the map equals 25,000 cm in reality
1 cm on the map equals 25,000 m in reality
1 m on the map equals 25,000 km in reality
1 km on the map equals 25,000 cm in reality
54704.e: The scale tells you how much things have been reduced. At 1:25,000, everything in reality is 25,000 times bigger than on the map.
54704.m: The scale tells you how much reality has been shrunk on the map.

54705.q: On a map with a scale of 1:25,000, a distance measures 6 cm. How long is it in reality?
54705.e: 6 cm times 25,000 gives 150,000 cm. That is 1500 m or 1.5 km.
54705.m: Map distance times the scale number gives the real distance.

54706.q: Two places are 3 km apart in reality. How far apart are they on a 1:50,000 map?
54706.e: 3 km is 300,000 cm. 300,000 divided by 50,000 gives 6 cm.
54706.m: For the map distance, divide the real distance by the scale number.

54707.q: At which scale does 1 cm on the map equal exactly 1 km in reality?
54707.e: 1 km is 100,000 cm. So at 1:100,000, 1 cm stands for exactly 1 km.
54707.m: At 1:100,000, one centimetre on the map is one kilometre on the ground.

54708.q: Which map has the largest scale?
54708.e: The smaller the scale number, the larger the scale. A 1:10,000 map shows a small area in a lot of detail.
54708.m: A large scale shows a small area very precisely.

54709.q: On a map, 4 cm equals exactly 1 km in reality. What is the map's scale?
54709.e: 1 km is 100,000 cm. 100,000 divided by 4 gives 25,000, so 1:25,000.
54709.m: You can work out the scale from the map distance and the real distance.

54710.q: What is the drawn line with kilometre markings called, which you use to measure distances on a map?
54710.e: The scale bar shows distances as a line. You can compare distances directly with a ruler or a piece of string.
54710.m: With the scale bar you can measure distances without doing sums.

54711.q: On a 1:200,000 map you measure 5 cm. How long is the distance in reality?
54711.e: 5 cm times 200,000 gives 1,000,000 cm. That is 10,000 m or 10 km.
54711.m: At 1:200,000, one centimetre stands for two kilometres.

54712.q: What is the explanation of symbols on a map called?
54712.e: The key, also called the legend, explains what the colours, lines and symbols on the map mean.
54712.m: Without a key you cannot understand a map's symbols.

54713.q: What are the simplified map signs, for example for a church or a railway station, called?
54713.e: Map symbols are fixed signs for things like buildings, roads or forests. Their meaning is given in the key.
54713.m: Map symbols are the simplified picture signs of a map.

54714.q: What colour are lakes and rivers almost always shown in on maps?
54714.e: Water is traditionally drawn in blue on maps. That way you recognise it straight away.
54714.m: On maps, water is almost always blue.

54715.q: How is a forest usually shown on Switzerland's national maps?
54715.e: On the national maps from swisstopo, forests are green areas. The key explains this colour.
54715.m: Green areas on national maps usually stand for forest.

54716.q: Why are the keys of different maps often different?
a: Each map uses its own signs and colours
Keys are exactly the same worldwide
54716.e: There is no single worldwide sign language for maps. That is why you have to read the key first for every map.
54716.m: With every new map, read the key first.

54717.q: What does a line made of dashes and dots on a map very often show?
54717.e: Borders of countries or cantons are often drawn as dash-dot lines. The exact meaning is given in the key.
54717.m: Dash-dot lines on maps often mark borders.

54718.q: What does a small dot or circle with a name on an overview map usually stand for?
54718.e: On overview maps, towns and villages are often drawn as dots or circles. Bigger circles usually stand for bigger cities.
54718.m: Dots with names on maps usually mark towns and villages.

54719.q: Which Swiss canton lies furthest west?
54719.e: Switzerland's westernmost point is near Chancy in the canton of Geneva.

54720.q: Which direction is on the right of a map that is oriented to north?
54720.e: When north is at the top, east is on the right and west is on the left.
54720.m: On a map oriented to north, east is on the right.

54722.q: Which direction is meant by the old word “Occident”?
54722.e: The sun sets in the west in the evening. That is why the Occident stands for the West, and the Orient for the East.
54722.m: The Occident lies where the sun sets.

54723.q: In which direction does Geneva lie as seen from Zurich?
54723.e: Geneva lies right in the west of Switzerland and a little further south than Zurich. That is why it lies to the south-west of Zurich.

54724.q: Which Swiss canton lies furthest south?
54724.e: Switzerland's southernmost point is near Chiasso in the canton of Ticino.

54725.q: Which direction is marked with the letter “E” on many compasses?
54725.e: “E” stands for the English “East” or the French “Est”. On German-language maps, “O” for “Ost” is used instead.

54726.q: Which word comes from the Latin word for “east” and today means “to find your bearings”?
54726.e: “Oriens” means “east” or “rising sun” in Latin. In the past, maps were often lined up towards the east.
54726.m: To orientate originally meant to line yourself up towards the east.

54727.q: Where does a compass needle point?
54727.e: A compass needle is a small magnet. It lines up with the Earth's magnetic field and points to the magnetic North Pole.
54727.m: A compass needle lines up with the Earth's magnetic field.

54728.q: What is the angle in degrees between north and the direction you are walking called?
54728.e: The azimuth is measured clockwise from north. You set it on the compass and then follow that direction.
54728.m: The azimuth gives your walking direction in degrees from north.

54729.q: Why does a compass needle not point exactly to the geographic North Pole?
a: The magnetic North Pole is in a different place
The moon pulls the needle aside
The Earth is flat at the North Pole
54729.e: The magnetic and geographic North Poles are not in the same place. The difference is called magnetic declination.
54729.m: The magnetic and geographic North Poles are not in the same place.

54730.q: Why should you not hold a compass right next to a mobile phone or an iron knife?
54730.e: Iron, magnets and electronic devices disturb the magnetic field near the needle. Then it shows the wrong direction.
54730.m: Iron and magnets deflect the compass needle.

54731.q: What does it mean to “orient” a map to north?
a: Turn the map so that its north points north
Mark the north on the map in colour
Extend the map towards the north
Use only the northern part of the map
54731.e: To orient a map, you turn it until its north matches the real north. Then the map lines up with the landscape.
54731.m: An oriented map lines up the same way as the landscape.

54732.q: How many degrees does the full circle on an ordinary compass have?
54732.e: A full circle has 360 degrees. North is 0 degrees, east 90 degrees, south 180 degrees and west 270 degrees.

54733.q: What colour is the north-pointing end of a compass needle often marked?
54733.e: On most compasses the north tip of the needle is red. That way you do not mix up the two ends.
54733.m: The red tip of a compass needle usually points north.

54734.q: Which type of compass with a transparent base plate is often used for hiking and orienteering?
54734.e: A baseplate compass has a transparent plate with rulers. You can lay it directly on the map.
54734.m: The baseplate compass is good for working with a map.

54735.q: How many degrees are there between north and north-east on the compass rose?
54735.e: The 8 directions divide the 360-degree circle evenly. 360 divided by 8 gives 45 degrees.
54735.m: Neighbouring main and in-between directions are 45 degrees apart.

54736.q: Which direction is the opposite of south-west?
54736.e: Opposite directions are 180 degrees apart on the compass rose. Opposite south-west is north-east.

54737.q: How many degrees does the direction south-west correspond to on the compass rose?
54737.e: South is at 180 degrees and west at 270 degrees. South-west lies exactly in between, at 225 degrees.

54738.q: How many directions does a compass rose with main and in-between directions show?
54738.e: To the 4 main directions you add the 4 in-between directions NE, SE, SW and NW. Together that makes 8.
54738.m: Main and in-between directions together make eight directions.

a: The wind comes from the west
The wind blows towards the west
The wind only blows in the evening
54739.e: Winds are named after the direction they come from. So a west wind blows from the west.
54739.m: A wind is named after the direction it comes from.

54740.q: From which direction does the cold bise blow in Switzerland?
54740.e: The bise is a cold, dry wind from the north-east to east. It blows mainly across the Central Plateau and over Lake Geneva.
54740.m: The bise blows cold from the north-east.

54741.q: Which direction lies between north and north-east on a 16-point compass rose?
54741.e: The 16-point compass rose divides the in-between directions once more. Between north and north-east lies north-north-east.
54741.m: North-north-east lies between north and north-east.

54742.q: What do contour lines on a map connect?
54742.e: A contour line runs through all the points that are at the same height above sea level.
54742.m: All points on a contour line are at the same height.

54743.q: What does it mean when contour lines are very close together?
54743.e: Contour lines close together show that the height increases a lot over a short distance. The ground is steep.
54743.m: The closer the contour lines, the steeper the ground.

54744.q: What is the difference in height between two neighbouring contour lines called?
54744.e: The contour interval tells you how many metres apart in height two neighbouring contour lines are.
54744.m: The contour interval is the height gap between two contour lines.

54745.q: How many metres is the contour interval on Switzerland's 1:25,000 national map?
54745.e: On swisstopo's 1:25,000 national map, the contour lines are 10 m apart. On the 1:50,000 map it is 20 m.
54745.m: On the 1:25,000 national map, contour lines are 10 metres apart.

54746.q: What are the thicker, labelled contour lines that make reading easier called?
54746.e: Every fifth or tenth contour line is drawn thicker and is often labelled with its height. These are called index contours.
54746.m: Index contours help you read heights quickly.

54747.q: What do several closed contour lines show if they lie inside each other like rings and get higher towards the middle?
54747.e: The innermost contour line is the highest. That is why such rings show a raised area like a hill or a peak.
54747.m: Ring-shaped contour lines rising in height show a peak.

54748.q: Which way does the tip of the V-shaped contour lines point in a stream valley?
54748.e: In valleys, the contour lines bend upwards because the stream has cut into the ground. So the tip of the V points uphill.
54748.m: In valleys, the tips of contour lines point uphill.

54749.q: What do heights such as “1200 m above sea level” refer to?
54749.e: The height tells you how many metres a place lies above sea level. In Switzerland, this is measured from the Pierre du Niton in Lake Geneva.
54749.m: Heights are measured from sea level.

54750.q: What does a physical map mainly show?
a: The shapes of the land such as mountains and plains
54750.e: A physical map shows the relief of the Earth, that is mountains, valleys, plains and water.
54750.m: Physical maps show the shapes of the Earth's surface.

54751.q: Which colour usually stands for low-lying land on physical maps?
54751.e: Lowland is usually shown in green. As the height increases, the colours change through yellow to brown.
54751.m: On physical maps, green means low land.

54752.q: Which colour usually shows high mountains on physical maps?
54752.e: The higher the ground, the darker the brown. Glaciers and permanent snow are often white.
54752.m: High mountains are dark brown on physical maps.

54753.q: What are the coloured height bands on a physical map called?
54753.e: With layer tints, each range of height gets its own colour. That way you can see high and low areas at a glance.
54753.m: Layer tints use colours to make differences in height visible.

54754.q: What is the technique of light and shadow that makes mountains look three-dimensional on maps called?
54754.e: With hill shading, slopes are shaded as if light were falling on them from one side. Swiss maps are famous for their hill shading.
54754.m: Hill shading makes mountains look three-dimensional on a map.

54755.q: From which direction does the imagined light fall in the hill shading on Swiss maps?
54755.e: On Swiss maps, the imagined light comes from the top left, that is from the north-west. This makes the relief look natural to the eye.
54755.m: In hill shading, the light usually comes from the top left.

54756.q: What does a political map mainly show?
54756.e: Political maps show how the Earth is divided into countries or administrative areas.
54756.m: Political maps show countries and their borders.

54757.q: Why do neighbouring countries have different colours on a political map?
a: So that you can tell the countries apart easily
Because the colour shows the height
Because the colour shows the population
Because every country has a compulsory colour
54757.e: On political maps the colours usually have no further meaning. They just help you tell neighbouring areas apart.
54757.m: On political maps, colours separate neighbouring areas.

54758.q: How many neighbouring countries of Switzerland does a political map show?
54758.e: Switzerland borders Germany, France, Italy, Austria and Liechtenstein.

54759.q: How are capital cities often highlighted on political maps?
a: With a special sign, such as a circle with a dot or a star
54759.e: Capitals often get their own sign or especially eye-catching lettering. What it means is given in the key.
54759.m: Capitals often have a special sign on maps.

54760.q: Apart from the national border, which borders does a political map of Switzerland usually also show?
54760.e: Switzerland is divided into 26 cantons. A political map of Switzerland shows their borders.
54760.m: A political map of Switzerland shows the borders of the 26 cantons.

a: A map on a particular topic, such as climate or population
A map with only contour lines
54761.e: Thematic maps show a particular topic, for example rainfall, languages or the economy.
54761.m: Thematic maps show a chosen topic.

54762.q: Which map is an example of a thematic map?
a: A map of Switzerland's national languages
A town plan with no extra information
54762.e: A language map shows a particular topic, namely where which language is spoken.
54762.m: A language map is a thematic map.

54763.q: What are the lines on weather maps that connect places with the same air pressure called?
54763.e: Isobars connect places with the same air pressure. They help you spot areas of high and low pressure.
54763.m: Isobars connect places with the same air pressure.

54764.q: What are lines that connect places with the same temperature called?
54764.e: “Iso” means equal and “therm” means heat. Isotherms connect places with the same temperature.
54764.m: Isotherms connect places with the same temperature.

54765.q: What do darker colours on a population density map usually show?
54765.e: On such maps, each area gets a colour according to its value. Darker colours usually show higher values, here more densely populated areas.
54765.m: On thematic maps, darker colours usually show higher values.

54766.q: What does a precipitation map show?
a: Where how much rain and snow falls
54766.e: A precipitation map is a thematic map. Lines or colours show where the same amount of rain or snow falls.
54766.m: Precipitation maps show where how much rain falls.

54767.q: What do pie charts on a thematic map usually show?
a: Shares, for example how a country's economy is divided up
The exact height of a mountain
54767.e: Pie charts on maps show shares of a whole. This lets you compare areas directly.
54767.m: Charts on maps show amounts and shares at a place.

54768.q: Why is every flat world map distorted in some way?
a: Because a sphere's surface cannot be shown flat without distortion
Because the Earth is a disc
Because the continents move every day
54768.e: The Earth is roughly a sphere. A curved surface cannot be transferred onto a flat one without stretching or squashing it.
54768.m: Only a globe shows the Earth without distortion.

54769.q: Which cartographer designed a famous angle-true world map for navigation at sea in 1569?
54769.e: Gerardus Mercator published his world map in 1569. Because it keeps angles correct, it was well suited to navigation at sea.
54769.m: The Mercator map keeps angles correct and was made for sailors.

54770.q: Which island appears far too big on the Mercator world map?
54770.e: The Mercator projection greatly enlarges areas near the poles. Greenland looks almost as big as Africa there, but it is about 14 times smaller.
54770.m: In the Mercator projection, areas near the poles look far too big.

54771.q: What does it mean when a map projection is “equal-area”?
a: The relative sizes of the areas are correct
54771.e: An equal-area map shows areas of the same size as the same size. In return, the shapes are distorted.
54771.m: Equal-area maps show areas in their correct relative sizes.

54772.q: Which continent looks smaller on many familiar world maps than it really is?
54772.e: On the Mercator map, areas near the poles are enlarged. In 1973 Arno Peters presented an equal-area map on which Africa appears at its real size.
54772.m: Equal-area maps show Africa at its real size.

54773.q: What is the line that divides the Earth into a Northern and a Southern Hemisphere called?
54773.e: The equator lies at 0 degrees latitude, exactly halfway between the North and South Poles.
54773.m: The equator divides the Earth into the Northern and Southern Hemispheres.

54774.q: What is the network of lines of latitude and longitude on a map or globe called?
54774.e: Circles of latitude and meridians together form the graticule. With it, any place on Earth can be pinpointed exactly.
54774.m: The graticule is made up of circles of latitude and meridians.

a: A collection of maps in book form
54775.e: An atlas brings many maps together in a book or a digital collection. It often contains physical, political and thematic maps.
54775.m: An atlas is a collection of many maps.

54776.q: Which figure from Greek myth is the atlas named after?
a: The Titan Atlas, who holds up the sky
54776.e: In Greek myth, the Titan Atlas has to hold up the sky. Later his name was used for collections of maps.
54776.m: The atlas is named after a Titan from Greek myth.

54777.q: What is the index of an atlas for?
a: To find places and names quickly on the right map
54777.e: In the index, names are listed alphabetically. Next to them are the page number and the square on the map.
54777.m: With the index you can find any place in the atlas quickly.

54778.q: How is the index of an atlas arranged?
a: By continent from north to south
54778.e: The index lists all the names from A to Z. So you can look up any name like in a dictionary.
54778.m: An atlas index is in alphabetical order.

54779.q: What does “p. 24, C3” in the index of an atlas mean?
a: Page 24, square in column C and row 3
54779.e: The maps in an atlas are divided into squares called grid squares. Letters and numbers along the edge of the map name the column and row.
54779.m: A grid square is given with a letter and a number.

54780.q: What is the atlas used in many Swiss schools called?
54780.e: The Swiss World Atlas is published by the Swiss Conference of Cantonal Ministers of Education. Many schools work with it.
54780.m: The Swiss World Atlas is Switzerland's school atlas.

54781.q: What are the squares that an atlas map is divided into by lines and letter and number labels called?
54781.e: Grid squares are search squares. With their letter and number, you can find a place on the map more quickly.
54781.m: Grid squares help you search on a map.

54782.q: What does the abbreviation GPS stand for?
54782.e: GPS is a satellite system for finding your own location. The name means roughly “worldwide location system”.
54782.m: GPS is a worldwide system for finding your position.

54783.e: GPS was developed by the US Department of Defense and is run there. It is free to use worldwide.

54784.q: What is the European satellite navigation system called?
54784.e: The European Union runs its own system, Galileo. GLONASS belongs to Russia, BeiDou to China.

54785.q: From at least how many satellites does a GPS receiver need signals to work out its position including height?
54785.e: For longitude, latitude and height you need three satellites. A fourth is needed to correct the inaccurate clock in the receiver.
54785.m: An accurate GPS position needs at least four satellites.

54786.q: How does a GPS receiver work out how far away it is from a satellite?
a: From the travel time of the radio signal
From the colour of the satellite
From the loudness of a sound
From the weight of the satellite
54786.e: The satellites send out their exact time. From how long the signal takes to arrive, the receiver calculates the distance.
54786.m: GPS measures distances using the travel time of signals.

54787.q: At roughly what height do GPS satellites orbit the Earth?
54787.e: GPS satellites fly at a height of about 20,200 km. They circle the Earth about twice a day.
54787.m: GPS satellites orbit at a height of about 20,000 kilometres.

54788.q: Which very precise devices do GPS satellites carry on board?
54788.e: To measure travel times, the time must be extremely accurate. That is why the satellites have atomic clocks on board.
54788.m: Atomic clocks make GPS timing very accurate.

54789.q: What is the leisure game called in which you use GPS coordinates to search for hidden boxes?
54789.e: In geocaching, hiding places are described with coordinates. You search for them with a GPS device or a mobile phone.
54789.m: In geocaching you find hiding places using coordinates.

54790.q: What is exploring the Earth's surface from a distance, for example with satellites, called?
54790.e: Remote sensing gathers information about the Earth without touching it. Satellites or aircraft are used to do this.
54790.m: Satellite images are part of remote sensing.

54791.q: Why are weather satellites like Meteosat positioned about 36,000 km above the equator?
a: Because there they always stay above the same area
Because there is no gravity there
Because they are closer to the sun there
54791.e: At this height, a satellite takes exactly as long to go round the Earth as the Earth takes to turn. It appears to stand still above one point.
54791.m: Geostationary satellites appear to stand still above the Earth.

54792.q: Roughly since when have satellites been regularly photographing the Earth from space?
54792.e: The first Landsat satellite was launched in 1972. Since then, images of the Earth's surface have been taken all the time, so changes can be compared.
54792.m: Satellites have been watching the Earth for about 50 years.

54793.q: What can you see well on satellite images taken with infrared light?
54793.e: Healthy plants reflect a lot of infrared light. So on such images you can see where forests and fields are healthy or dry.
54793.m: Infrared images show how healthy plants are.

54794.q: Which satellites can take pictures of the Earth even through clouds?
54794.e: Radar satellites send out microwaves themselves and receive the echo. These waves pass through clouds.

54795.q: Which federal office produces Switzerland's national maps and aerial photos?
54795.e: The Federal Office of Topography, swisstopo, surveys Switzerland. It provides maps and corrected aerial photos for the whole country.

54796.q: What, for example, is watched with Earth observation satellites?
a: The melting of glaciers and polar ice
54796.e: With its Sentinel satellites, Europe observes the climate, oceans, ice and forests. That way changes can be seen over many years.
54796.m: Satellites show how the Earth is changing.

54797.q: Which star in the night sky shows roughly where north is?
54797.e: The Pole Star is almost exactly above the Earth's North Pole. That is why it shows the direction of north at night.
54797.m: The Pole Star shows the way north.

54798.q: How do you find the Pole Star using the Plough?
a: Extend the back edge of the Plough's box about five times
Extend the handle of the Plough to double its length
Look for the brightest star in the Plough
Look straight up from the moon
54798.e: You extend the line joining the two back stars of the box by about five times its length. That is where the Pole Star is.
54798.m: You can find the Pole Star using the Plough.

54799.q: In which direction is the sun in Switzerland around midday?
54799.e: In the Northern Hemisphere outside the tropics, the sun is in the south at midday. During summer time that is around 1.30 pm.
54799.m: At midday the sun is in the south here.

54800.q: In which direction does the shadow of a stick point in Switzerland at midday?
54800.e: A shadow always falls on the side facing away from the sun. At midday it is also at its shortest.
54800.m: Here, the midday shadow points north.

54801.q: Which constellation helps you find south in the Southern Hemisphere?
54801.e: The northern guide star cannot be seen in the Southern Hemisphere. There people use the constellation of the Southern Cross.
54801.m: In the Southern Hemisphere, the Southern Cross points south.

54802.q: On which days does the sun rise exactly in the east?
a: At the equinoxes in spring and autumn
On the longest day in summer
On the shortest day in winter
On every day of the year
54802.e: Only around 20 March and 22 September does the sun rise exactly in the east. In summer it rises in the north-east, in winter in the south-east.
54802.m: The sun rises exactly in the east only at the equinoxes.

54803.q: What is the sport called in which you use a map and compass to find control points in the countryside as fast as possible?
54803.e: In orienteering, runners look for control points with the help of a detailed map. Orienteering is very popular in Switzerland.
54803.m: In orienteering, map reading counts as much as speed.

54804.q: Where do most earthquakes on Earth happen?
a: At the boundaries of the tectonic plates
In the middle of large deserts
Only at the North and South Poles
54804.e: The Earth's crust is made of plates that move against each other. Tension builds up at their boundaries and is released suddenly as earthquakes.
54804.m: Most earthquakes happen where tectonic plates meet.

54805.q: What is the instrument that records earthquake waves called?
54805.e: A seismograph records the movements of the ground during an earthquake. The recording is called a seismogram.
54805.m: The seismograph records the movements of the ground.

54806.q: At which university is the Swiss Seismological Service based?
54806.e: The Swiss Seismological Service (SED) is part of ETH Zurich. It monitors earthquakes in Switzerland and assesses the earthquake risk.
54806.m: The Swiss Seismological Service works at ETH Zurich.

54807.q: What is the science of earthquakes and how their waves spread called?
54807.e: Seismology studies earthquakes and the waves that spread through the Earth when they happen. Experts in this field are called seismologists.
54807.m: Seismology is the science of earthquakes.

54808.q: What are the smaller tremors that follow a strong earthquake called?
54808.e: After a strong earthquake, the Earth's crust settles again. This often causes smaller quakes for days or weeks afterwards, called aftershocks.
54808.m: A strong earthquake is often followed by many aftershocks.

54809.q: What should you do if you are inside a building during an earthquake?
a: Crawl under a sturdy table and protect your head
Get into the lift straight away
54809.e: The biggest dangers are falling objects and shattering glass. Under a sturdy table you are best protected from them until the quake is over.
54809.m: In an earthquake, crawl under a sturdy table and protect your head.

54810.q: Who is the Richter scale named after?
54810.e: The American seismologist Charles Francis Richter developed the scale in 1935 together with Beno Gutenberg. It gives the strength of an earthquake.
54810.m: The Richter scale is named after the seismologist Charles Richter.

54811.q: What is the value that gives the strength of an earthquake on the Richter scale called?
54811.e: The Richter scale gives the magnitude, that is the strength of a quake at its source. Intensity, on the other hand, describes the effects at a particular place.
54811.m: The strength of an earthquake is called its magnitude.

54812.q: How much bigger is the swing on a seismogram at magnitude 6 compared with magnitude 5?
54812.e: The Richter scale is logarithmic. Each whole step up means a ten times bigger swing of the seismograph.
54812.m: One step up on the Richter scale means a ten times bigger swing.

54813.q: What is true of a magnitude 7 earthquake compared with a magnitude 6 one?
a: It releases the same amount of energy
54813.e: For each whole step, the energy released increases about 32 times. So even one step up makes a huge difference.
54813.m: One step up on the scale means much more energy.

54814.q: Why is the damage usually greatest near the epicentre?
a: The earthquake waves are least weakened there
The ground there is always sand
There are always the most houses there
The weather is especially bad there
54814.e: Earthquake waves lose strength as they travel further. Near the epicentre they therefore hit with the greatest force.
54814.m: The closer to the epicentre, the stronger the shaking.

54815.q: What is the place inside the Earth where an earthquake starts called?
54815.e: The hypocentre is the actual source of the earthquake deep underground. From there, the earthquake waves spread out in all directions.
54815.m: The hypocentre is the source of an earthquake deep down.

54816.q: What is the minimum number of measuring stations needed to locate an earthquake's epicentre?
54816.e: Each station only knows its distance from the epicentre, which gives a circle around it. Only three circles cross at one single point.
54816.m: With three measuring stations, the epicentre can be pinpointed.

54817.q: Which earthquake waves arrive at a measuring station first?
54817.e: P waves (primary waves) are the fastest earthquake waves. That is why measuring stations always record them first.
54817.m: In an earthquake, the P waves always arrive first.

54818.q: Which earthquake waves usually cause the most damage at the Earth's surface?
54818.e: Surface waves travel along the Earth's surface and make the ground sway strongly. They arrive last but are the most destructive.
54818.m: Surface waves cause the most damage in earthquakes.

54819.q: A station measures a long time gap between the first and the second earthquake waves. What does that mean?
54819.e: The two kinds of wave travel at different speeds. The longer the journey, the bigger the gap between their arrivals.
54819.m: The bigger the time gap between the waves, the further away the epicentre.

54820.q: Why do earthquakes with a source near the surface often cause great damage?
a: The waves are hardly weakened on the way to the surface
The rock there is always soft
Such quakes always last for days
54820.e: The shorter the path from the source to the surface, the less strength the waves lose. Shallow quakes therefore often cause especially great damage.
54820.m: Shallow earthquakes are often especially destructive at the surface.

54821.q: What does the Japanese word “tsunami” mean in English?
54821.e: Tsunami is made from the Japanese words for harbour and wave. Fishermen often only noticed the wave once it had wrecked their harbour.

54822.q: What is the most common cause of a tsunami?
54822.e: In an undersea earthquake, the seabed suddenly rises or sinks. This sets a huge amount of water in motion.
54822.m: Most tsunamis are triggered by undersea earthquakes.

54823.q: How fast can a tsunami travel in the deep open ocean?
54823.e: In deep water, a tsunami moves about as fast as an airliner. In shallow water near the coast it slows down but gets much higher.
54823.m: In the deep ocean, a tsunami is as fast as a plane.

54824.q: Which warning sign can appear on the coast shortly before a tsunami?
a: The sea suddenly draws back a long way
The water suddenly becomes very warm
The waves become very small and calm
54824.e: Often the trough of the wave reaches the coast first, and the water draws back a long way. Anyone who sees this should immediately flee to higher ground.
54824.m: If the sea suddenly draws back, flee to higher ground at once.

54825.q: Which ocean was hit by the devastating tsunami of 26 December 2004?
54825.e: An undersea earthquake off Sumatra triggered the tsunami. It hit many coasts around the Indian Ocean, for example in Indonesia, Sri Lanka and Thailand.
54825.m: The 2004 tsunami devastated the coasts of the Indian Ocean.

54826.q: What does a tsunami usually consist of?
54826.e: A tsunami usually consists of a series of waves that arrive minutes apart. The first wave is often not the highest, so you must not go back too early.
54826.m: A tsunami comes in several waves, and the first is often not the biggest.

54827.q: Why do ships on the open ocean hardly notice a tsunami?
a: The wave there is very low and very long
The wave there is hidden under water
The wave there is very slow
The wave only forms at the coast
54827.e: On the high seas, a tsunami is often less than a metre high but hundreds of kilometres long. Only in shallow coastal water does it pile up high.
54827.m: On the open sea a tsunami is low; at the coast it becomes dangerously high.

54828.q: Which Swiss lake was hit by a flood wave in the year 563 after a rockslide in the Rhône valley?
54828.e: In the Tauredunum event, a mountain collapsed in the Rhône valley. The falling masses set off a flood wave in Lake Geneva that caused great damage as far as Geneva.
54828.m: Even lakes like Lake Geneva can be hit by flood waves.

54829.q: Apart from an undersea earthquake, what else can trigger a tsunami?
a: A large landslide into the sea
54829.e: Landslides, volcanic eruptions or meteorite impacts can also suddenly push aside large amounts of water. This also creates a tsunami wave.
54829.m: A landslide into the sea can also trigger a tsunami.

54830.q: What is molten rock called that flows onto the Earth's surface during a volcanic eruption?
54830.e: Inside the Earth, molten rock is called magma. As soon as it comes out at the surface, it is called lava.
54830.m: Magma that comes out at the surface is called lava.

54831.q: What is the opening at the top of a volcano called, from which lava, ash and gases come out?
54831.e: The crater is the funnel-shaped opening at the top of a volcano. Magma rises up to it through the vent inside.
54831.m: Lava, ash and gases come out of a volcano's crater.

54832.q: Which volcano buried the Roman town of Pompeii in AD 79?
54832.e: When Vesuvius erupted, Pompeii was buried under a layer of ash and pumice several metres thick. That is why the town is still well preserved today.
54832.m: Vesuvius buried the town of Pompeii in AD 79.

54833.q: Which volcano in the Philippines erupted in 1991 and then cooled the Earth's climate for a while?
54833.e: Pinatubo hurled large amounts of sulphur gases high into the atmosphere. These blocked out sunlight, and the Earth cooled slightly for one to two years.
54833.m: The eruption of Pinatubo in 1991 briefly cooled the Earth.

54834.q: The eruption of which volcano in 1815 led to the “Year Without a Summer” in 1816, including in Switzerland?
54834.e: Tambora in Indonesia hurled huge amounts of ash and gases into the atmosphere. These darkened the sun, and in 1816 Switzerland suffered failed harvests and hunger.
54834.m: Because of the Tambora eruption, 1816 became the year without a summer.

54835.q: Which volcano in Indonesia exploded so violently in 1883 that the bang was heard thousands of kilometres away?
54835.e: The explosion of Krakatoa is thought to be one of the loudest sounds in history. Most of the island was destroyed.
54835.m: Krakatoa exploded in 1883 with a tremendous bang.

54836.q: Why do many people live at the foot of volcanoes despite the danger?
a: Weathered volcanic ash makes the soil very fertile
It is always cool and shady there
54836.e: Volcanic ash contains many minerals that turn into fertile soil as they weather. That is why grapes, fruit and vegetables often grow especially well on volcanic slopes.
54836.m: Volcanic soils are often especially fertile.

54837.q: Which type of volcano has gentle slopes and is formed from runny lava, as on Hawaii?
54837.e: Runny lava flows a long way before it hardens. This creates wide, flat volcanoes that look like a shield lying on the ground.
54837.m: Shield volcanoes are formed from runny lava and have gentle slopes.

54838.q: What is a tropical cyclone in the north-west Pacific, for example near Japan or the Philippines, called?
54838.e: Tropical cyclones have different names depending on the region. In the north-west Pacific they are called typhoons.
54838.m: In the north-west Pacific, a tropical cyclone is called a typhoon.

54839.q: What is a tropical storm in the Indian Ocean, for example near India or Bangladesh, called?
54839.e: In the Indian Ocean and the South Pacific, tropical storms are called cyclones. They often bring storm surges to low-lying coasts.
54839.m: In the Indian Ocean, a tropical storm is called a cyclone.

54840.q: What is the almost windless centre of a hurricane called?
54840.e: In the eye of a hurricane it is often calm and the sky can be clear. All around it, the strongest winds rage in the eyewall.
54840.m: The calm centre of a hurricane is called the eye.

54841.q: Roughly how warm does sea water need to be at least for a tropical cyclone to form?
54841.e: Tropical cyclones only form over warm tropical seas. They need water temperatures of about 26.5 °C down to a depth of several tens of metres.
54841.m: Tropical cyclones need sea water of at least about 26 degrees.

54842.q: Which way do hurricanes turn in the Northern Hemisphere?
a: They do not turn at all
54842.e: The Earth's rotation deflects air currents; this is called the Coriolis effect. That is why storms in the Northern Hemisphere turn anticlockwise.
54842.m: In the Northern Hemisphere, cyclones turn anticlockwise.

54843.q: Why does a hurricane weaken when it moves over land?
a: It loses its supply of warm sea water
The mountains soak up the wind
The sun shines more weakly over land
54843.e: A hurricane's energy comes from warm, evaporating sea water. Over land this energy source is missing, and the storm loses strength.
54843.m: Without warm sea water, a hurricane loses its strength.

54844.q: Which US city was widely flooded by Hurricane Katrina in 2005?
54844.e: Hurricane Katrina brought a storm surge that broke the levees in New Orleans. Large parts of the city were under water.
54844.m: Hurricane Katrina flooded the city of New Orleans in 2005.

54845.q: From what wind speed does a tropical cyclone count as a hurricane?
54845.e: A hurricane has at least force 12 on the Beaufort scale. That means wind speeds of about 119 km/h or more.
54845.m: A hurricane brings winds of at least about 119 km/h.

54846.q: From which kind of clouds do most strong tornadoes form?
54846.e: Supercells are large thunderstorms with a rotating updraught. Strong tornadoes can form from this rotation.
54846.m: Strong tornadoes usually form from rotating supercells.

54847.q: What is the strength of a tornado usually classified by?
a: By the month in which it occurs
54847.e: The wind in a tornado can rarely be measured directly. That is why the Fujita scale ranks tornadoes by the damage they cause; the strongest get level 5.
54847.m: Tornadoes are ranked by their damage.

54848.q: What makes a tornado different from a hurricane?
a: A tornado is much smaller and usually lasts only minutes
A tornado is much bigger and lasts for weeks
A tornado only forms over the sea
54848.e: A tornado is usually only a few dozen to a hundred metres wide and often lasts only minutes. A hurricane is hundreds of kilometres across and can last for days.
54848.m: A tornado is small and short-lived; a hurricane is huge and long-lived.

54849.q: What is a tornado that forms over a lake or the sea called?
54849.e: A waterspout is a whirlwind over a body of water. Waterspouts are occasionally seen over Swiss lakes too.
54849.m: A tornado over water is called a waterspout.

54850.q: Where is the best place to shelter during a tornado?
a: In the cellar or a windowless inner room
In a car on the road
54850.e: The main dangers are flying debris and shattering glass. A low-lying room without windows offers the best protection.
54850.m: In a tornado, shelter in the cellar or a room without windows.

54851.q: What wind speeds can the strongest tornadoes reach?
54851.e: Radar has measured wind speeds of over 400 km/h in the strongest tornadoes. That makes them some of the most violent winds on Earth.
54851.m: The strongest tornadoes bring winds of over 400 km/h.

54852.q: What is the tube-shaped cloud that reaches down to the ground in a tornado called?
54852.e: In a tornado, a rotating tube of cloud forms that looks like a funnel. It becomes visible through water vapour, dust and debris.
54852.m: The trunk of a tornado is a funnel cloud.

54853.q: What caused major flooding in Switzerland in August 2005?
a: A storm surge from the sea
54853.e: In August 2005 it rained very heavily for days on the north side of the Alps. Rivers burst their banks, and the damage came to about 3 billion francs.
54853.m: Days of heavy rain led to major floods in Switzerland in 2005.

54854.q: Why were the yearly floods of the Nile useful to the ancient Egyptians?
a: They brought fertile mud to the fields
They filled the pyramids with water
They brought gold from the mountains
54854.e: Every year the Nile flood left behind nutrient-rich mud. On it, farmers could grow rich harvests.
54854.m: The Nile flood brought the Egyptians fertile mud.

54855.q: Why do tarmac and concrete surfaces make floods worse?
54855.e: On sealed ground, rain runs straight off instead of soaking into the soil. So a lot of water reaches streams and rivers all at once.
54855.m: Sealed ground makes rain run off quickly and worsens floods.

54856.q: What measure is used today on many Swiss rivers to reduce the risk of flooding?
a: Cutting down all the trees on the banks
Building houses right on the banks
54856.e: When rivers are restored to a more natural state, they are widened and get floodplains. There, flood water can spread out without flooding settlements.
54856.m: Rivers with more space can take in flood water better.

54857.q: What is a sudden flood after very heavy rain called?
54857.e: In a flash flood, the water rises a lot in a short time. This is especially dangerous in narrow valleys and dried-up stream beds.
54857.m: A flash flood comes suddenly after heavy rain.

54858.q: Which country had floods in 2022 after an extremely strong monsoon, affecting about 33 million people?
54858.e: An extremely strong monsoon caused huge floods in Pakistan in 2022. More than two million people lost their homes.

54859.q: What is a flood retention basin for?
a: It holds back water during floods and releases it slowly
It supplies drinking water to cities
It is used as a swimming pool in summer
54859.e: A retention basin fills up during heavy rain and stores the water for a while. That way the river downstream swells less.
54859.m: Retention basins catch flood water and release it slowly.

54860.q: What is meant by a drought?
a: A long period with far too little rain or snow
A period with especially heavy snow
54860.e: In a drought, much less rain falls than usual for weeks or months. The soil dries out and plants suffer from lack of water.
54860.m: A drought is a long period with far too little rain.

54861.q: Which region on the southern edge of the Sahara suffered severe droughts in the 1970s and 1980s?
54861.e: In the Sahel, far too little rain fell for years. The droughts led to famines in which very many people died.
54861.m: The Sahel was hit by severe droughts in the 1970s and 1980s.

54862.q: What is it called when desert-like areas spread because of drought and overuse?
54862.e: In desertification, soils lose their fertility. The causes are droughts, but also overgrazing and deforestation.
54862.m: Desertification means that desert-like areas are spreading.

54863.q: In the drought summer of 2018, the Swiss Army transported water by helicopter. What for?
a: For indoor swimming pools in cities
54863.e: In 2018 many Alpine pastures had no water left for the livestock. So the army flew water to the animals on the pastures.
54863.m: In the drought summer of 2018, the army brought water to cows on the Alpine pastures.

54864.q: What is the drought and dust storm disaster on the Great Plains of the USA in the 1930s called?
54864.e: Long dry spells and poor farming methods made the topsoil dry out. The wind carried it away in huge dust storms.
54864.m: The Dust Bowl was a drought with dust storms in the USA in the 1930s.

54865.q: What do farmers measure to spot a drought early?
54865.e: Soil moisture shows how much water is available to plants in the ground. If it drops sharply, crop failures threaten.
54865.m: Soil moisture shows whether plants have enough water.

54866.q: What problem does a long drought cause for shipping on the Rhine?
a: Ships can carry less because the water level is low
54866.e: When the water is low, cargo ships have less depth to float in. So they may only take part of their load.
54866.m: When the water is low, Rhine ships can carry less cargo.

54867.q: Which climate phenomenon in the Pacific often leads to droughts in Australia and Indonesia?
54867.e: During El Niño, the eastern Pacific warms up unusually strongly. This shifts the rain areas, and the western Pacific becomes drier.
54867.m: El Niño often brings droughts to Australia and Indonesia.

54868.q: What is the most common natural cause of forest fires?
54868.e: Lightning can set dry wood or grass alight. However, most forest fires are caused by people.
54868.m: Lightning is the most common natural cause of forest fires.

54869.q: Which three things does a fire need to burn?
54869.e: These three conditions are called the fire triangle. If one of them is missing, the fire goes out.
54869.m: A fire needs fuel, oxygen and heat.

54870.q: In which canton are there especially many forest fires, often in winter and spring when the dry north föhn blows?
54870.e: On the south side of the Alps, the north föhn dries out leaves and soil a great deal. That is why the risk of forest fires in Ticino is often already high in winter.
54870.m: In Ticino the risk of forest fires is especially high when the north föhn blows.

54871.q: Why is the risk of forest fires especially high in very hot and dry summers?
a: Grass, leaves and wood have dried out
54871.e: Without rain, plants and soil dry out and burn easily. In the heatwave summer of 2003, for example, large forest fires raged in Valais.
54871.m: Dryness makes forests catch fire easily.

54872.q: In which country did huge bushfires rage during the “Black Summer” of 2019 and 2020?
54872.e: After a long drought, huge areas of bush and forest burnt in Australia. Countless wild animals such as koalas died.
54872.m: In the Black Summer of 2019 and 2020, large parts of Australia burnt.

54873.q: What is a firebreak in a forest for?
a: It is meant to stop a fire spreading
It is used as a playground
54873.e: A firebreak is a strip with no trees or bushes. Because nothing can burn there, the fire is stopped.
54873.m: A firebreak stops a fire because nothing burns there.

54874.q: What role do fires play in some ecosystems?
a: Some plants need fire for their seeds to sprout
Fire makes the soil infertile for ever
54874.e: Some plants, such as certain pines or eucalyptus species, only open their seed capsules in heat. After the fire, the seedlings find plenty of light and ash as fertiliser.
54874.m: Some plants only sprout after a fire.

54875.q: How are forest fires often fought on the steep slopes of the Swiss mountains?
a: With helicopters dropping water from containers
54875.e: Fire engines can hardly reach steep terrain. Helicopters collect water from lakes or rivers and release it precisely over the fire.
54875.m: In the mountains, forest fires are often put out with helicopters.

54876.q: Which type of avalanche causes the most fatal accidents among skiers and ski tourers?
54876.e: In a slab avalanche, a whole layer of snow breaks away at once. It is usually triggered by the victims themselves.
54876.m: Slab avalanches are the most dangerous for winter sports fans.

54877.q: In which town is the WSL Institute for Snow and Avalanche Research SLF located?
54877.e: The SLF in Davos researches snow and avalanches. In winter it publishes the daily avalanche bulletin for Switzerland.
54877.m: Switzerland's avalanche bulletin comes from the SLF in Davos.

54878.q: How many levels does the European avalanche danger scale have?
54878.e: The scale goes from level 1 (low) to level 5 (very high). Many accidents already happen at level 3 (considerable).
54878.m: The avalanche danger scale has five levels.

54879.q: Roughly from what slope angle can slab avalanches be triggered?
54879.e: Most slab avalanches release on slopes of about 30 degrees or steeper. The steeper the slope, the greater the danger.
54879.m: From about 30 degrees of slope, avalanches become a danger.

54880.q: Which device helps find people buried by an avalanche quickly?
54880.e: An avalanche transceiver sends a radio signal that other devices can locate. A shovel and a probe are also part of the emergency kit.
54880.m: An avalanche transceiver helps locate buried people quickly.

54881.q: Within what time should people buried by an avalanche ideally be freed so that their chance of survival is high?
54881.e: Most buried people survive the first few minutes. After that, the chance of survival drops quickly, mainly because of lack of oxygen.
54881.m: For avalanche victims every minute counts, especially the first 15.

54882.q: What happened in the avalanche winter of 1999 in the Alps?
a: Many avalanches buried houses and roads
54882.e: In February 1999 an extreme amount of snow fell in a short time. People died in Galtür in Austria and in Evolène in Valais.
54882.m: The avalanche winter of 1999 claimed many victims in the Alps.

54883.q: What naturally protects many mountain villages in Switzerland from avalanches?
54883.e: The trees hold the snow in place on the slope and slow down small avalanches. That is why protection forests are specially protected in Switzerland.
54883.m: Protection forests hold the snow in place and protect villages from avalanches.

54884.q: What most often triggers a landslide?
54884.e: Rainwater soaks the ground and makes it heavy and slippery. As a result, the slope loses its grip.
54884.m: Heavy rain is the most common trigger of landslides.

54885.q: Which village in the canton of Schwyz was buried by a huge rockslide in 1806?
54885.e: On 2 September 1806, a huge mass of rock broke away from the Rossberg. It buried Goldau and several hamlets, and almost 500 people died.
54885.m: The Goldau rockslide of 1806 was one of the worst natural disasters in Switzerland.

54886.q: Which village in the Bregaglia was hit by debris flows in 2017 after a rockslide on Piz Cengalo?
54886.e: In 2017 about three million cubic metres of rock fell from Piz Cengalo. The debris flows that followed reached the village of Bondo in the Grisons.
54886.m: Bondo was hit by debris flows after a rockslide in 2017.

a: A fast stream of water, mud and rock
A hiking trail in the mountains
54887.e: A debris flow pours like a thick sludge down stream beds into the valley. In Switzerland it is also called a “Rüfe”.
54887.m: A debris flow is a stream of water, mud and stones.

54888.q: Which village in the Lötschental in Valais was mostly buried by a glacier collapse in May 2025?
