55194.m: There is sticky rice in the mortar of the Great Wall of China.

55195.q: Roughly how high is the Great Wall of China near Beijing?
55195.e: At well-known sections near Beijing, the wall is almost 8 metres high. That is about as high as a house with two or three storeys.
55195.m: Near Beijing, the Great Wall of China is about 7 to 8 metres high.

55196.q: Is the Great Wall of China well preserved everywhere today?
a: Yes, it is like new everywhere
Yes, because it is made of metal
55196.e: Wind, rain and people have damaged many sections. Only some parts have been restored for visitors.
55196.m: Many parts of the Great Wall of China have crumbled today.

55197.q: Is the Great Wall of China one single, continuous wall?
a: No, it has many separate sections
Yes, it is one big circle
55197.e: The wall is made up of many sections from different times. Some run side by side, and in other places there are gaps.
55197.m: The Great Wall of China is made up of many separate sections.

55199.q: What lies at the feet of the Statue of Liberty?
55199.e: The broken chains show that the people are free. You can only see them well from above.
55199.m: Broken chains lie at the feet of the Statue of Liberty.

55200.q: Roughly how tall is the Statue of Liberty including its base?
a: As tall as a high-rise building
As tall as a garden shed
55200.e: Including the base, the Statue of Liberty is about 93 metres tall. That is as tall as a high-rise building.
55200.m: The Statue of Liberty is as tall as a high-rise building.

55201.q: Who does the Statue of Liberty represent?
55201.e: The figure shows Libertas, the goddess of freedom from ancient Rome. That is why it is called the Statue of Liberty.
55201.m: The Statue of Liberty represents a goddess of freedom.

55202.q: How did the Statue of Liberty get across the ocean to America?
a: In one piece on a ship
In one piece on lots of rowing boats
55202.e: In 1885 the statue was taken apart into about 350 pieces and shipped in more than 200 crates. In America it was put back together.
55202.m: The Statue of Liberty came to America in pieces by ship.

55203.q: What is there in the crown of the Statue of Liberty?
55203.e: There are small windows in the crown. From there, visitors have a wide view over the harbour.
55203.m: There are windows in the crown of the Statue of Liberty.

55204.q: Who did the Statue of Liberty greet first in the past?
55204.e: Many people came to America by ship to start a new life there. For them, the statue was the first sign of their new home.
55204.m: In the past, the Statue of Liberty greeted many immigrants.

55205.q: In which city does a smaller copy of the Statue of Liberty stand on an island in a river?
55205.e: A copy about 11 metres tall stands on a narrow island in the River Seine. It looks towards the big statue in America.
55205.m: A small copy of the Statue of Liberty stands in Paris.

55206.q: What shape is the big roof in the middle of the Taj Mahal?
55206.e: A large white dome rises above the main building. It looks a little like an onion.
55206.m: The Taj Mahal has a large dome in the middle.

55207.q: Roughly how many years ago was the Taj Mahal built?
55207.e: Building began around 1632 and took about 20 years. That is almost 400 years ago now.
55207.m: The Taj Mahal is almost 400 years old.

55208.q: What lies in the garden in front of the Taj Mahal?
55208.e: There is a long pool of water in the garden. The building is reflected in it like in a mirror.
55208.m: A long pool of water lies in front of the Taj Mahal.

55209.q: What was set into the white stone of the Taj Mahal?
55209.e: Craftsmen set coloured gemstones into the stone. This created delicate flower patterns.
55209.m: Colourful gemstones are set into the stone of the Taj Mahal.

55210.q: Roughly how many craftsmen worked on building the Taj Mahal?
55210.e: About 20,000 craftsmen from many countries worked on it. Among them were stonemasons, painters and scribes.
55210.m: About 20,000 craftsmen worked on the Taj Mahal.

55211.q: Which animals helped carry heavy loads when the Taj Mahal was built?
55211.e: Elephants and oxen pulled carts with stones and building materials. Without lorries, strong animals were very important.
55211.m: Elephants carried heavy loads when the Taj Mahal was built.

55212.q: What colour is the great tomb, the Taj Mahal?
55212.e: The Taj Mahal is built of white marble. That is why it shines brightly in the sun.

55213.q: What is special about the shape of the Taj Mahal?
a: It is round like a ball
55213.e: The Taj Mahal is built symmetrically. The left and right halves look almost exactly the same.
55213.m: The Taj Mahal is built the same on both sides.

55214.q: What colour is the mosque that stands next to the Taj Mahal?
55214.e: The mosque is built of red sandstone. This makes the pale main building in the middle stand out especially well.
55214.m: The mosque next to the Taj Mahal is red.

55215.q: What kind of landscape is Petra in?
55215.e: Petra lies between bare rocky mountains in a desert-like area. It rarely rains there.
55215.m: Petra lies in a dry, mountainous landscape.

55217.q: Which building for spectators was carved out of the rock in Petra?
55217.e: The rows of seats of the theatre were carved into a rocky slope. Several thousand people could fit there.
55217.m: There is a theatre carved from rock in Petra.

55218.q: How did the people of Petra get water in that dry area?
a: From a large lake in the city
55218.e: The people led rainwater through channels and canals into large stores. That way they had water all year round.
55218.m: The people of Petra collected rainwater in stores.

55219.q: What does the name Petra mean in Greek?
55219.e: The Greek word ‘petra’ means rock or stone. The name suits the city made of rock.

55220.q: What were many of the magnificent rock façades in Petra?
55220.e: Behind many façades there are burial chambers. Important families were buried there.
55220.m: Many rock façades in Petra are tombs.

55221.q: What did the people of Petra trade in, among other things?
55221.e: Petra lay on important trade routes for caravans. Precious incense and spices from Arabia made the city rich.
55221.m: Petra became rich through trading incense and spices.

55222.q: Roughly how old are the rock buildings of Petra?
55222.e: Most of the big buildings were made about 2000 years ago. At that time the city flourished through trade.
55222.m: The rock buildings of Petra are about 2000 years old.

55223.q: In which country does the statue of Christ the Redeemer stand?
55223.e: The statue is the best-known landmark of Brazil. People there speak Portuguese.
55223.m: Christ the Redeemer stands in Brazil.

55224.q: What strikes the statue of Christ the Redeemer several times every year?
55224.e: Because the statue stands high up on a mountain, lightning often strikes it during thunderstorms. A lightning conductor protects it.
55224.m: The statue of Christ is often struck by lightning.

55225.q: What happens to the statue of Christ the Redeemer at night?
a: It is lit up with floodlights
It is moved into a tower
55225.e: Floodlights light up the statue at night. That way you can see it from far away even in the dark.
55225.m: At night the statue of Christ is lit up.

55226.q: What does the statue of Christ in Rio do with its arms?
a: It folds them across its chest
55226.e: The statue spreads its arms wide, as if it wanted to hug the whole city. It was designed by the French sculptor Paul Landowski.
55226.m: The statue of Christ in Rio spreads its arms wide.

55227.q: What is the statue of Christ the Redeemer made of on the inside?
55227.e: Inside, the statue is built of reinforced concrete. This material is very strong and stands up to wind and weather.
55227.m: The statue of Christ is made of reinforced concrete inside.

55228.q: How far does the statue of Christ the Redeemer measure from one hand to the other?
55228.e: From fingertip to fingertip the statue measures about 28 metres. That is almost as wide as it is tall.
55228.m: From hand to hand the statue of Christ measures about 28 metres.

55229.q: What grows on the mountain around the statue of Christ the Redeemer?
55229.e: The mountain lies in Tijuca National Park. One of the largest city forests in the world grows there.
55229.m: A rainforest grows around the statue of Christ.

55230.q: Roughly how heavy is the statue of Christ the Redeemer?
55230.e: The statue weighs about 635 tonnes. That is as heavy as about 100 elephants.
55230.m: The statue of Christ weighs over 600 tonnes.

55231.q: Where does the Sydney Opera House stand?
a: At the harbour, right by the water
In the middle of the desert
55231.e: The Opera House stands on a headland in the harbour. It is surrounded by water on three sides.
55231.m: The Sydney Opera House stands right by the water.

55232.q: Roughly how long did it take to build the Sydney Opera House?
55232.e: Building began in 1959 and took about 14 years. The curved roofs were difficult to build.
55232.m: Building the Sydney Opera House took about 14 years.

55233.q: How much did building the Sydney Opera House cost compared with the plan?
55233.e: About 7 million dollars was planned, but in the end it cost over 100 million. That was about fourteen times more.
55233.m: The Sydney Opera House cost much more than planned.

55234.q: Who officially opened the Sydney Opera House?
55234.e: Queen Elizabeth II opened the Opera House on 20 October 1973. She was also Queen of Australia.
55234.m: Queen Elizabeth II opened the Sydney Opera House.

55235.q: What colour are the roofs of the Sydney Opera House?
55235.e: The curved roofs are covered with more than a million white tiles. They shine brightly in the sun.
55235.m: The Sydney Opera House has white roofs.

55236.q: Which huge musical instrument stands in the main concert hall of the Sydney Opera House?
55236.e: The organ has more than 10,000 pipes. It is one of the largest of its kind in the world.
55236.m: A huge organ stands in the Opera House’s concert hall.

55237.q: What happens to the roofs of the Opera House during Sydney’s yearly light festival?
a: Colourful pictures are projected onto them
55237.e: During the festival ‘Vivid Sydney’, colourful pictures and patterns are projected onto the white roofs. Lots of people watch at night.
55237.m: During the light festival, the Opera House roofs glow in colour.

55238.q: What can visitors see at the Sydney Opera House on New Year’s Eve?
55238.e: On New Year’s Eve there is a huge firework display over the harbour. In Sydney it is summer then.
55238.m: On New Year’s Eve there is a big firework display at the Sydney Opera House.

55239.q: Roughly how long is the Golden Gate Bridge?
55239.e: Including all its approaches, the bridge is about 2.7 kilometres long. Walking across takes about half an hour.
55239.m: The Golden Gate Bridge is about 2.7 kilometres long.

55240.q: How many tall towers does the Golden Gate Bridge have?
55240.e: The bridge has two tall towers. The thick main cables, from which the road hangs, run over them.
55240.m: The Golden Gate Bridge has two tall towers.

55241.q: How high do the towers of the Golden Gate Bridge rise above the water?
55241.e: The towers are about 227 metres above the water. That is taller than any building in Switzerland.
55241.m: The towers of the Golden Gate Bridge are about 230 metres high.

55243.q: What do workers on the Golden Gate Bridge do again and again?
55243.e: Salty sea air makes steel rust. That is why painters are constantly touching up the paint.
55243.m: The Golden Gate Bridge is repainted again and again.

55244.q: What record did the Golden Gate Bridge hold when it opened?
a: Longest suspension bridge in the world
55244.e: Between its towers it was longer than any other suspension bridge at that time. Today there are longer ones.
55244.m: When it opened, the Golden Gate Bridge was the longest suspension bridge in the world.

55245.q: What are the thick main cables of the Golden Gate Bridge made of?
55245.e: Each main cable is made of more than 27,000 thin steel wires. Together they are very strong.
55245.m: The main cables of the Golden Gate Bridge are made of lots of steel wires.

55246.q: Who is allowed to cross the Golden Gate Bridge?
55246.e: Lots of cars drive across the bridge. Next to the road there are paths for pedestrians and bikes.
55246.m: Cars and bikes cross the Golden Gate Bridge, and people walk across it too.

55247.q: In which country is the Leaning Tower of Pisa?
55247.e: Pisa is a city in Tuscany. The tower is one of the country’s best-known buildings.
55247.m: The Leaning Tower of Pisa is in Italy.

55248.q: How long did it take to build the Leaning Tower of Pisa?
55248.e: Building began in 1173 and was stopped several times for long periods. The tower was only finished about 200 years later.
55248.m: The Tower of Pisa took about 200 years to build.

55249.q: When did the Tower of Pisa start to lean?
a: While it was still being built
55249.e: The lean was noticed after the first few storeys. The builders tried to make up for it by building the upper storeys slightly slanted.
55249.m: The Tower of Pisa was already leaning while it was being built.

55250.q: Which famous scientist from Pisa is said to have dropped balls from the Leaning Tower?
55250.e: Galileo Galilei was born in Pisa in 1564. He is said to have studied from the tower how objects fall, but it is not certain that this really happened.
55250.m: Galileo Galilei is said to have done falling experiments at the Tower of Pisa.

55251.q: Are you allowed to climb the Leaning Tower of Pisa?
a: Yes, but only with a ladder
55251.e: Visitors climb a staircase with almost 300 steps to the top. Because of the lean, walking feels a bit strange.
55251.m: You can climb the Leaning Tower of Pisa by a staircase.

55252.q: What stone is the Leaning Tower of Pisa built of?
55252.e: The tower is faced with pale marble. That is why it shines white in the sun.
55252.m: The Leaning Tower of Pisa is made of white marble.

55253.q: What was the Leaning Tower of Pisa built for?
a: As a bell tower for the cathedral
As a watchtower in the city wall
55253.e: The Leaning Tower is the bell tower of Pisa Cathedral. The bells hang on the top floor.
55253.m: The Leaning Tower of Pisa is a bell tower.

55254.q: Roughly how far does the top of the Leaning Tower of Pisa hang to one side?
55254.e: Today the top is just under 4 metres to the side of the base. Before the tower was made safe, it was a little more.
55254.m: The top of the Tower of Pisa hangs about 4 metres to one side.

55255.q: Which famous fairy-tale castle was Neuschwanstein a model for?
55255.e: Walt Disney was inspired by Neuschwanstein. His Sleeping Beauty Castle in the theme park looks similar.
55255.m: Neuschwanstein was a model for Sleeping Beauty Castle at Disneyland.

55256.q: In which German state is Neuschwanstein Castle?
55256.e: The castle is in Bavaria, near the town of Füssen. The king had it built in his home region.

55257.q: Which animal is hidden in the name Neuschwanstein?
55257.e: ‘Schwan’ is German for swan, and the king loved swans. In the castle you find many swans in pictures and decorations.
55257.m: The swan is hidden in the name Neuschwanstein.

55258.q: In which year did building start on Neuschwanstein Castle?
55258.e: The foundation stone was laid in 1869. The castle looks like a castle from the Middle Ages, but it is much younger.

55261.q: Roughly how many people visit Neuschwanstein Castle every year?
55261.e: Every year well over a million visitors come from all over the world. It is one of the most popular sights in Europe.
55261.m: Over a million people visit Neuschwanstein every year.

55262.q: What was very modern for its time in Neuschwanstein Castle?
55262.e: The castle had modern technology for its time. There was warm-air heating, running water and flushing toilets. Moats and dungeons belong to old knights’ castles.
55262.m: Neuschwanstein already had modern technology such as heating.

55263.q: Which king had Neuschwanstein Castle built?
55263.e: King Ludwig II of Bavaria loved fairy tales and legends. Shortly after his death in 1886, the castle was opened to visitors.

55264.q: In which country is the Burj Khalifa?
55264.e: The tower stands in a country made up of seven emirates on the Arabian Peninsula. It is named after that country’s president at the time.
55264.m: The Burj Khalifa is in the United Arab Emirates.

55265.q: What was a model for the shape of the Burj Khalifa?
55265.e: The architects were inspired by a flower from the desert. The floor plan is reminiscent of its petals.
55265.m: A desert flower was a model for the Burj Khalifa.

55266.q: What is the outer wall of the Burj Khalifa mainly made of?
55266.e: The façade is made of thousands of glass panels and metal parts. They reflect the sunlight and protect against the great heat.
55266.m: The Burj Khalifa has an outer wall of glass and metal.

55267.q: Roughly how long does it take to clean all the windows of the Burj Khalifa once?
55267.e: Window cleaners work with machines that hang on the façade. To do all the windows they need about three to four months.
55267.m: Cleaning all the windows of the Burj Khalifa takes several months.

55268.q: What is at the very top of the Burj Khalifa?
55268.e: The top part is a slender steel spire. It makes the building much taller still.
55268.m: At the very top of the Burj Khalifa is a steel spire.

55269.q: What is there in the Burj Khalifa?
55269.e: In the tower there are flats, offices, a hotel and restaurants. High up there are viewing platforms.
55269.m: There are flats, offices and a hotel in the Burj Khalifa.

55270.q: Roughly how long did it take to build the Burj Khalifa?
55270.e: Construction began in 2004. The tower opened at the beginning of 2010.
55270.m: Building the Burj Khalifa took about six years.

55271.q: What does the Arabic word ‘Burj’ mean?
55271.e: ‘Burj’ is the Arabic word for tower. The second part of the name honours a ruler.

55272.q: At what time of day do especially many visitors come to the temple of Angkor Wat?
55272.e: Early in the morning the sun rises behind the towers. The temple is then reflected in the water in front of it.
55272.m: Many visitors watch the sunrise at Angkor Wat.

55273.q: What stone is Angkor Wat mainly built of?
55273.e: The builders used large blocks of sandstone. Fine pictures could be carved into this stone.
55273.m: Angkor Wat is mainly built of sandstone.

55274.q: Which figures are very often carved into the walls of Angkor Wat?
55274.e: On the walls you can see more than 1700 female figures. They are goddesses and heavenly dancers called apsaras.
55274.m: Many goddesses and dancers can be seen on the walls of Angkor Wat.

55275.q: What does the name Angkor Wat roughly mean?
55275.e: ‘Angkor’ comes from a word for city, and ‘Wat’ means temple. Together it means something like temple city.
55275.m: Angkor Wat roughly means temple city.

55276.q: Roughly how tall is the central tower of Angkor Wat?
55276.e: The central tower rises about 65 metres above the ground. It is the highest point of the complex.
55276.m: The central tower of Angkor Wat is about 65 metres tall.

55277.q: What lies all around the temple complex of Angkor Wat?
55277.e: A moat full of water, about 190 metres wide, surrounds the whole complex. A stone causeway leads to the temple.
55277.m: A wide moat surrounds Angkor Wat.

55278.q: Which animals can often be seen climbing around the temples of Angkor?
55278.e: Lots of macaques live in the forests around the temples. These monkeys love climbing on the old walls.
55278.m: Many monkeys live at the temples of Angkor.

55279.q: On which continent is Angkor Wat?
55279.e: Angkor Wat is in Southeast Asia. It is warm there all year round.

55280.q: What was the Colosseum voted in 2007?
a: One of the New Seven Wonders of the World
The most beautiful railway station in the world
The largest museum in the world
55280.e: In a worldwide vote, the Colosseum was chosen as one of the New Seven Wonders of the World. Millions of people had voted.
55280.m: The Colosseum is one of the New Seven Wonders of the World.

55281.q: Why is part of the outer wall of the Colosseum missing today?
a: Because of earthquakes and stone theft
55281.e: Earthquakes made parts of the wall collapse. Later, people took the stones to build other buildings.
55281.m: Earthquakes and stone theft damaged the Colosseum.

55282.q: Why did the Colosseum have so many entrances all the way round?
a: So that the many spectators could get in and out quickly
So that the wind could cool the arena
So that every gladiator had his own door
So that it could be guarded from all sides
55282.e: The Colosseum held tens of thousands of people. Through its 80 arched entrances they got in and out quickly.
55282.m: The Colosseum had many entrances for its many spectators.

55283.q: What was the Colosseum mainly used for in ancient Rome?
55283.e: In the Colosseum, up to 50,000 spectators watched gladiator fights and animal hunts. The outer wall is made of pale limestone called travertine.

55284.q: What does the Pope traditionally hold at the Colosseum on Good Friday?
55284.e: On the evening of Good Friday, the Stations of the Cross are prayed at the Colosseum, usually with the Pope. They remember the suffering of Jesus on his way to the cross.
55284.m: On Good Friday the Pope prays the Stations of the Cross at the Colosseum.

55285.q: Who sat at the very top of the stands in the Colosseum?
55285.e: The important people sat at the bottom, close to the arena. The poorer people sat right at the top.
55285.m: In the Colosseum, the poorer people sat right at the top.

55286.q: Where does the Colosseum probably get its name from?
55286.e: Next to the building stood a huge statue, a ‘colossus’ of the emperor Nero. The Colosseum probably got its name from it.
55286.m: The Colosseum is probably named after a huge statue.

55287.q: What was the floor of the arena in the Colosseum covered with?
55287.e: The Latin word ‘arena’ means sand. The sand was meant to stop the fighters slipping.
55287.m: The floor of the Colosseum was covered with sand.

55289.q: Which country in Africa is known for especially fine cotton?
55289.e: Along the Nile in Egypt, cotton grows with especially long, fine fibres. Very soft fabrics are made from it.
55289.m: Egypt is known for fine cotton.

55290.q: Where are the soft fibres of the cotton plant found?
55290.e: The fruit of the cotton plant is a boll. When it is ripe, it bursts open and the white fluffy fibres puff out.
55290.m: Cotton fibres are found in a boll.

55293.q: What is made from cotton for the first aid kit?
55293.e: Cotton wool is usually made of soft cotton fibres. It is used, for example, to clean small wounds.
55293.m: Cotton wool is usually made from cotton.

55294.q: What is the thread called that is spun from cotton fibres?
55294.e: The short fibres are spun into a long thread. This thread is called yarn.
55294.m: Yarn is spun from cotton fibres.

55295.q: What can be obtained from cotton seeds?
55295.e: Cotton seeds contain oil. It is pressed out and used, for example, for cooking.
55295.m: Oil is obtained from cotton seeds.

55296.q: What kind of fibre is cotton?
55296.e: Cotton comes from nature, namely from a plant. That is why it is a natural fibre.

55297.q: How many coffee beans are usually inside a coffee cherry?
55297.e: There are usually two beans in a coffee cherry. They lie with their flat sides against each other.
55297.m: There are usually two beans in a coffee cherry.

55298.q: What colour is a ripe coffee cherry usually?
55298.e: At first, coffee cherries are green. When they are ripe, they usually turn bright red.
55298.m: Ripe coffee cherries are usually red.

55299.q: Which country in Asia harvests a lot of coffee?
55299.e: Vietnam is one of the biggest coffee producers in the world. Mostly robusta beans grow there.
55299.m: Vietnam harvests a lot of coffee.

55300.e: Coffee needs warmth and rain. It grows in tropical countries around the equator.
55300.m: Coffee grows in warm, tropical countries.

55301.q: How do the green coffee beans turn brown?
55301.e: Fresh coffee beans are greenish. Only when they are roasted at great heat do they turn brown and smell good.
55301.m: Coffee beans turn brown when they are roasted.

55302.q: What is a large farm where coffee is grown called?
55302.e: On a coffee plantation there are lots of coffee bushes in long rows.

55303.q: What is a coffee bean really?
55303.e: The coffee bean is the seed inside the fruit of the coffee bush. It is not related to real beans such as garden beans.
55303.m: A coffee bean is a seed.

55304.q: Which of these is a well-known type of coffee?
55304.e: The two most important types of coffee are called arabica and robusta. Darjeeling, Assam and rooibos, on the other hand, are types of tea.
55304.m: Arabica is a well-known type of coffee.

55305.q: How are coffee cherries often harvested?
55305.e: Coffee cherries do not all ripen at the same time. That is why workers often pick them by hand.
55305.m: Coffee cherries are often picked by hand.

55309.q: Which country is one of the biggest rice growers in the world?
55309.e: China grows a lot of rice, and so does India. Rice does not grow in cold countries like Iceland.
55309.m: China is one of the biggest rice growers.

55310.q: Which dish from Japan is made from rice and fish?
55310.e: For sushi, sticky rice is combined with fish or vegetables. It comes from Japan.
55310.m: Sushi is a rice dish from Japan.

55312.q: Which rice dish comes from Italy and Ticino?
55312.e: Risotto is a creamy rice dish from northern Italy. People in Ticino love eating it too.
55312.m: Risotto is a rice dish from Italy.

55313.q: What do people in China often use to eat rice?
55313.e: In China, Japan and other Asian countries, people often eat rice with two chopsticks.
55313.m: In China people often eat rice with chopsticks.

55314.q: Which animal often helps with work in the rice fields in Asia?
55314.e: Water buffalo like wet ground. In many parts of Asia they pull the plough through the rice fields.
55314.m: Water buffalo help in the rice fields in Asia.

55315.q: What did crude oil form from millions of years ago?
55315.e: Tiny creatures in the sea sank to the bottom when they died. Over millions of years, pressure and heat turned them into crude oil.
55315.m: Crude oil formed from tiny sea creatures.

55316.q: What colour is crude oil usually?
55316.e: Crude oil is a thick liquid. It is usually dark brown to black.

55317.q: Which raw material is petrol made from?
55317.e: Petrol for cars is made from crude oil. To do this, the oil is separated in a factory.
55317.m: Petrol is made from crude oil.

55318.q: What is the platform called that is used to drill for oil at sea?
55318.e: An oil rig stands in the middle of the sea. From there, people drill deep into the seabed to extract oil.
55318.m: At sea, people drill for oil with an oil rig.

55319.q: What is a large ship that carries crude oil called?
55319.e: Oil tankers are huge ships with large tanks. They carry crude oil across the seas.
55319.m: Oil tankers carry crude oil across the sea.

55320.q: What is a long pipe that crude oil flows through called?
55320.e: Crude oil is pumped over long distances through a pipeline. Some pipelines are thousands of kilometres long.
55320.m: A pipeline carries crude oil through a pipe.

55321.q: What is often made from crude oil?
55321.e: Crude oil is used to make not only fuel but also plastic. That is why many plastic things are made from oil.
55321.m: Plastic is often made from crude oil.

55322.q: What is the factory called where crude oil is processed?
55322.e: In a refinery, crude oil is heated and separated into many different substances.
55322.m: Crude oil is processed in a refinery.

55323.q: Which country is known for its large oil reserves?
55323.e: There is a great deal of oil under the desert of Saudi Arabia. The country sells oil all over the world.
55323.m: Saudi Arabia has a lot of oil.

55324.q: What is it called when you get gold out of river sand?
55324.e: You swirl sand and water in a pan. The heavy gold stays at the bottom. This is called panning for gold.
55324.m: When panning for gold, you get gold out of sand.

55325.q: In which area of Switzerland can you pan for gold?
55325.e: In the streams around the Napf, between Bern and Lucerne, you can find tiny grains of gold.
55325.m: You can pan for gold in the Napf area.

55326.q: What happens to gold if it is left in the air for a long time?
55326.e: Gold hardly reacts with air and water. That is why it does not rust and stays nice and shiny.

55327.q: Which place do you get a gold medal for?
55327.e: In competitions there is gold for winning, silver for second place and bronze for third place.
55327.m: A gold medal is for first place.

55328.q: What is a cast block of gold called?
55328.e: Gold is often cast into rectangular blocks. These blocks are called gold bars.
55328.m: A block of gold is called a gold bar.

55329.q: What is gold often used for?
55329.e: Gold shines beautifully and is very valuable. That is why rings, necklaces and other jewellery are made from it.
55329.m: Gold is often made into jewellery.

55330.q: What is a place where gold is dug out of the ground called?
55330.e: In a gold mine, people dig deep into the earth to get out rock that contains gold.
55330.m: Gold is mined in a gold mine.

55331.q: Where was there a famous gold rush from 1848?
55331.e: In 1848 gold was found in California. Afterwards hundreds of thousands of people rushed there to get rich. Alaska and South Africa only had gold rushes decades later.
55331.m: From 1848 there was a gold rush in California.

55332.q: Which natural substance is the hardest?
55332.e: Diamond is the hardest natural material. It can scratch almost anything.
55332.m: Diamond is the hardest natural substance.

55333.q: What substance is a diamond made of?
55333.e: A diamond is made only of carbon. The lead in a pencil, graphite, is also made of carbon.
55333.m: A diamond is made of carbon.

55334.e: Diamonds form deep inside the earth. There is enormous pressure and great heat there.
55334.m: Diamonds form deep inside the earth.

55335.q: What do you do to a diamond to make it sparkle?
55335.e: A rough diamond looks plain. Only when lots of small faces are cut into it does it sparkle in the light.
55335.m: A diamond only sparkles once it has been cut.

55336.q: What is a round-cut diamond with many faces called?
55336.e: A brilliant is a diamond with a special round cut. It has many small faces and glitters a lot.
55336.m: A diamond with a special cut is called a brilliant.

55337.q: Which unit is used to measure the weight of diamonds?
55337.e: Gemstones are weighed in carats. One carat is 0.2 grams.

55338.q: In which African country are especially many diamonds found?
55338.e: Botswana in southern Africa has some of the richest diamond mines in the world.

55339.q: Which piece of jewellery with a diamond is often given for an engagement?
55339.e: When two people get engaged, they promise to marry each other. Often a ring with a sparkling diamond is given.
55339.m: A diamond ring is often given for an engagement.

55340.q: How is salt obtained from the sea?
a: The water is left to evaporate
The water is filtered through sand
55340.e: Seawater is led into shallow pools. The sun makes the water evaporate and the salt is left behind.
55340.m: Sea salt is made when seawater evaporates.

55341.q: What is salt that is taken from a mine called?
55341.e: Under the ground there are old layers of salt from ancient seas. The salt from them is called rock salt.
55341.m: Salt from a mine is called rock salt.

55342.q: In which place in Vaud can you visit a salt mine?
55342.e: Salt has been produced in Bex for centuries. Visitors can ride into the mine on a little train.
55342.m: You can visit a salt mine in Bex.

55343.q: Why is salt spread on the roads in winter?
55343.e: Salt makes ice and snow melt even below zero degrees. That makes the road less slippery.
55343.m: Salt on the road makes the ice melt.

55344.q: Why did people salt meat and fish in the past?
a: To keep it for a long time
55344.e: In the past there were no fridges. Salt was used to preserve meat and fish.

55345.q: What was salt called in the past because it was so valuable?
55345.e: In the past, salt was rare and expensive. That is why it was called ‘white gold’.
55345.m: Salt used to be called white gold.

55346.q: What shape are salt crystals under a magnifying glass?
55346.e: Table salt forms small crystals in the shape of cubes. You can see them well with a magnifying glass.
55346.m: Salt crystals are shaped like cubes.

55347.q: What happens when you bathe in the very salty Dead Sea?
a: You sink straight to the bottom
You have to swim very fast
55347.e: The water in the Dead Sea contains a huge amount of salt. It holds the body up so well that you float almost like a cork.
55347.m: In the Dead Sea you float on the surface.

55348.e: Wood is the hard part of trees and bushes. It is taken from the trunks.

55349.q: What do the growth rings in a tree trunk show?
55349.e: Every year a new ring grows in the trunk. If you count the rings, you know how old the tree is.
55349.m: The growth rings show the age of a tree.

55350.e: Wood is broken down into fine fibres. Paper and cardboard are made from this pulp.

55351.q: Roughly how much of Switzerland is covered with forest?
55351.e: About a third of Switzerland’s area is forest. Most of it is in the Jura, the Prealps and the Alps.
55351.m: About a third of Switzerland is forest.

55352.q: Which tree is the most common in Swiss forests?
55352.e: The spruce is the most common tree in Swiss forests. Its wood is often used for building.
55352.m: The spruce is the most common tree in Switzerland.

55353.q: What is the job called in Switzerland where people look after and fell trees in the forest?
55353.e: Forestry workers work in the forest. They fell trees, plant new ones and look after the forest.
55353.m: A forestry worker looks after and fells trees in the forest.

55354.q: Where are tree trunks sawn into planks?
55354.e: At the sawmill, big saws cut the trunks into planks and beams.
55354.m: Tree trunks are turned into planks at the sawmill.

55355.q: Which very light wood is used for model aeroplanes?
55355.e: Balsa wood comes from a tree from South America. It is very light and easy to cut.

55356.q: Why is wood called a renewable raw material?
a: Because it comes from the sea
Because it is made in a laboratory
55356.e: When trees are felled, new trees can grow in their place. So wood does not run out if the forest is looked after well.
55356.m: Wood is a renewable raw material.

55357.q: What do fishermen at sea use to catch lots of fish at once?
55357.e: Fishermen cast out big nets. Lots of fish get caught in them at once.
55357.m: Fishermen catch lots of fish with a net.

55358.q: What is a smaller fishing boat on the coast called?
55358.e: A trawler is a smaller, sturdy boat. Fishermen use it to go out to sea near the coast.
55358.m: A trawler is a fishing boat.

55359.q: What do you put on the hook when fishing to attract the fish?
55359.e: Bait can be, for example, a worm or a shiny piece of metal. The fish bites and gets caught on the hook.
55359.m: When fishing, bait attracts the fish.

55360.q: What is it called when fish are raised in tanks?
55360.e: In fish farming, fish grow up in tanks or net pens. That way they do not have to be caught in the sea.
55360.m: In fish farming, fish are raised.

55361.q: Which country produces especially large amounts of farmed salmon?
55361.e: Along the coast of Norway, huge numbers of salmon are farmed in large net pens.
55361.m: Norway farms a lot of salmon.

55362.q: Which large sea fish often comes in tins in the shops?
55362.e: Tuna lives in the open sea. It is often cooked and sold in tins.

55363.q: What do you usually need in Switzerland to fish at a lake?
55363.e: Anyone who wants to fish in most Swiss waters needs permission. This is called a fishing licence.
55363.m: To fish, you usually need a fishing licence.

55364.q: Where do many farmers in Switzerland take their cows in summer?
a: To the barn by the lake
55364.e: In summer, fresh grass grows on the alpine pastures in the mountains. That is why many cows move up to the alp for the summer.
55364.m: In summer many cows go up to the alp.

55365.q: What are cattle herders in Argentina called?
55365.e: In Argentina there are huge pastures with lots of cattle. The riders who herd them are called gauchos.
55365.m: Cattle herders in Argentina are called gauchos.

55366.q: In which country are there more sheep than people?
55366.e: In 2024 just over 5 million people lived in New Zealand, but about 23 million sheep.
55366.m: In New Zealand there are more sheep than people.

55367.q: What do sheep provide apart from milk and meat?
55367.e: Sheep are shorn once or twice a year. Wool is obtained from their fleece.

55368.q: Which animal is kept in the desert for carrying loads and for its milk?
55368.e: Camels can go a long time without water. They carry loads through the desert and give milk.
55368.m: Camels are kept in the desert.

55369.q: What is the man called who looks after the cows on the alp in summer and makes cheese?
55369.e: The alpine dairyman lives on the alp in summer. He milks the cows and makes cheese from the milk.
55369.m: The alpine dairyman looks after the cows on the alp.

55371.q: Which spice is the most expensive in the world?
55371.e: For saffron, tiny threads are picked by hand from crocus flowers. Because this is so much work, saffron is very expensive.
55371.m: Saffron is the most expensive spice in the world.

55372.q: Which spice is often grated over mashed potato?
55372.e: Nutmeg is the seed of a tropical tree. It is grated finely over mashed potato or sauces.
55372.m: Nutmeg goes well with mashed potato.

55373.q: Which plant family does vanilla belong to?
55373.e: Vanilla is the fruit of a climbing plant from the orchid family. The pod is dried for a long time.
55373.m: Vanilla is the fruit of an orchid.

55374.q: Which country harvests the most vanilla?
55374.e: The island of Madagascar off Africa is the biggest vanilla producer in the world (as of 2023).

55376.e: Cloves are the buds of a tree. They are picked before the flowers open and are then dried.

55377.e: Peppercorns grow as small fruits on a climbing plant. When dried, they turn black and wrinkly.
55377.m: A peppercorn is a dried fruit.

55378.q: Which group of plants does sugar cane belong to?
55378.e: Sugar cane is a very tall grass. Its thick stalks are full of sweet juice.

55379.q: Which country grows the most sugar cane?
55379.e: Brazil is the biggest sugar cane producer in the world. It is warm and wet enough there.
55379.m: Brazil grows the most sugar cane.

55380.q: Which plant is sugar made from in Switzerland?
55380.e: Sugar cane does not grow here because it is too cold. In Switzerland, sugar is made from sugar beet.
55380.m: In Switzerland sugar is made from sugar beet.

55381.q: How is the sweet juice obtained from sugar cane?
55381.e: The stalks are chopped up and pressed. Then the juice is boiled to make sugar.
55381.m: Sugar cane juice is pressed out of the stalks.

55382.e: Sugar cane needs lots of warmth, sun and rain. It grows in the tropics and subtropics.
55382.m: Sugar cane grows in warm countries.

55383.q: How tall can sugar cane grow?
55383.e: Sugar cane usually grows three to six metres tall. So it is much taller than a person.
55383.m: Sugar cane grows several metres tall.

55384.q: What is brown sugar from sugar cane often called?
55384.e: Sugar from sugar cane is called cane sugar. If it is not fully refined, it is brown.
55384.m: Sugar from sugar cane is called cane sugar.

55385.q: What is made from sugar cane in Brazil apart from sugar?
55385.e: Alcohol can be made from sugar cane. In Brazil many cars run on this fuel, ethanol.
55385.m: In Brazil cars also run on fuel made from sugar cane.

55386.q: What is the Norwegian parliament called?
55386.e: The Norwegian parliament is called the Storting, which means something like “great assembly”. It meets in Oslo.
55386.m: The Norwegian parliament is called the Storting.

55387.q: Roughly how deep is the Sognefjord at its deepest point?
55387.e: The Sognefjord is 1308 metres deep at its deepest point. This makes it one of the deepest fjords in the world.
55387.m: The Sognefjord is over a kilometre deep.

55388.q: What is a fjord like the Lysefjord in Norway?
a: A long arm of the sea between steep mountains
A volcanic crater with a lake
A sandy desert by the sea
55388.e: Fjords were carved out by glaciers in the Ice Age and later filled by the sea. Preikestolen rises above the Lysefjord.
55388.m: Fjords are arms of the sea shaped by glaciers.

55389.q: Which organisation is Norway a member of, like Switzerland?
55389.e: Like Switzerland, Norway is not a member of the EU, but it is a member of the European Free Trade Association, EFTA. Iceland and Liechtenstein also belong to EFTA.
55389.m: Norway and Switzerland are both members of EFTA.

55390.q: Which raw materials make Norway a rich country?
55390.e: Since the 1970s Norway has extracted large amounts of oil and natural gas from the North Sea. The state invests part of the income in a huge fund.
55390.m: Oil and natural gas from the North Sea made Norway rich.

55391.q: Which group of islands in northern Norway is known for steep mountains and dried stockfish?
55391.e: The Lofoten Islands lie north of the Arctic Circle off the coast of Norway. For centuries, cod has been dried there on wooden racks to make stockfish.
55391.m: Stockfish is dried on the Lofoten Islands.

55392.q: In 1905 Norway left a union with which country?
55392.e: From 1814 to 1905, Norway and Sweden were joined in a union under one shared king. In 1905 Norway became fully independent.

55393.q: Why is a fjord often less deep at its mouth to the sea than further in?
a: There is a sill of rock and glacial debris there
Rivers deposit a lot of sand there
The tide lifts the seabed there
The fjord was filled in artificially there
55393.e: The glacier scraped the valley out deepest further inland and lost strength at its end. That is why a sill of rock and moraine debris was left behind at the mouth.
55393.m: Many fjords have a shallow sill at their mouth.

55394.q: In which country is the Göta Canal with its many locks?
55394.e: The Göta Canal was completed in 1832 and has 58 locks. Together with rivers and lakes it connects Gothenburg with the Baltic Sea.
55394.m: The Göta Canal runs right across Sweden.

55395.q: What is the second largest city in Sweden, on the west coast, called?
55395.e: Gothenburg lies on the Kattegat and has the largest port in Scandinavia. Malmö is the third largest city in Sweden.
55395.m: Gothenburg is the second largest city in Sweden.

55396.q: What is Vättern, a large lake in Sweden, especially known for?
55396.e: Vättern is in southern Sweden and is the country’s second largest lake. Its water is so clean that you could drink it almost anywhere.
55396.m: Vättern is a large lake with very clear water.

55397.q: In which city does the Riksdag, the Swedish parliament, meet?
55397.e: The Riksdag is the Swedish parliament with 349 seats. It meets in the capital, Stockholm.
55397.m: The Swedish parliament, the Riksdag, meets in Stockholm.

55398.q: What are the many small rocky islands off the coast of Stockholm called?
55398.e: Off Stockholm there are about 30,000 islands and rocks, the Stockholm archipelago. The skerries were worn smooth by glaciers.
55398.m: There are thousands of skerries off Stockholm.

55399.q: After France and Spain, which country is the largest in the EU by area?
55399.e: Sweden covers about 450,000 square kilometres. This puts it in third place in the EU, just ahead of Germany with about 357,000 square kilometres.
55399.m: Sweden is the third largest country in the EU.

55400.q: In which year did Sweden and Finland join the European Union?
55400.e: Sweden, Finland and Austria became members of the EU on 1 January 1995. Norway rejected joining in a referendum.
55400.m: Sweden and Finland have been in the EU since 1995.

55401.q: What is the Stockholm underground especially known for?
55401.e: Over 90 of its roughly 100 stations are decorated with paintings, sculptures or mosaics. That is why the Tunnelbana is called the longest art gallery in the world.
55401.m: The Stockholm underground is full of art.

55402.q: In which year did Sweden join NATO?
55402.e: Sweden became a member of NATO in March 2024. Before that it had stayed out of military alliances for over 200 years.
55402.m: Sweden has been in NATO since 2024.

55403.q: What do the Finns call their country in their own language?
55403.e: In Finnish, Finland is called Suomi. That is why euro coins and stamps often say “Suomi Finland”.
55403.m: Finland is called Suomi in Finnish.

55404.q: Which language is Finnish closely related to?
55404.e: Finnish is not an Indo-European language but belongs to the Uralic language family. It is most closely related to Estonian, and distantly also to Hungarian.
55404.m: Finnish and Estonian are closely related languages.

55405.q: Which group of islands between Finland and Sweden belongs to Finland but speaks Swedish?
55405.e: The Åland Islands are an autonomous region of Finland with over 6700 islands and skerries. The only official language there is Swedish.
55405.m: Swedish is spoken on the Åland Islands, even though they belong to Finland.

55406.q: From which country did Finland become independent in 1917?
55406.e: From 1809 Finland was a Grand Duchy under the Russian tsar. On 6 December 1917 it declared its independence.
55406.m: Finland became independent from Russia in 1917.

55407.q: Which realm did Finland belong to when Helsinki was founded in 1550?
55407.e: The Swedish king Gustav I Vasa founded Helsinki in 1550 as a trading town. At that time Finland had already belonged to Sweden for centuries.
55407.m: Helsinki was founded by a Swedish king.

55408.q: Which city was the capital of Finland before Helsinki?
55408.e: Turku is the oldest city in Finland and was the centre of the country for a long time. In 1812 the capital was moved to Helsinki.
55408.m: Turku used to be the capital of Finland.

55409.q: In which year did Finland become a member of NATO?
55409.e: Finland joined NATO in April 2023. Before that the country stayed out of military alliances for a long time.
55409.m: Finland has been a member of NATO since 2023.

55410.q: What is the Kalevala from Finland?
a: A collection of old heroic songs
55410.e: The Kalevala was put together from old folk songs by Elias Lönnrot in the 19th century. It is Finland’s national epic.
55410.m: The Kalevala is Finland’s national epic.

55411.q: In which city does the Danish parliament meet?
55411.e: The Danish parliament meets in Christiansborg Palace in the capital, Copenhagen.
55411.m: The Danish parliament sits in Copenhagen.

55412.q: The Danish parliament is called the Folketing. What does this name mean?
55412.e: “Folk” means people and “ting” means assembly. The Folketing also includes two members each from Greenland and the Faroe Islands.
55412.m: The Danish parliament is called the Folketing.

55413.q: Roughly how high is the highest natural point in Denmark?
55413.e: Denmark’s highest point, Møllehøj in Jutland, is only about 171 metres high. Denmark is one of the flattest countries in Europe.
55413.m: Denmark has no hill higher than 200 metres.

55414.q: Which Danish island lies far to the east in the middle of the Baltic Sea?
55414.e: Bornholm lies between Sweden and Poland, about 150 kilometres east of Copenhagen. The island is known for its round churches.
55414.m: Bornholm is a Danish island far to the east.

55415.q: What does the Danish name København mean in English?
55415.e: Even in the Middle Ages, Copenhagen was an important trading place on the Øresund. That is why the name means “merchants’ harbour”.

55416.q: From which energy source does a very large share of Denmark’s electricity come?
55416.e: Denmark has many wind farms on land and at sea. For some years now, about half of its electricity has come from wind power.
55416.m: Denmark produces a lot of electricity with wind power.

55417.q: In which country do long bridges such as the Great Belt link lead from island to island?
55417.e: Denmark is made up of many islands. The Great Belt link crosses the Great Belt from Zealand to Funen.
55417.m: The Great Belt link is in Denmark.

55418.q: Which famous play by Shakespeare is set in Denmark?
55418.e: Hamlet is the Prince of Denmark. The play is set in Kronborg Castle north of Copenhagen.
55418.m: Shakespeare’s Hamlet is set in Denmark.

55419.q: Roughly how much bigger than Switzerland is Iceland?
a: About two and a half times
55419.e: Iceland covers about 103,000 square kilometres, Switzerland about 41,000. 103,000 divided by 41,000 is about 2.5.
55419.m: Iceland is about two and a half times the size of Switzerland.

55420.q: In which Icelandic national park can you walk in a rift between two tectonic plates?
55420.e: In Þingvellir National Park you can clearly see how the North American and the Eurasian plates are drifting apart. The park is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
55420.m: In Þingvellir you can see the edge of two tectonic plates.

55421.q: What does the name Reykjavík mean in English?
55421.e: The first settlers saw steam rising from hot springs and thought it was smoke. So they named the place “smoky bay”.

55422.q: In which capital city is Hallgrímskirkja, whose shape is reminiscent of basalt columns?
55422.e: Hallgrímskirkja is about 75 metres high and one of the tallest buildings in Iceland. It is the landmark of Reykjavík.
55422.m: Hallgrímskirkja is the landmark of Reykjavík.

55423.q: What does the ending “-dóttir” in many Icelandic surnames mean?
55423.e: In Iceland most people form their surname from their father’s first name. A daughter of Jón, for example, is called Jónsdóttir, a son Jónsson.
55423.m: Icelandic surnames say whose child you are.

55424.q: Which island south of Iceland was formed from 1963 onwards by a volcanic eruption in the sea?
55424.e: Surtsey grew out of the sea during an eruption from 1963 to 1967. Researchers there watch how plants and animals settle on new land.
55424.m: Surtsey is a young volcanic island.

55425.q: What is the Althing in Iceland?
55425.e: The Althing is the parliament of Iceland. It was founded in 930 and is considered one of the oldest parliaments in the world.
55425.m: Iceland’s parliament is called the Althing.

55426.q: What does Iceland not have, even though it is a NATO member?
55426.e: Iceland is a founding member of NATO, but it has no armed forces of its own. The Icelandic Coast Guard looks after safety at sea.
55426.m: Iceland has no army of its own.

55427.q: Where does almost all of Iceland’s electricity come from?
55427.e: Iceland uses its many rivers and the heat from inside the Earth. Most houses are also heated with geothermal energy.
55427.m: Iceland gets its electricity from hydropower and geothermal energy.

55428.q: Norway’s highest mountains are in Jotunheimen. What does this name mean?
55428.e: In old Norse legends the Jotuns are giants. In Jotunheimen there are over 250 peaks higher than 1900 metres.
55428.m: Jotunheimen means home of the giants.

55429.q: Which animal with long, thick fur lives in the wild in Norway’s Dovrefjell mountains?
55429.e: Musk oxen were brought from Greenland to the Dovrefjell in the 20th century. Their fur protects them from icy cold.
55429.m: Musk oxen live in the Dovrefjell.

55430.q: What else are the Scandinavian Mountains called?
55430.e: The Scandinavian Mountains are also called the Scandes. They stretch for about 1700 kilometres through Norway and Sweden.
55430.m: The Scandinavian Mountains are also called the Scandes.

55431.q: What is the treeless upland above the tree line called in Norway?
55431.e: A fjell is a wide, bare upland above the tree line. It is typical of the Scandinavian Mountains.
55431.m: A fjell is a treeless upland in Scandinavia.

55432.q: How old are the Scandinavian Mountains compared with the Alps?
a: Only formed after the Ice Age
55432.e: The Scandinavian Mountains formed about 400 million years ago and have been worn down a great deal since then. The Alps are much younger and therefore higher and more rugged.
55432.m: The Scandinavian Mountains are much older than the Alps.

55433.q: What is the steep Norwegian mountain road with eleven hairpin bends called?
55433.e: Trollstigen winds up a steep rock face in eleven tight bends. In winter the road is closed because of snow.
55433.m: Trollstigen is a winding mountain road in Norway.

55434.q: Which wild animals live in large herds on the Hardangervidda in Norway?
55434.e: The Hardangervidda is considered the largest plateau in Europe. The largest herds of wild reindeer in Europe live there.
55434.m: Wild reindeer live on the Hardangervidda.

55435.q: Which side of the Scandinavian Mountains gets the most rain?
a: The western side facing the Atlantic
The eastern side facing the Baltic Sea
55435.e: Moist air from the Atlantic rises on the western side, cools down and falls as rain. That is why Bergen is one of the rainiest cities in Europe.
55435.m: It rains most on the western side of the mountains.

55436.q: Which animals do many Sami traditionally breed?
55436.e: The Sami live in the far north of Europe. Reindeer herding is an important part of their culture.

a: In the north of Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia
55437.e: The Sami are a people of the far north of Europe. They call their area Sápmi, often called Lapland in English.
55437.m: The Sami live in the north of Europe.

55438.q: What do the Sami call the area where they live in their own language?
55438.e: Sápmi covers the north of Norway, Sweden and Finland as well as the Russian Kola Peninsula. In English it is often called Lapland.
55438.m: The land of the Sami is called Sápmi.

55439.q: Across how many countries is the area where the Sami live spread?
55439.e: The Sami live in Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia. That makes four countries.
55439.m: The Sami area stretches across four countries.

55440.q: Which Finnish town lies on the Arctic Circle and is seen as the home of Father Christmas?
55440.e: Rovaniemi is the capital of Finnish Lapland. The well-known Santa Claus Village lies there on the Arctic Circle.
55440.m: Rovaniemi lies on the Arctic Circle in Finland.

55441.q: Which animals did the Sami herd when they lived in tents called lavvu?
55441.e: The Sami in northern Europe moved around with their reindeer herds. A lavvu could be put up and taken down quickly.

55442.q: What are the elected assemblies of the Sami in Norway, Sweden and Finland called?
55442.e: In all three countries the Sami elect their own parliament, the Sami Parliament. It deals with Sami language, culture and reindeer herding.
55442.m: The Sami have their own parliament.

55443.q: Which raw material is mined near the town of Kiruna in northern Sweden?
55443.e: Beneath Kiruna lies one of the largest iron ore mines in the world. Because the ground is sinking, the town is being rebuilt further east.
55443.m: Iron ore is mined in Kiruna.

55444.q: What is the traditional singing of the Sami called?
55444.e: A joik is a song that sings about a person, an animal or a landscape. It is one of the oldest musical traditions in Europe.
55444.m: The traditional song of the Sami is called a joik.

55445.q: When did the Baltic Sea take on its present form?
a: In the time of the dinosaurs
55445.e: After the glaciers melted about 10,000 years ago, the basin filled with meltwater and seawater. This makes the Baltic Sea a very young sea.
55445.m: The Baltic Sea formed after the last Ice Age.

55446.q: What is the largest island in the Baltic Sea called?
55446.e: Gotland belongs to Sweden and covers about 3000 square kilometres. Its capital, Visby, has a medieval town wall.
55446.m: Gotland is the largest island in the Baltic Sea.

55447.q: What is the northern part of the Baltic Sea between Sweden and Finland, which often freezes in winter, called?
55447.e: The Gulf of Bothnia has very little salt and lies far to the north. That is why it is often covered with ice in winter.
55447.m: The Gulf of Bothnia lies between Sweden and Finland.

55448.q: On which part of the Baltic Sea are Helsinki, Tallinn and St Petersburg?
55448.e: The Gulf of Finland reaches far east to St Petersburg. Helsinki is on its northern coast, Tallinn on its southern coast.
55448.m: Helsinki and Tallinn are on the Gulf of Finland.

55449.q: How many countries border the Baltic Sea?
55449.e: The countries on its shores are Germany, Denmark, Sweden, Finland, Russia, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania and Poland. That makes nine countries.
55449.m: Nine countries border the Baltic Sea.

55450.q: Which is the largest city on the Baltic coast?
55450.e: St Petersburg has over five million inhabitants and lies at the mouth of the Neva. No other Baltic city is as big.
55450.m: St Petersburg is the largest city on the Baltic Sea.

55451.q: Roughly how deep is the Baltic Sea on average?
55451.e: On average the Baltic Sea is only about 52 metres deep. The deepest point, the Landsort Deep off Sweden, is about 460 metres.
55451.m: The Baltic Sea is a shallow sea.

55452.q: Which medieval league of towns controlled trade on the Baltic Sea for a long time?
55452.e: The Hanseatic League was an alliance of merchants and towns such as Lübeck, Gdańsk and Visby. It traded in fish, salt, grain and furs.
55452.m: The Hanseatic League shaped trade on the Baltic Sea.

55453.q: In which country is the North Cape?
55453.e: The North Cape is in the very north of Norway on the island of Magerøya. A tunnel under the sea connects the island with the mainland.
55453.m: The North Cape is in Norway.

55454.q: What can visitors to the North Cape experience in summer?
55454.e: In summer the sun does not set at the North Cape for weeks. You can even see it in the sky at midnight.
55454.m: The midnight sun shines at the North Cape in summer.

55455.q: Which well-known cape in the north of Norway is often seen as the northernmost point of Europe?
55455.e: The North Cape is a famous rock high above the sea. Strictly speaking it is on an island; the northernmost point of the mainland is Kinnarodden.
55455.m: The North Cape is in the far north of Europe.

55456.q: Roughly how high is the cliff of the North Cape?
55456.e: The North Cape is a rock plateau that rises steeply about 307 metres out of the sea. From the top you look out over the Arctic Ocean.
55456.m: The cliff of the North Cape is about 300 metres high.

55457.q: Which well-known monument stands on the plateau of the North Cape?
a: A model of the Eiffel Tower
55457.e: The steel globe is the landmark of the North Cape. Almost every visitor takes a photo there.
55457.m: There is a steel globe on the North Cape.

55458.q: Who gave the North Cape its name in 1553?
55458.e: The English seafarer Richard Chancellor sailed past it in 1553 while searching for a sea route to Asia. He named the rock “North Cape”.
55458.m: An English seafarer named the North Cape.

55459.q: Where is the North Cape in relation to the Arctic Circle?
55459.e: The North Cape lies at about 71 degrees north, the Arctic Circle at about 66.5 degrees north. So the North Cape lies clearly further north.
55459.m: The North Cape lies north of the Arctic Circle.

55460.q: Which sea lies east of the North Cape?
55460.e: At the North Cape the Norwegian Sea meets the Barents Sea. The Barents Sea reaches as far as the Russian coast.
55460.m: The Barents Sea begins east of the North Cape.

55462.q: Roughly how many people live on the Faroe Islands (as of 2025)?
55462.e: About 55,000 people live on the Faroe Islands. That is about as many as in the town of Biel/Bienne.
55462.m: Only a few tens of thousands of people live on the Faroe Islands.

55463.q: Which country do the Faroe Islands belong to?
55463.e: The Faroe Islands lie in the North Atlantic between Iceland and Norway. They belong to Denmark but largely govern themselves.
55463.m: The Faroe Islands belong to Denmark.

55464.q: What is special about the Eysturoy Tunnel on the Faroe Islands?
a: A railway station under the sea
55464.e: The Eysturoy Tunnel was opened in 2020 and connects three places. Its branches meet in a roundabout under the seabed.
55464.m: There is a roundabout under the sea in the Faroe Islands.

55465.q: What is special about the Faroe Islands with regard to the EU?
a: They are not part of the EU
They are an EU country of their own
55465.e: Denmark is a member of the EU, but the Faroe Islands decided against joining. This lets them manage their fishing themselves.
55465.m: The Faroe Islands are not part of the EU, even though Denmark is a member.

55466.q: What is almost completely missing from the landscape of the Faroe Islands?
55466.e: Because of the strong wind, the cool climate and the many sheep, hardly any trees grow on the Faroe Islands. The islands are covered with grass and moss.
55466.m: There are hardly any trees on the Faroe Islands.

55467.q: Which language is spoken in everyday life on the Faroe Islands?
55467.e: Faroese is a North Germanic language related to Icelandic. At school the children also learn Danish.
55467.m: Faroese is spoken on the Faroe Islands.

55468.q: Which branch of the economy is the most important for the Faroe Islands?
55468.e: Fish and fish products, including from salmon farming, make up most of the exports. The sea is the most important source of livelihood for the Faroe Islands.
55468.m: Fishing is the most important industry for the Faroe Islands.

55469.q: Roughly how many lakes are there in Finland?
55469.e: Finland is called the “land of a thousand lakes”, but it has far more. About 188,000 lakes larger than 500 square metres are counted.
55469.m: Finland has far more than a thousand lakes.

55470.q: What is the largest lake in Finland called?
55470.e: Saimaa is in south-eastern Finland and is made up of many connected lake basins with thousands of islands. It is the largest lake in the country.
55470.m: Saimaa is the largest lake in Finland.

55471.q: Which rare animal lives only in Finland’s Lake Saimaa?
55471.e: The Saimaa ringed seal is a seal that lives only in the fresh water of this lake. It is highly endangered and strictly protected.
55471.m: A rare freshwater seal lives in Saimaa.

55472.q: How were most of Finland’s lakes formed?
55472.e: Ice Age glaciers ground hollows into the rock and left debris behind. After the ice melted, the hollows filled with water.
55472.m: Finland’s lakes were formed by the Ice Age.

55473.q: What covers about three quarters of Finland’s area?
55473.e: Finland is one of the most forested countries in Europe. That is why wood and paper are important exports.
55473.m: Most of Finland is covered with forest.

55474.q: What is the largest lake in Europe called?
55474.e: Lake Ladoga is in Russia near St Petersburg. It is much bigger than any lake in central Europe.
55474.m: Lake Ladoga is the largest lake in Europe.

55475.q: In which country is the large lake Päijänne?
55475.e: Päijänne is the second largest lake in Finland. A long rock tunnel carries its water to Helsinki as drinking water.
55475.m: Päijänne is a large lake in Finland.

55476.q: What shaped Finland’s landscape with its many lakes and long gravel ridges?
55476.e: In the Ice Age Finland lay under thick ice. Glaciers dug out lake basins, and meltwater left behind long gravel ridges called eskers.
55476.m: Ice Age glaciers shaped Finland’s lakes.

55478.q: Which two countries does the Øresund Bridge connect?
55478.e: The Øresund link was opened in 2000. Before that, only ferries ran between Denmark and Sweden here.
55478.m: The Øresund Bridge connects Denmark and Sweden.

55479.q: Roughly how long is the Øresund Bridge itself?
55479.e: The bridge itself is about 7.8 kilometres long. Together with an island and a tunnel, the whole link is about 16 kilometres long.
55479.m: The Øresund Bridge is about 8 kilometres long.

55480.q: Which two countries does the Øresund link with its bridge and tunnel connect?
55480.e: The Øresund link runs from Copenhagen to Malmö. On the artificial island of Peberholm the route changes from tunnel to bridge.
55480.m: The Øresund link connects Denmark and Sweden.

55481.q: Why does part of the Øresund link run through a tunnel?
a: Because of the airport and shipping
55481.e: Tall bridge towers would have disturbed nearby Copenhagen Airport. Also, large ships needed to be able to sail freely through the Øresund.
55481.m: The tunnel protects air traffic and shipping.

55482.q: How is the Øresund Bridge built?
a: Railway on top, cycle path below
55482.e: The bridge has two levels. Cars drive on the upper deck and trains run on the lower deck.
55482.m: On the Øresund Bridge, cars go on top and trains below.

55483.q: Which two cities does the Øresund link connect?
55483.e: The link runs from Copenhagen on the island of Zealand to Malmö in southern Sweden.
55483.m: The Øresund Bridge connects Copenhagen and Malmö.

55484.q: What type of bridge is the main part of the Øresund Bridge?
55484.e: In the main part, steel cables stretched at an angle from tall pylons to the roadway carry the bridge. The pylons are about 200 metres high.
55484.m: The Øresund Bridge is a cable-stayed bridge.

55485.q: Which four parts together make up the United Kingdom?
55485.e: Three parts are on the large island, one is in the north-east of the island of Ireland. The Republic of Ireland is a separate country.
55485.m: The United Kingdom has four parts.

55486.q: What is the difference between “Great Britain” and the “United Kingdom”?
a: Only the United Kingdom includes Northern Ireland
Only the United Kingdom includes Wales
55486.e: Great Britain is the large island with England, Scotland and Wales. The United Kingdom also includes Northern Ireland.
55486.m: The United Kingdom is Great Britain plus Northern Ireland.

55487.q: What is the flag of the United Kingdom called?
55487.e: The flag is called the Union Jack or Union Flag. It combines the crosses of the patron saints of England, Scotland and Ireland.
55487.m: The Union Jack combines the crosses of several parts of the country.

55488.q: Which cross in the flag of the United Kingdom stands for Scotland?
a: The white cross of St Andrew
The red cross of St George
The red cross of St Patrick
The yellow cross of St David
55488.e: Scotland’s flag shows a white diagonal St Andrew’s cross on a blue background. It forms the background of the Union Jack.
55488.m: Scotland’s symbol is the diagonal St Andrew’s cross.

55489.q: What form of government does the United Kingdom have?
55489.e: The head of state is a king or queen, but the country is governed by Parliament and the Prime Minister. Charles III has been king since 2022.
55489.m: In the United Kingdom, Parliament governs under the Crown.

55490.q: Which is the largest island of the British Isles?
55490.e: Great Britain is the largest island of the British Isles and the largest island in Europe. Ireland is the second largest.
55490.m: Great Britain is the largest island in Europe.

55491.q: Roughly how many people live in the United Kingdom (as of 2024)?
55491.e: In mid-2024 about 69 million people lived in the United Kingdom. That is almost eight times as many as in Switzerland.
55491.m: Almost eight times as many people live in the United Kingdom as in Switzerland.

55492.q: Which people founded the settlement that grew into London?
55492.e: The Romans founded the settlement of Londinium around the year AD 50. Today's capital grew out of it.

55493.q: What is special about the London Underground, the “Tube”?
a: It is the oldest underground railway in the world
It runs under the sea to France
55493.e: The London Underground opened in 1863. It is the oldest underground railway in the world.
55493.m: The London Tube is the oldest underground railway in the world.

55494.q: What is kept in the Tower of London?
55494.e: The British Crown Jewels are displayed in the Tower of London, an old fortress on the Thames. It was once also used as a prison.
55494.m: The Crown Jewels are kept in the Tower of London.

55495.q: Which part of London is famous for the Prime Meridian?
55495.e: The Prime Meridian runs through the observatory in Greenwich. Lines of longitude and world time are counted from there.
55495.m: The counting of longitude starts in Greenwich.

55496.q: What is the name of London's largest airport?
55496.e: Heathrow in west London is the largest airport in the United Kingdom. It is one of the busiest airports in the world.

55497.q: Which big city lies on the Thames?
55497.e: The Thames rises in the west of England and flows east right through London to the North Sea.

55498.q: Which two universities hold a famous rowing race on the Thames every year?
55498.e: In the Boat Race, eights from Oxford and Cambridge row against each other on the Thames in London. The race has been held since 1829.
55498.m: Oxford and Cambridge row against each other in the Boat Race.

55499.q: Which London bridge over the Thames can be raised in the middle?
55499.e: Tower Bridge has two towers and a bascule bridge that opens for large ships. It opened in 1894.
55499.m: Tower Bridge can open for ships.

55500.q: What is the name for the mouth of the Thames, which gets wider and wider?
55500.e: The Thames flows into the sea through an estuary, a funnel-shaped river mouth. There, river water mixes with seawater because of the tides.
55500.m: A funnel-shaped river mouth is called an estuary.

55501.q: Which part of the United Kingdom has the most inhabitants?
55501.e: Over 80 per cent of the population of the United Kingdom live in England. It is also the largest part by area.
55501.m: England is the largest part of the United Kingdom.

55502.q: Which cross is shown on the flag of England?
a: A red cross on a white background
A white cross on a red background
A white cross on a blue background
A yellow cross on a green background
55502.e: The flag of England is the Cross of St George: a red cross on a white background. The Swiss flag has exactly the opposite colours.
55502.m: England's flag is a red cross on white.

55503.q: Which is the largest city in Scotland?
55503.e: Glasgow lies on the River Clyde in the west of Scotland. About a third of Scotland's population live in the Greater Glasgow area.

55504.q: What is the capital of Northern Ireland?
55504.e: Belfast is the capital and largest city of Northern Ireland. It lies at the mouth of the River Lagan.
55504.m: Belfast is the capital of Northern Ireland.

55505.q: Which famous ship was built in Belfast?
55505.e: The Titanic was built at the Harland and Wolff shipyard in Belfast. It sank on its first voyage in 1912.
55505.m: The Titanic came from a shipyard in Belfast.

55506.q: What is the name of the coast in Northern Ireland with thousands of six-sided basalt columns?
55506.e: The Giant's Causeway is made up of about 40,000 basalt columns. They formed when lava cooled slowly.
55506.m: The Giant's Causeway was formed from cooled lava.

55507.q: Which country does Northern Ireland belong to?
55507.e: Like England, Scotland and Wales, Northern Ireland is part of the United Kingdom. The rest of the island forms the country of Ireland.
55507.m: Northern Ireland is part of the United Kingdom.

55508.q: Which city is known as the “capital of the Highlands”?
55508.e: Inverness lies at the northern end of the Great Glen by the Moray Firth. It is the administrative and shopping centre of the Highlands.
55508.m: Inverness is the capital of the Highlands.

55509.q: How do the Highlands differ from the Lowlands in Scotland?
a: The Highlands are mountainous and thinly populated
The Highlands are flat and densely populated
The Highlands are on an island
55509.e: The Highlands in the north are rugged, mountainous and thinly populated. The big cities such as Glasgow and Edinburgh lie in the flatter Lowlands in the south.
55509.m: The Highlands are Scotland's mountainous uplands.

55510.q: Which famous loch lies in the long valley of the Great Glen in the Scottish Highlands?
55510.e: The Great Glen runs right across Scotland. It contains several lochs, the best known being Loch Ness with its legendary monster.
55510.m: Loch Ness lies in the Great Glen.

55511.q: Which canal runs through the Great Glen, linking the east and west coasts of Scotland?
55511.e: The Caledonian Canal links several lochs in the Great Glen, including Loch Ness. It was built in the 19th century.
55511.m: The Caledonian Canal runs right across the Highlands.

55512.e: A clan is a large family group sharing a name, for example MacDonald. Each clan has its own checked tartan pattern.
55512.m: A Scottish clan is a large family sharing a name.

55513.q: Which large wild animals live in the Scottish Highlands?
55513.e: Many red deer live in the Highlands. In the Cairngorms National Park, the largest national park in Britain, there are even reindeer.
55513.m: Many red deer live in the Highlands.

55514.q: Which Swiss peak is about 1150 metres higher than Ben Nevis at 1345 metres?
55514.e: 2502 minus 1345 is 1157 metres. So the Säntis is about 1150 metres higher than the highest mountain in Britain.
55514.m: The Säntis is more than 1000 metres higher than Ben Nevis.

55515.q: In which part of the United Kingdom is Ben Nevis?
55515.e: Ben Nevis lies in the Scottish Highlands on the west coast of Scotland.

55516.q: Why is there often snow or fog on the summit of Ben Nevis, even in summer?
a: Because of the damp, cool maritime climate
Because it is at the North Pole
Because it is over 4000 metres high
55516.e: Westerly winds bring a lot of damp air from the Atlantic to the mountain. So the summit is usually in cloud, and snow lasts a long time.
55516.m: The maritime climate often makes Ben Nevis foggy and wet.

55517.q: What stood on the summit of Ben Nevis from 1883 to 1904?
55517.e: A weather observatory was run on the summit from 1883 to 1904. Its ruins can still be seen today.
55517.m: The weather used to be measured on Ben Nevis.

55518.q: What is Ben Nevis known for?
a: It is the highest mountain in Britain
It is the highest mountain in Europe
It is on an island in the Atlantic
55518.e: At 1345 metres, Ben Nevis is the highest mountain in Britain. By Swiss standards it is rather small.
55518.m: Ben Nevis is the highest mountain in Britain.

55519.q: Which type of rock makes up a large part of Ben Nevis?
55519.e: Ben Nevis is the remains of an ancient volcano that collapsed about 350 million years ago. Ice Age glaciers later shaped it.
55519.m: Ben Nevis is the remains of an ancient volcano.

55520.q: What does Edinburgh Castle stand on?
55520.e: The castle stands on Castle Rock, the remains of an extinct volcano. From there it looks out over the whole Old Town.
55520.m: Edinburgh Castle sits on an old volcanic rock.

55521.q: What is the name of the main street of Edinburgh's Old Town between the castle and the palace?
55521.e: The Royal Mile runs from Edinburgh Castle down to Holyrood Palace. It is about one Scottish mile long.
55521.m: The Royal Mile links the castle and the palace in Edinburgh.

55522.q: Which big cultural festival takes place in Edinburgh every August?
55522.e: The Edinburgh International Festival and the Fringe take place in August. The Fringe is said to be the largest arts festival in the world.
55522.m: In August, Edinburgh becomes a festival city.

55523.q: What is the name of the hill in the middle of Edinburgh that is an old volcano?
55523.e: Arthur's Seat is 251 metres high and lies in Holyrood Park. You can climb it right in the middle of the city.
55523.m: Arthur's Seat is a volcanic hill in Edinburgh.

55524.q: Edinburgh is the capital of which part of the United Kingdom?
55524.e: Edinburgh is the capital of Scotland. But Scotland's largest city is Glasgow.
55524.m: Edinburgh is the capital of Scotland.

55525.q: Where does the Scottish Parliament meet in Edinburgh?
55525.e: The Scottish Parliament has its building in the Holyrood area. It has existed in this form since 1999.
55525.m: Holyrood is the seat of the Scottish Parliament.

55526.q: Which well-known children's author wrote parts of her wizard novels in cafés in Edinburgh?
55526.e: J. K. Rowling lived in Edinburgh and worked on the Harry Potter books there. Some places in the city are said to have inspired her.
55526.m: Harry Potter was partly written in Edinburgh.

55527.q: Which is the longest river in Ireland and the British Isles?
55527.e: The Shannon is about 360 kilometres long and flows through Ireland from north to south. It is a little longer than the Thames.
55527.m: The Shannon is the longest river in the British Isles.

55528.q: Who was the first person to cross the English Channel by aeroplane in 1909?
55528.e: The Frenchman Louis Blériot flew from Calais to Dover on 25 July 1909. The flight took about 37 minutes.
55528.m: Louis Blériot was the first to fly across the English Channel in 1909.

55529.q: Which group of islands in the English Channel lies close to France but belongs to the British Crown?
55529.e: The Channel Islands, including Jersey and Guernsey, lie off the coast of Normandy. They are not part of the United Kingdom, but belong to the British Crown.
55529.m: Jersey and Guernsey are Channel Islands of the British Crown.

55530.q: Under which sea does the Channel Tunnel run?
55530.e: The Channel Tunnel runs under the English Channel from Folkestone in England to Coquelles near Calais in France.
55530.m: The Channel Tunnel lies under the English Channel.

55531.q: Off which coast of Scotland are the Hebrides?
55531.e: The Hebrides lie in the Atlantic off the west coast of Scotland. There are the Inner and the Outer Hebrides.
55531.m: The Hebrides lie off Scotland's west coast.

55532.q: Which well-known island of the Inner Hebrides is linked to the mainland by a bridge?
55532.e: The Isle of Skye has been reachable by the Skye Bridge since 1995. It is the largest island of the Inner Hebrides.
55532.m: Skye is the largest island of the Inner Hebrides.

55533.q: Which language is still spoken by many people in the Outer Hebrides?
55533.e: Scottish Gaelic is more widespread in the Outer Hebrides than anywhere else in Scotland. Place signs are often in two languages.
55533.m: The Gaelic language lives on in the Outer Hebrides.

55534.q: What is Harris Tweed from the Outer Hebrides?
55534.e: Harris Tweed is woven by hand at home in the Outer Hebrides. Only cloth woven this way may carry the name.
55534.m: Harris Tweed is a woollen cloth from the Hebrides.

55535.q: Who mainly lives on the abandoned islands of St Kilda today?
55535.e: The islands of St Kilda lie far out in the Atlantic. In 1930 the last inhabitants were taken to the mainland; today huge colonies of seabirds nest there.
55535.m: Today St Kilda is home mainly to seabirds.

a: Off the north coast of Scotland
Off the south coast of England
Off the west coast of Ireland
55536.e: The Orkney Islands lie north of the Scottish mainland between the Atlantic and the North Sea. Further north still are the Shetland Islands.
55536.m: Orkney lies north of the Scottish mainland.

55537.q: What did a storm uncover on the Orkney Islands in 1850?
a: A Roman town made of marble
A Viking ship made of gold
55537.e: The Stone Age village of Skara Brae is about 5000 years old. You can still see beds and shelves made of stone there.
